#3566. The Lord Of The Rings: The Rings Of Power Season 3 Opening Credits Have A Hidden Connection To HBO's White Lotus [Exclusive]

As viewers make their long-awaited return to Middle-earth in Season 3 of "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power," they will inevitably find things a bit different compared to where they last left off. The war that was teased at the conclusion of Season 2 has finally arrived, led by Charlie Vickers' Sauron unmasked in all his Dark Lord, uh, lordliness. A five-year time jump has reset the board considerably, putting heroes like Elrond (Robert Aramayo) and Galadriel (Morfydd Clark) on their back foot. But, as of Episode 2, fans will notice a significant tweak has been made to the opening credits sequence — one which contains an unseen connection to another popular streaming series.

Prior to the premiere, I recently attended the press junket for "The Rings of Power" and spoke with co-showrunner Patrick McKay about the third season. In our limited time together, I wanted to address the noticeably darker edge to the title sequence this time around and whether there might be any Easter eggs worth paying attention to, as has been the case in the prior two seasons. The creative team worked with studio and creative consultant Plains of Yonder, who crafted the sand-based vibrational look for the opening credits of "The Rings of Power" and apparently pitched a new approach for Season 3. Here's a behind-the-scenes featurette showcasing their previous work:

But observant fans may recognize the fingerprints of another haunting title sequence. Fans of HBO's "White Lotus," this one's for you. As proudly displayed on their website, Plains of Yonder was also involved in everyone's favorite dramedy about "when everybody goes to the hotel" (as McKay hilariously put it in our interview) and, specifically, the wallpaper-focused title sequence with some seriously unsettling imagery. Not surprisingly, the designers pulled a similar trick with "The Rings of Power."

In keeping with the theme of Season 3 of "The Rings of Power," Patrick McKay explained that Plains of Yonder pitched a different approach for the episodes to come. Where Seasons 1 and 2 contained hidden references and symbols pointing towards specific events of the story, the designers felt called to go in another direction. "They're really serious artists," McKay told me with obvious admiration for their skills. "They're really wonderful people to work with. I mean, we find [their work on Season 2] hypnotic."

Episode 2 provides our first glimpse of the newly-revamped opening credits sequence, with the familiar-looking particulates now taking on a much darker color palette as they reform into all sorts of different visuals: evocative landscapes, elemental imagery, and plenty more examples of abstract art. According to McKay:

"Season 3, they're like, 'We want to do something different. We want to change the entire thing. We want to revisit the concept and make it feel like this season feels [emotionally], rather than reference things that happen in the season.' So it's a little different this time. It's a little more dramatic, has a little more darkness to it."

The visuals certainly help strike a different tone for Season 3, although the stirring musical theme by "The Lord of the Rings" trilogy composer Howard Shore remains perfectly intact. This seems to suggest that, even in its darkest moments, Middle-earth always retains a glimmer of hope. New episodes of "The Rings of Power" stream on Prime Video every Wednesday.

#3564. These 10 New Features Are Coming to iOS 27.3

Apple dropped the first developer beta for iOS 27.3 on Tuesday. While this update isn't as large as iOS 27 proper, it's surprisingly feature-filled for a 0.3 update. This is only a beta, so anything could (and likely will) change before Apple officially launches the update. But, as it stands, iOS 27.3 tests 10 new features—including one feature the company trialed in the previous beta.

Technically, anyone with a compatible iPhone can try out iOS 27.3 right now—assuming you enroll your Apple Account in the developer program. But a word of warning: Betas can be temperamental, and could be risky. As such, I'd recommend avoiding the beta until Apple releases the public beta, which comes after a bit more testing to iron out larger issues. Either way, make sure to make a full backup of your iPhone to a Mac or PC first, as issues with the beta could result in permanent data loss.

With watchOS 27, Apple released "Audio Intelligence," a new set of features for Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. Audio Intelligence uses the watches' new S11 chip, along with on-device AI and cloud-based AI, to run new features, like Sound Recognition and Shazam (music recognition).

With iOS 27.3, however, the company is now officially testing the other two Audio Intelligence features it originally announced with watchOS 27. First, there's Live Rewind: By double-clicking the watch crown, you can pull up a transcript of the last 15 seconds of a conversation. Siri Recap, on the other hand, displays summaries of conversations you had that day, in case you need a refresher on any chats you might have otherwise forgotten about,

The company generated some controversy when it first announced these two Audio Intelligence features, since, on the surface, it sounds like these new Apple Watches are essentially spying on people all day long. According to Apple, however, that isn't really the case. The company says Audio Intelligence is private, and never records or stores any audio. No speakers are ever identified, and text results (both transcripts and summaries) are deleted automatically after a set period of time unless the user saves them to the Siri app. You can read more about how Audio Intelligence works here.

Despite their claims, I'm sure there will still be strong feelings surrounding these Audio Intelligence features. We'll have to see whether Apple can prove Live Rewind and Siri Recap aren't all that creepy throughout the iOS 27.3 beta process.

iOS 27.3 also introduces app actions for Siri AI. Apple is testing new abilities for Siri AI, including organizing files, planning events, or adding photos to albums. You could ask Siri to organize your Downloads folder, or delete files that haven't been opened in more than a year. You could ask Siri to find a coffee shop you went to last week, or to save an article to your Reading List in Safari. You could ask Siri to check your calendar and set up a time for an event based on when you're free. You can even ask the assistant to schedule, edit, or unsend messages.

For example, you could ask Siri AI to help you plan a trip with your friends. You could ask the AI to put together a themed playlist in Apple Music, schedule a message to a group about an upcoming trip, organize the websites you've been visiting in Safari into a tab group, and, after the trip, ask Siri to move your best photos to your favorites album. These new actions work in the following apps: Calendar, Files, Finder, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather. Developers can also add Siri AI app actions support to their own apps.

Apple started testing its new Health app with the iOS 27.2 beta, but pulled the redesign before the official release. Now, with iOS 27.3, the new app is back. The new Health app has a health dashboard for the first time, as well as new features like Health Age and movement assessments. It seems to be pulling from some popular competitor services, hopefully, for the better. For more on the new Health app, check out Lifehacker health editor Beth Skwarecki's explainer.

Continuing on the Health track, iOS 27.3 also introduces "Gym Strength." This is a new Fitness+ feature that offers a personalized four-week strength-training plan. You can customize these plans to meet your goals, experience level, and schedule, and they adapt as you progress. You'll get recommendations based on your experience with exercises, reps, and sets, including video demos for exercises. You can access Gym Strength on both iPhone and iPad, and Apple Watches are optional—though you can log your progress with the wearable if you have it.

Vertical tabs have been a favorite among browser aficionados, as they give you more screen real estate in your browser while keeping your tabs off the side. Apple hasn't made the jump—until now. This feature works with iPads running iPadOS 27.3 as well as Macs running macOS 27.3.

Another new Safari feature in testing is "Adaptive Dark Mode." This feature forces websites into a dark theme, if they don't have a native theme of their own. There are third-party apps that can do this, but this is the first time Apple has offered this feature built into Safari.

Apple is also testing new StandBy experiences with iOS 27.3, which were previously only available on the iPhone Duo. When you turn your iPhone sideways while plugged in, you'll find new Analog and Digital Clock faces with new customization options. There's also a new Photos face, with the option to pull images from Shared Albums.

"Reachability" pulls your iPhone's display down towards the bottom of the screen, so you can access items towards the top of the display with one hand. It's a useful feature for those of us with big iPhones, and now, there's no iPhone bigger than the Duo. With iOS 27.3, Apple is testing Reachability for its first foldable phone. It's a bit like the inverse of how Reachability currently works: You can swipe on the left or right side of your Duo's display to shift the other side of the screen towards your current position. If you're holding your Duo in your left hand, a swipe of the left side will pull the right side over to the left, and vice versa.

Apple is also rolling out new languages for Siri AI in iOS 27.3. Now, Apple's smart assistant supports Traditional Chinese, Vietnamese, Turkish, and Norwegian.

If you have an Apple Intelligence-compatible iPad running iPadOS 27.3, you now have access to Siri Mode in Camera. As with iOS, you can open the Camera app on iPadOS to access Siri Mode, and ask Siri about your surroundings.

#3563. Stephen Miller Into the Breach: How Susie Wiles’s Failures Portend Miller’s Future

There’s a time-honored tradition for new White House chiefs of staff: The outgoing chief invites former holders of the office, Republicans and Democrats, to a get-together (usually in the West Wing), where the newcomer is offered advice. But Donald Trump’s new chief, Stephen Miller—appointed in a jaw-dropping Truth Social post on Friday—won’t be getting a party. First, because the tradition applies only to a president’s first chief. Second, because no Democratic chief would likely want to be caught dead with Miller, a longtime basher of the opposition party. Shortly after hearing that Trump had picked the hard-right firebrand as his new chief, James Carville sent me a text that summed up the prevailing attitude: “This is like Caligula’s appointment of his horse as consul.”

It was different when Susie Wiles came to town. On the evening of November 19, 2024, she was the guest of honor at a dinner party thrown by Jeffrey Zients, Joe Biden’s outgoing White House chief of staff. They were joined by eight of Zients’s predecessors. It was an occasion for bipartisan bonhomie, a tradition started in 2008 by George W. Bush’s chief Joshua Bolten. In a spirit of goodwill and generosity, Bolten had thrown a gathering in his West Wing office for Barack Obama’s incoming chief, Rahm Emanuel. The informal meetup was intended as a way to convey the chiefs’ collective wisdom and experience—and to offer, in miniature, a nuts-and-bolts version of the transition of executive power that is a hallmark of American democracy.

Now evicted from her West Wing corner office, with the president’s agenda in tatters, Wiles has learned that fealty to Trump almost always ends badly.

On the night of the dinner for Wiles, however, a cloud hung over the occasion. Virtually no one at the table thought she could succeed as Donald Trump’s chief of staff.

For almost two years, Wiles was the second most powerful person in the West Wing. Had Trump been interested in governing, she might have helped him solidify a GOP majority in Congress for years to come. But she was unwilling, or unable, to save Trump from himself. On Wiles’s watch, he squandered his second term with a reign of revenge, retribution, and recklessness. Now evicted from her West Wing corner office, with the president’s agenda in tatters, Wiles has learned that fealty to Trump almost always ends badly.

And if past experience is any guide, Wiles’s replacement, Stephen Miller, may well crash and burn in even more spectacular fashion.

There was no one the president relied on or trusted more than Wiles. From their first meeting in 2015 at Trump Tower to her impressive stint as his winning 2024 presidential campaign co-manager, the “ice maiden” had Trump’s back. And he had hers—until last Tuesday’s epic Democratic blowout. Wiles would resign two days later. Indeed, the Republicans’ midterm apocalypse was an extinction event that not even Wiles could have survived.

Ironically, Trump’s savvy political strategist was the architect of what turned out to be a big blue bloodbath. “We’re going to win the midterms,” Wiles told me boldly when I interviewed her for Vanity Fair just a year ago. Even then, three months before Trump initiated a war on Iran, that was a ridiculously rosy prediction. The president’s approval rating was in the gutter. He’d failed to address, much less solve, voters’ primary concerns: affordability, inflation, health care, and housing—and had still not released the remaining Epstein files. How could a battle-hardened political pro like Wiles be so starry-eyed? The answer, I believe, is that in the fog of MAGA-land, she’d lost touch with the real world.

In almost every presidency, the West Wing is a bubble where like-minded acolytes engage in groupthink. But in Trump’s West Wing this phenomenon is exponentially magnified. It’s a parallel universe, one in which the 2020 election was stolen, violent insurrectionists are “patriots,” and the prosecution of political enemies—with scant evidence—is a presidential perk. (“Who would blame him?” Wiles said to me of Trump’s campaign to settle scores.) That, to my mind, is why Wiles seemed so stunned by the firestorm that erupted when her words appeared in my 10,000-word Vanity Fair series last December. She had no idea they would land like bombs on planet Earth.

Wiles invested Trump with almost otherworldly powers. He would lead the GOP to victory in the 2026 midterms, she believed, because of his preternatural ability to rally his base. That’s why, on the eve of the midterms, Wiles was all-in on sending Trump almost everywhere all at once, admonishing people to “vote like I’m on the ballot.” The trouble was voters saw all too clearly what she apparently couldn’t see: Trump was deeply unpopular; on his watch, the country was coming apart.

A year ago, when Wiles made her electoral prediction, I challenged her. “I admire your confidence about the midterms,” I said, “but the stakes are huge, right? And history is not encouraging. Incumbents do stuff and there’s a reaction. And usually, as Obama said, you get shellacked.”

Wiles seemed to shrug off that possibility. “Can you ever imagine Donald Trump saying that?” she said. “No, no.”

Wiles was right. Trump could never say such a thing—because he could never accept the fact that his electoral magic had waned. Neither, it seemed, could Wiles. But as his chief of staff and top political strategist, she was paid to know better.

Even before the election debacle, Trump had reportedly started privately inquiring about her on phone calls, although he lashed out at accounts of such purported conversations. Then, once the carnage sunk in, the die was cast. Wiles offered her resignation. And Trump accepted it.

At the start of her West Wing tenure, I believed Wiles stood a chance of succeeding. If Trump would listen to anyone, I thought, it was the loyal, organized, no-nonsense Wiles. Yet during 10 conversations with her over 10 months, I watched as she abdicated the most important duty of the White House chief: telling the president hard truths. Wiles told me she’d read my book, The Gatekeepers: How the White House Chiefs of Staff Define Every Presidency, and she understood the importance of heeding Reagan chief James Baker’s advice. “You do not serve your president well if you are just a yes man,” he said. In a phone call, she told me, Baker “reminded me that my job wasn’t to be a fangirl.” I asked Wiles, “Have you had any gut check moments where you had to tell the president something he didn’t want to hear?” She paused. “I probably have one a day,” she said. “But they’re over little things, not big.”

Wiles should have known that the midterms would spell disaster. She carried around a list of her priorities, on an index card. Number five: “Don’t forget about organized labor. Don’t forget about young Black men and women and Hispanics…because that’s the future of the country and the backbone of his support. And if we don’t convert those people to being enthusiastic Republicans, then if the Democrats were even just a little bit better, they might win an election.”

Miller is a zealot, a hard-boiled ideologue—an advocate of Trump’s notorious first-term Muslim ban, the brutal paramilitary tactics of ICE, the deployment of the National Guard to Democrat-run cities, and the lethal air strikes on boats in the Caribbean.

They might—and they did. And now Wiles is out, taking up shop, so Trump himself has said, within his political operation. Last November she hinted that she knew this day might come: “You go to bed at night, you say your prayers, you take stock of what the day was and what your day is tomorrow, and you get up and do it again…. So as long as that’s the case and the president’s pleased…” Wiles paused. “He could fire you tomorrow.”

She’s sensitive about her legacy as the first female White House chief. “I’m not an enabler,” she insisted. “I’m also, like, not a bitch. I try to be thoughtful about what I engage in, and what I disagree [with the president] about. I guess time will tell whether I’ve been effective.”

What about Wiles’s successor, Stephen Miller?

Miller is the antithesis of Ronald Reagan’s chief James Baker, a cool pragmatist who could push back on the president’s half-baked ideas. Miller, by contrast, is a zealot, a hard-boiled ideologue—an advocate of Trump’s notorious first-term Muslim ban, the brutal paramilitary tactics of ICE, the deployment of the National Guard to Democrat-run cities, and the lethal air strikes on boats in the Caribbean. He believes in a Hobbesian world, he has stated, “that is governed by strength, that is governed by force, that is governed by power.” Now he’ll be the last person in the room when Trump makes life-and-death decisions about law and order and war and peace.

The man who decreed that the president’s powers “are very substantial and will not be questioned” is now the official charged with questioning the president’s decisions. It’s hard to imagine Miller doing that without a personality transplant. He’s already alienated the House minority leader, and soon to be Speaker, Hakeem Jeffries, who has called Miller “a dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist who has American blood on his hands,” insisting, “I’ve got zero interest in working with that kind of individual.”

At the White House last November, after a Vanity Fair photo session, I spoke with Miller at length about the midterms, still a year away; about his portfolio in the Trump administration; and about the role of the White House chief of staff. Perched on a chair in the Roosevelt Room, he eyed me warily. He seemed impatient to get back to work. “I understand that your need for me is quite limited, right?” he said.

I asked Miller about his interactions with the president—specifically an Oval Office meeting in which he and Trump reportedly talked about blowing up boats in the Caribbean. “I would never talk about…whether a meeting occurred or didn’t occur,” he said, “or whether it was in a meeting that did occur, or was not in that meeting if it occurred, which I would never say either way.”

Miller was more forthcoming about Wiles’s prediction—that Trump and the GOP would triumph at the polls in 2026. “What about you?” I asked him. “I am confident that we’ll win the midterms,” he replied. History might be against them, he said, “but we have every expectation that we’re going to defy that history.” “Why?” I asked. Miller replied, “Because of the president’s unprecedentedly successful first nine months in office.”

What followed was a black-is-white, up-is-down litany of Trump’s accomplishments, a revisionist history that might have made Karoline Leavitt, another world-class propagandist, blush. “In no particular order,” Miller said, “the taming and defeating of inflation. As you know, we inherited record double-digit inflation and the president made his first priority to bring down the cost of living…cutting the price of energy by high double digits. For many Americans, gas prices have been cut in half since we took over.” None of this, of course, has proved true—but Miller was just warming up.

“And the passage of the largest package of tax cuts and reforms in American history in the form of the One Big Beautiful Bill. Fully securing the Southern border, the most secure border in history, zero illegal crossings, four months in a row. And also the largest number of deportations in American history…. The president has…achieved more in foreign policy than any president in our lifetimes, ending eight wars in eight months—which includes, but is not limited to, securing the historic peace deal between Israel and Gaza, Thailand and Cambodia, Congo and Rwanda, Azerbaijan and Armenia, Israel and Iran, and so on…”

Miller still wasn’t done. The president, he said, “has executed on every promise he’s made to the American people and that includes also taking back our culture and fighting against whether you call it radical leftism or woke or Marxism—a lot of people just call it plain crazy—but taking back our culture and restoring sanity to American life.

“It is my extraordinary privilege and blessing,” Miller added, “to be able to work for the president of the United States, to implement an agenda that I believe in wholly and completely and with every fiber of my being.”

I was there, of course, because I was writing a story on Susie Wiles and her West Wing team. I asked him, point-blank: “Would you agree, though, that it’s also the chief of staff’s job to tell the president what he doesn’t want to hear?”

“No, I wouldn’t say that,” Miller replied, finding fault with my framing of the question and insisting that this president wants to hear everything. “The chief of staff would never have to encounter the scenario you’re describing.” Miller said. “President Trump craves, he loves the every-minute detail of management, having every piece of information, having every side of everything, having inputs into the Oval Office from every square, every quarter, every person.”

As for the president’s staff, Miller said, their job is “implementing the president’s vision, the president’s directions, the president’s agenda, the president’s plans for the future…. We’re just here on his behalf to see that that is done.”

As the great political columnist Molly Ivins once wrote, “It probably sounded better in the original German.”

Chris Whipple is a contributing writer at Vanity Fair and a Fall 2026 Resident Fellow at Harvard’s Kennedy School Institute of Politics. You can follow him on Substack.

#3562. 32 Years Later, The Santa Clause's Line On Believing Is Still The Greatest Christmas Quote

Ah, "The Santa Clause." The holiday classic where Tim Allen (making his leading man debut in a movie) accidentally murders Jolly Old Saint Nick, featuring a title that tricked an entire generation into misspelling "Santa Claus." In the 1994 film (which ended up having to cut a risque joke), Allen plays Scott Calvin (Get it? His name has the same initials as SANTA CLAUS!), a divorced, work-obsessed marketing exec spending the holidays with his son, Charlie (Eric Lloyd).

Christmas Eve rolls around, and when the real Santa accidentally falls off Scott's roof and dies, Scott is forced to become the new Santa. Scott doesn't like this idea, especially when he starts growing a magical beard and a magical fat belly. It doesn't help that everyone around him — except Charlie — thinks he's gone insane. The film then unfolds over a year leading up to the following Christmas, where Scott has to come to terms with his new career.

Will Scott learn to be a better father, embrace the Christmas spirit, and thrive as the new Santa Claus? Of course he will, and then they'll make a string of sequels (and a streaming TV series reboot as well)! Happy holidays!

"Seeing isn't believing. Believing is seeing."

"Seeing is believing" is an age-old saying, but "The Santa Clause" flips this a bit. When Scott becomes Santa, he ends up in the North Pole, where the Elves who toil away in the workshop try to give him some help. One of those elves, Judy (Paige Tamada), utters our quote of the day: "Seeing isn't believing. Believing is seeing." This quote is later embraced wholeheartedly by Scott's son Charlie, who has to keep reminding Scott that all he has to do is look around to witness the reality of his new magical life.

Belief is a big part of "The Santa Clause." Scott has to believe in himself, while everyone around Scott has to believe he's really the new Santa. The hard-headed realists of the world understandably have trouble with all of this, and that includes Scott himself. He's a gruff American businessman! He doesn't believe in Christmas magic, gosh darn it! All Scott needs to do is open his eyes, both literally and metaphorically, to see the reality of his new situation. And isn't that what Christmas is all about? That and drinking way too much nog? Thank you,"The Santa Clause," for making us believe in Christmas.

"You want me to take the toys down the chimney into a strange house, IN MY UNDERWEAR?"

"Merry Christmas to all, and to all a good night! And when I wake up, I'm gettin' a CAT scan!"

"We're your worst nightmare. Elves with attitude."

"Everybody likes Denny's, it's an American institution."

"You see, children hold the spirit of Christmas within their hearts. You don't wanna be responsible for killing the spirit of Christmas, now would you ... Santa?"

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

90 Day: Florida is the latest entry in the 90 Day Fiancé franchise, and I have to ask if we've lost the plot. Sure, it seems and feels like the average TLC spinoff we'd expect to see on the 2026 TV schedule, minus the cornerstones of what makes this franchise what it is. Yes, beginning Monday, December 14th, those with TLC or an HBO Max subscription can see all the 90 Day couples living in Florida jam-packed into one show. This season teases a wedding between Cortney Reardanz and Phil, as well as a celebration for Jasmine Pineda. It sounds fun, but I'm still on the fence about it due to these two principles.

90 Day: Florida gives me pause for a couple of reasons, and they have to do with the foundation of the franchise. One detail is the fact that this entire spinoff takes place in one location. While we've seen this done before with 90 Day: The Last Resort or Hunt For Love, the resort was a matter of convenience rather than a series focused on individuals all living in one area. I mean, should a franchise that focuses on people finding love abroad have a spinoff based solely in one part of the United States?

It doesn't feel like we're going to get the best storylines with couples in the franchise, or that this is a handpicked selection of the best 90 Day has to offer. It's just all the cast members who live in Florida, which feels like this was just made out of convenience rather than actual fan interest.

90 Day: Florida feels like TLC attempting to make 90 Day Fiancé like the Real Housewives franchise. The problem is, what they're doing already exists, and in making a spinoff based solely on the fact that all these couples live in the same state, I question if it'll pull in the core audience that shows up for these shows.

I'm Shocked By How Much 90 Day Fiancé's Sarper Reportedly Made Doing Stand-Up Comedy

All this to say, it's not my money, so I'm curious to see how 90 Day: Florida will do and how audiences will respond. I do know there are rumors that Yara Dufren will be accused of cheating on Jovi, which is something I would love to know more about.

I also can't help but notice the timing of this spinoff lines up perfectly with Libby and Andrei Castravet announcing their exit from the franchise. They're also based in Florida, so is it possible they ended up leaving after not receiving an invite to appear? I'd love to know the details on that, especially in the aftermath of their feud with Alexei and Loren Brovarnik.

Whether I'm on board or not, though, I'll be watching 90 Day: Florida when it premieres, and I hope I'm wrong about this franchise not really feeling like it falls under the 90 Day Fiancé umbrella. I'll be eager to see what other viewers say as well, and if this ends up being a format that TLC sticks with for other states.

#3559. The Role of the “Queen Mother” in Monarchies Around the World: Queen Sofía, Sonia of Norway, and Beatrix of the Netherlands

Queen Sofía celebrated her 88th birthday on November 2 and remains a pillar of the Spanish royal family, with a demanding schedule that includes at least one official engagement per week. Queen Sofía has never set aside her institutional role, unlike some other European “queen mothers” (this official title is used only in the United Kingdom but is commonly used to refer to the mothers of kings), who, to a greater or lesser extent, continue to work for the monarchy in their respective countries.

This week, Queen Sofía will be in San Fernando, Cádiz, where she will serve as patroness of the ceremony to present the National Ensign to the Marine Corps, a special unit within the Navy and the world’s oldest marine corps, created in 1537 by Emperor Charles I. Far from retiring from public life, the Queen Emerita continues to play an important role within the Crown; she retains her office at Zarzuela and receives an official stipend.

She also remains closely involved in the day-to-day activities of the Queen Sofía Foundation and regularly visits the provincial offices of the Spanish Federation of Food Banks to learn about its charitable work, among other projects. Always discreet, Felipe VI’s mother has weathered the controversies surrounding Juan Carlos and maintained a professional image dedicated to serving the Spanish people—one that her family circumstances have not tarnished.

Queen Sonja, a great source of support today for her son, King Haakon.

Following the death of her husband, King Harald, in late August, and with the newly crowned Queen Mette-Marit on medical leave, Queen Sonja of Norway has become a pillar of support for her son, Haakon VIII. Sonia of Norway is 89 years old and in recent months has had minor health scares that led to her being hospitalized for a few days in the hospital. But despite everything, she continues her duties as a member of the Norwegian royal family. Just a few days ago, Queen Sonja traveled to Málaga to attend the opening of an exhibition on Picasso and Munch at the Picasso Museum in the Andalusian city, and was all smiles during a visit to a Norwegian school in Benalmádena.

On November 3, Queen Sonja accompanied her son Haakon to an official dinner to welcome the provincial governors at the Royal Palace—an important event at which the king will have his mother’s support in the absence of his wife and his daughter, Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra, who is currently focused on her university studies in Oslo. Two days later, Queen Sonja will visit the Furniture Maker School in Askim, attend the opening of a furniture exhibition at the Center for Democracy at Fort Høytorp, and meet with members of the Indre Østfold Women’s Group and young people at the Re:læx youth center in Askim.

After more than three decades as queen, Sonia of Norway has stayed by her son’s side, at a time when he needs her support more than ever. Since her accession to the throne, Queen Sonia—whom Haakon stripped of the title “Her Majesty,” now simply Queen Sonia—has become a cornerstone of institutional and family support for the new monarch.

Beatrix of the Netherlands served as queen for 33 years.

At 88 years old, Beatrix of the Netherlands does not have a schedule as busy as those of Queen Sofía or Queen Sonja of Norway, but she has continued to attend institutional events and fulfill some official engagements since her abdication in 2013. King Willem-Alexander’s mother actively participates in award ceremonies linked to the Crown, such as the Appeltjes van Oranje awards presented by the Oranje Fonds foundation—awards whose bronze statuettes she designed herself and which she attends each year alongside King Willem-Alexander and Queen Máxima.

In addition, Princess Beatrix continues to make official trips to the Dutch Caribbean territories (such as her recent visits to Bonaire, St. Eustatius, and Saba) to preside over events dedicated to nature conservation, sustainable development, and education. She also continues to attend certain cultural and charitable events in her home country, such as the Dutch Ballet Gala hosted by the Dansersfonds Foundation, which she attended in mid-October.

Beatrix of the Netherlands, who now resides at Drakenstein Castle, was Queen of the Netherlands for 33 years, from 1980 to 2013. Following the coronation of her son Willem, she regained the title of princess, and today her official title is Her Royal Highness Princess Beatrix of the Netherlands, Princess of Orange-Nassau, and Princess of Lippe-Biesterfeld. Beatrix of the Netherlands remains deeply loved and respected by the people, and within the Orange-Nassau royal family, she continues to support and guide her son, King Willem-Alexander.

Princess Beatrix is a great role model for her granddaughter, Princess Amalia.

Queen Sofía, Queen Sonja of Norway, and Beatrix of the Netherlands all embody the key institutional values essential to preserving the monarchy in their respective countries. Loyal to the crown in one capacity or another and having dedicated their lives to public service for decades, all three are great examples of institutional loyalty for their granddaughters— Princess Leonor, Princess Ingrid Alexandra, and Princess Amalia—who will one day become queens.

#3558. VisionQuest's Avengers: Doomsday Post-Credits Scene Explained: [SPOILER] Returns

This article contains spoilers for "VisionQuest" Season 1, Episode 8, "Forever."

The season (series?) finale of "VisionQuest" teases that the Vision-Maximoff family still has a future in the Marvel Cinematic Universe. There are two post-credits scenes in "VisionQuest." One is vaguer: Ultron (James Spader), now free and convinced not to kill all of humanity for now, has a backup drive of Jocasta (T'Nia Miller). So, yeah, it looks like this isn't the last we've seen of the Living Automaton in the MCU.

Towards the end of the episode, Tommy Shepherd (Ruaridh Mollica) asks Vision (Paul Bettany) if they'll ever see his mom, Wanda Maximoff/The Scarlet Witch (Elizabeth Olsen) again. The second post-credit scene all but confirms, yes, they will.

The scene replays the climax of 2022's "Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness," where Wanda buries herself under the rubble of Mount Wundagore to destroy the grimoire, the Darkhold. But then the scene shows green energy telekinetically lifting the rubble away, as a shadowed, hooded figure stands over Wanda. "Scarlet Witch, awaken. Your power will be mine," he says in a European accent as green light bathes Wanda, and her eyes shoot open. Three guesses who Wanda's savior is and the first two don't count. (But you will get a hint — his name rhymes with "zoom.")

This basically confirms Olsen will be appearing as Wanda in "Avengers: Doomsday," and as a servant of Doctor Doom (Robert Downey Jr.) This scene also aligns rather well with a post-credits scene included in the "Avengers Endgame: Encore" rerelease earlier this year, which depicted Doom freeing Bruce Banner (Mark Ruffalo) from imprisonment after the events of "Spider-Man: Brand New Day."

Many now vindicated Marvel fans refused to believe that Wanda was really dead after Wundagore's destruction. Elizabeth Olsen had previously said she was open to returning as Scarlet Witch, and it seems Marvel must've given her a call.

In "Avengers: Doomsday," Doom will have at least three "Latverian witches" under his command, and they will wear steel masks much like their boss does. That'll be a fitting homage to the three Brides of Dracula — Doom, as a caped, castle-dwelling Eastern European king, is very much a villain modeled in Dracula's image. But there's also rampant speculation the witches' masks hide familiar faces, including Wanda's. This "VisionQuest" post-credits scene all but confirms it.

(In the "Time Runs Out" storyline that "Doomsday" is loosely adapting, Doom had all female acolytes called Black Swans serving him. The Latverian witches might be a simplified version of that concept.)

While I'm hoping Marvel doesn't make Doom, their greatest villain, a literal variant of Tony Stark, the fact is Robert Downey Jr.'s casting means a lot of the audience will read Doom as "evil Iron Man." There'd be some fitting narrative symmetry then if Doom has corrupted Avengers, like Hulk and Scarlet Witch, on his side.

Doom has manipulated Wanda before in the comics, too. "Young Avengers: The Children's Crusade" by Allan Heinberg and Jim Cheung revealed that, after Wanda's infamous "No more mutants" crash-out in "House of M," Doom sheltered her in Latveria to try and gain her powers. This is the storyline that reunited Wanda with Tommy and Billy as well. With how "VisionQuest" leaves the Maximoff boys, and with Marvel Studios having planted the seeds for Young Avengers, I think a "Children's Crusade" adaptation is in the near future.

Adam Driver and Miles Teller are the co-leads of a particularly thrilling entry on the 2026 movie schedule. The two actors – alongside the show-stopping Scarlett Johansson – headline Paper Tiger, the latest film from director James Gray. It tells the story of a family that gets wrapped up in shaky business dealings and, as a result, some characters keep secrets. CinemaBlend caught up with Teller and Driver and asked about their secret-keeping abilities, and it seems as far as their wives are concerned, they just can’t do it.

In the film, Teller and Driver play Irwin and Gary Pearl, respectively, who embark on a business venture (at Gary’s suggestion) involving the Gowanus Canal in 1980s New York. The two ultimately find themselves contending with the forces of the Russian mafia and, amid a portion of the conflict, Irwin’s wife, Hester (Johansson) is left in the dark. When CB caught up with the two leading men and asked if they would be able to keep big secrets from their significant other, and Driver dropped a funny take:

Would I have told her right away? Oh, yeah. Yeah, yeah, yeah…. My wife is kind of a [clairvoyant]. She can see into the future a little bit. No literally, but she can just tell….

Since 2013, Driver has been married to Joanne Tucker, with whom he shares two children. Based on his comments, it sounds like the Ferrari star knows better than to try to keep something from his wife. The sentiments drew laughs from Teller, but he also seemed to be able to empathize with the thoughts. Teller is married to Keleigh Sperry (who’s known for sharing fun videos online), and they’ve been married for over seven years. While discussing whether he’d keep a big secret from Sperry, Teller had this to say about his wife:

Yeah, Keleigh, can always sense when something’s… Even if I just eat something wrong, she's like, ‘Everything OK?’ I’m like, how did you…

It’s great to hear that the two stars strive to maintain transparency with their wives, though that also begs another question. Our Jeff McCobb went on to ask if the two would tell the truth only because they knew they couldn’t get away with a lie. However, they both clarified their thoughts on that front:

Considering their attitudes, I wonder if that tendency not to keep secrets also extends to the actors’ work. I mean, was Tucker aware that Driver was developing a Kylo Ren movie with Steven Soderbergh for a time, or is Sperry privy to any details regarding Teller’s involvement in Top Gun 3? I’d also like to know if the pair’s co-star, Johansson, also kept secrets from hubby Colin Jost while she was “wrapped up” in Marvel movies. I could just be overthinking this, and maybe the stars’ spouses don’t even care to know such information. Regardless, it’s still interesting to consider.

What isn’t a secret, though, is that Paper Tiger is proving to be an extremely buzzy title, and James Gray and co. are receiving considerable praise from critics. The Armageddon Time director seems to have delivered yet another classic, and it may even yield some recognition this awards season. For now, though, anyone who wants to see Adam Driver and Miles Teller keep secrets (on screen and not in real life) can check out their new movie, which opens in limited release on November 13 and opens nationwide on November 20.

#3555. Ryan Gosling's R-Rated 2016 Comedy Is Officially Apple TV's Biggest Streaming Hit

I have never seen an actor resist Hollywood stardom more stubbornly than Ryan Gosling. Three years after his 2001 breakout performance as a Jewish skinhead in Henry Bean's incendiary "The Believer," (for which he should've been nominated for an Academy Award), he was transformed into a big-screen heartthrob via his portrayal of Noah Calhoun in Nick Cassavetes' "The Notebook." Gosling could've dined out on hunky leading men roles for the next decade, but, over the next few years, he chose instead to play a freebasing high school teacher in "Half Nelson," a self-destructive husband in the soul-hollowing "Blue Valentine" and an emotionally remote getaway driver in "Drive." "Crazy, Stupid, Love" was a bright box-office spot, but it wasn't the showcase he needed. If he wanted to be a star. Which, in 2011, seemed to be in question.

In 2016, Gosling made a play to become a star on his own off-kilter terms as alcoholic private detective Holland March in Shane Black's "The Nice Guys." The legendary screenwriter behind "Lethal Weapon," "The Last Boy Scout" and "Kiss Kiss, Bang Bang" cooked up an elegantly seared filet mignon for Gosling, and he savored every moment. "The Nice Guys," which pairs Gosling with an over-it Russell Crowe (as a Yoo-hoo swilling enforcer) is an audience movie, but the audience, for whatever reason, didn't show up in 2016.

28 days after "The Nice Guys" went live on Apple TV, it's now the service's most watched movie. I'm thrilled that more people are discovering this shaggy detective classic 10 years after its release, but under Ellison's Skydance rule, Warner Bros. isn't trying to resuscitate commercial misfires. This is it. That said, it's got more going on in its 116 minutes than the entire Marvel Cinematic Universe oeuvre.

I read "The Nice Guys" when it was pitched as a network television pilot by Black and Anthony Bagarozzi (one of these men had the pleasure of watching a stray kitten urinate on my lap). It was sharp, hilarious and fertile ground for a series – if the writers could get around CBS' standards and practices. Not since "The Monster Squad" had Black written with such ease and eloquence at a PG-ish level.

When "The Nice Guys" got greenlit as a film, producer Joel Silver starred it up with Gosling and Crowe. The idea seemed to be that Crowe, a major movie star and Academy Award-winner, would play straight man to Gosling's goofball PI, and the film would sell itself. This just didn't happen. Set in the late 1970s, Black's stumblebum neo-noir is a skillfully plotted romp that finds Gosling and Crowe trying to piece together the disappearance of anti-pollution activist Amelia Kuttner (Margaret Qualley).

Gosling is dopey perfection as Holland March, a single father who's battling against a boozy haze to solve a case that could save his profession and his life. He's funny and heartbreaking in this role. As is Black's wont, you're left with a wacky, whimsically moralistic Donald Westlake riff with blockbuster trimmings. Gosling and Crowe are scrambling to take down men who abuse women. Spoiler: they get their dastardly dudes, and you'll shed tears along the way.

I'm thrilled that Gosling is now an A-lister making films for Lucasfilm, and he was wonderful in "Project Hail Mary," but we've yet to see his best. I just want to watch him blossom.

#3554. Lobbyists Are Preparing Silicon Valley Titans for Democratic Subpoenas and Congressional Crackdown

On Thursday, I was on the phone with a source when he suddenly sounded like he’d gotten the wind knocked out of him. We were in the middle of talking about antitrust policy when he exhaled and said, “Wow. Worst one-day destruction of value in history. Just got the Wall Street Journal alert.”

The tech world—and the markets built on top of it—is still figuring out how to feel about last week’s momentous Democratic midterm sweep. My Republican sources, unsurprisingly, reported that the vibes in their ranks are “horrendous.” Anyone who works with data centers is just about ready to throw in the towel on planet Earth and take their infrastructure efforts to space, with voters having opposed data center construction via 40 different ballot measures. And then there’s the more general rebuke of the future the tech industry is building, and the possible implications for an economy that’s increasingly come to revolve around it.

Indeed, it seems that the debate over AI has really, truly broken through to the mainstream this year: According to an NBC exit poll, 56% of voters called AI and data centers a “crucial or major factor” in their votes for Congress. Amid the free-for-all of President Trump’s first two years back in office, AI companies have been allowed to develop their technology largely free of regulatory oversight, but they may now be forced to pump the brakes.

In a lengthy interview with Ross Douthat on CBS’s 60 Minutes, Trump said he was open to working with Democrats to implement some AI guardrails. Still, no one I spoke to this week told me they expect to see sweeping AI legislation—unless, as two different tech Democrats suggested, there is an AI-caused catastrophe that “scares the shit out of us.”

Democratic Senators like Bernie Sanders and Elizabeth Warren have already begun making plans to investigate tech corporations.

In the absence of such an event, “we expect [new AI laws] to be narrow and bipartisan. Child safety, AI agent liability, and predeployment testing, for example, all have Republican cosponsors,” said Christina Ho, an executive at the financial auditing firm Oath Verified.

Meanwhile, even more explicitly MAGA-coded industries could see more concrete crackdowns. Those in “the crypto world,” who spent the first year of Trump 2.0 flying high, now “realize they’re screwed,” said an executive at a conservative think tank—especially as famed crypto critic Sherrod Brown makes his big return to the Senate with, as one Democratic strategist put it, an “axe to grind.”

Defense-tech founders and investors may also find themselves toning down their rhetoric as the testosterone-fueled “Department of War” era comes to an end with the possible impeachment of Secretary Pete Hegseth. In recent years, “dual use” has become a bit of a “dirty word,” said Cody Huggins, a partner at Scout Ventures. He suspects that promoting the commercial applications of military technologies, from satellites to drones, “will come back to be a little bit more sexy than it has been.”

Perhaps the biggest winners of the post-midterms period will be the DC law firms brought on to help manage the flood of subpoenas promised by politicians like Bernie Sanders and Elizabeth Warren. “AI executives might be called to testify,” said Ho, adding, “Companies would be wise to prepare their executives for the witness table before they prepare for any new laws.”

A Democratic tech lobbyist told me that one of his clients has already received a list of questions from a congressional committee. “They’re not waiting to have gavels,” he said.

Luther Lowe, the head of public policy at the start-up accelerator Y Combinator, is hoping to see a return to the antitrust revolution once promised by former FTC chair Lina Khan. “I think some of that stuff could come back online,” he said, referring to antitrust legislation that then Senate majority leader Chuck Schumer declined to bring to a vote in 2022.

In the future, tech executives who went all in on MAGA (right after going all in on woke) may want to consider some age-old advice: just be yourself. “Companies need to stop thinking about political outcomes as permanent conditions. Regulations change, governments change, and priorities change. That’s not new,” said Andrew Peek, CEO of the investing platform Tilt. “What’s different now is the sheer amount of money being committed to technologies whose economics are still evolving. If your entire strategy only works under one political scenario, that’s a pretty big risk to be taking.”

Still, there was one midterm fight in which the tech world definitively won out: the one over Proposition 40, or California’s so-called billionaire tax, which was defeated. Some suspect that the hundreds of millions of dollars spent by Silicon Valley billionaires to defeat the measure could backfire. “There’s a growing wave of anger and resentment from the working class that is coming for them,” said the Democratic strategist. The irony of spending so much money to fight the tax, he said, is that if it had passed, it could have “temporarily removed some of the pressure in the pressure cooker.” All that money having been spent to shut down the tax, he warned, “is gonna make things much worse.”

#3553. This Bose Portable Bluetooth Speaker Is 33% Off Right Now

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

A price drop always stands out more when the product in question already has a reputation for delivering above its size, and that’s the case with the Bose SoundLink Plus. It hasn’t been on the market for long, but it’s already earned strong reviews—CNET labeled it “the Goldilocks of Bose Bluetooth speakers.” And right now, ahead of Black Friday, it’s down to $179 from $269, which price trackers show is the lowest it’s ever been.

Bose positions it right in the middle of the SoundLink lineup, and you feel that balance in how it’s built. It’s compact enough to clip onto a backpack using its built-in nylon strap, and tough enough to handle getting knocked around, and sealed against dust and full water submersion with an IP67 rating. Battery life can last up to 20 hours, depending on the volume, which is sufficient for full-day outings. On the connectivity side, there’s Bluetooth 5.4 with AAC and AptX Adaptive support, as well as the ability to keep two devices paired for smoother switching. What you don’t get is a microphone, an aux port, or any voice assistant support, which is worth considering if you prefer wired options or use speakers for calls.

As for its sound profile, it leans into mid- and high-bass, which gives electronic and pop tracks a lively pulse, though at higher volumes, you may notice some compression (which is common in speakers this size). It also doesn’t reach into true low-bass territory, so anyone who wants thumping sub-bass may not get it here, but the punch it does deliver feels clean for its size, notes this PCMag review. And while you won't get the width and separation of a stereo mix since the SoundLink Plus plays audio in mono, its directivity is good—meaning its sound remains clear from different listening positions, so you don't have to sit directly in front of it to get a good experience.

But there’s also been some re-evaluating of the whole series now that it’s got five years under its belt and Kelly Clarkson seems to be pulling back from her own daytime show.

#3551. Why Prince William Is Reluctant to Become Head of the Commonwealth

Following King Charles’s successful nine-day tour to the Caribbean, the future of the Commonwealth has become a much debated subject. At last week’s Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) in Antigua and Barbuda, Charles, who was designated Head of the Commonwealth, a role he assumed after his late mother Queen Elizabeth, told assembled leaders he found the voluntary union of 56 nations to be a “source of enormous encouragement and pride.”

However, Buckingham Palace has made it clear this weekend that Charles will only serve as monarch in the Caribbean realms “for as long as they wish” and that the monarch is open to change. According to The Times, Charles is “fully open” to those realms removing him as head of state.

While Charles was in the Caribbean, there was ongoing debate about slave trade reparations, which the monarch addressed in his speech to CHOGM. Describing it as a “monstrous injustice” he expressed his “profound personal sorrow” but fell short of making a formal apology for Britain’s role in the slave trade. (Since King Charles is a ceremonial head of state, he is unable to apologize on behalf of Britain unless the government sanctions it.)

Amid calls for reparations, there are questions about the future of the Commonwealth and who its next head should be. In conversation with Vanity Fair, constitutional expert Ed Owens, author of After Elizabeth: Can the Monarchy Save Itself?, discusses what’s in store for the future.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

King Charles reacts near Antigua and Barbuda flags during a visit to Nelson's Dockyard, a historic naval base established in 1725, during his visit to Antigua and Barbuda on November 2, 2026 in St John's, Antigua and Barbuda.

Vanity Fair: Prince William has made it clear that he does not necessarily expect to follow his father as head of the Commonwealth, saying that the decision belongs to the Commonwealth itself.

Ed Owens: Prince William hinted after his difficult 2022 tour of Belize, the Bahamas, and Jamaica that he wasn’t focused on following his father as head of the Commonwealth. A couple of weeks ago The Times of London confirmed that the prince’s position was unchanged on this issue. Crucially, the position of head of the Commonwealth is not hereditary. King Charles got the role because his mother and predecessor, Queen Elizabeth II, actively lobbied Commonwealth heads of state to ensure that the role would pass to him when he became monarch, following her death. But it will not automatically transfer to William when Charles dies.

What is the Commonwealth and how significant is that statement?

The Commonwealth of Nations (as it’s officially known) is a voluntary association of 56 independent member states. Most of these member states were once colonies in the British empire. Decolonization began after World War II and most newly independent states—though no longer part of the empire—became part of the new Commonwealth. This new international body represented change but also continuity, enabling Britain to maintain a global (but mostly symbolic) presence at a time when its real geopolitical power was rapidly in retreat. The Commonwealth also provided a stage for the monarchy to continue to exercise an important international role. George VI was the last emperor and first Head of the Commonwealth. The latter role was invented by the British government to replace the former and allowed the monarch to maintain a semblance of global prestige while helping to facilitate the process of decolonization.

Although most member states have historical ties to Britain, any country can apply to join the Commonwealth—exemplified by recent members like Rwanda, Mozambique, Gabon, and Togo. Members commit to shared principles outlined in the Commonwealth charter, including democracy, human rights, the rule of law, and sustainable development. In reality, though, many member states have failed to live up to these principles, and the Commonwealth has, in recent years, felt morally directionless.

William’s reluctance to take on the mantle of Head of the Commonwealth isn’t that surprising: He and his advisers want to future-proof his reign. One way to do this is to identify potential problems in order to avoid them. The Commonwealth is one such potential problem, and William seems to have calculated that the headship of this organization likely represents more trouble than it is worth.

Does it represent a fundamental shift in the monarchy’s attitude toward the organization, or simply an acknowledgement that the old imperial relationship is no longer sustainable?

We have to remember that 15 members of the Commonwealth (including the UK) are also “realms”—i.e. their head of state is King Charles. I think it’s clear even to the current king that his position as monarch of the 14 realms beyond Britain is unsustainable. Eventually all 14 nations, and perhaps the UK too, will opt to become republics, cutting their ties with the crown. Those nations most likely to become republics soonest—owing to the fact that they have surging republican movements—are the Caribbean realms, two of which (the Bahamas and Antigua and Barbuda) King Charles visited during his recent tour to the Caribbean. Indeed, we can even interpret the tour as the king and his courtiers preparing the ground for this transition to republics. This is because, though former realms will no longer have as their head of state the incumbent monarch, they will almost certainly remain members of the wider Commonwealth.

What King Charles was trying to do with his latest tour was to inject energy and meaning into the idea of the Commonwealth, more than attempt to reinvigorate the personal bonds that connect him to his peoples in the Caribbean. In loudly acknowledging the injustices of the slave trade in which Britain was, for a long time, complicit, while also reminding his hosts that Britain was one of the first major powers to abolish and oppose slavery—the king has sought to address and ease concerns in ways that might enable the Commonwealth to function more cohesively in the future, irrespective of whether the UK’s monarch remains in post as head of the Commonwealth.

When Charles eventually leaves the throne, could the Commonwealth decide that it no longer needs a British monarch as its figurehead? What might replace that role? Will the Commonwealth continue?

I absolutely think [the] Commonwealth nations will look to replace the British monarch with a new figurehead. My sense is that many nations would already prefer to have a different kind of figurehead, for example a head who belongs to one of the 56 member states and is elected by member states for a set term. Alternatively, there could be some kind of “rolling” headship, whereby every member nation is invited to elect an official who will take a 12-month turn as head of the Commonwealth.

Whether or not the Commonwealth will continue is more difficult to say. Certainly one of the reasons it has survived until now is because of the energy and engagement of two British monarchs—Charles and Elizabeth II—who have viewed it as a potential force for good in the world. Without its connection to the British monarchy, it may lose what is left of its momentum. However, its survival also depends on wider geopolitical shifts: If individual governments within the Commonwealth view it as [a] useful arena for bringing together states who could benefit from closer association—be that economic, political, or military association—then it may continue long into the future.

There is an increasingly difficult conversation about Britain’s colonial past, slavery, and reparations. Charles has expressed personal sorrow over the slave trade, but the question of a formal apology remains politically and constitutionally complicated. How much freedom does the king actually have to address these issues, and could William take a different approach?

The king has very little freedom to apologize unless his government specifically sanctions and encourages such an apology. As the recent Caribbean tour made clear, I think Charles would prefer to strike a more nuanced line, reminding audiences that, despite the UK’s colonial past and its involvement in the horrors of slavery, Britain was one of the first major powers to abolish slavery and that it played an important role in bringing to an end the maritime trade in human chattel. Whether William takes a different approach will depend entirely on the UK government’s approach to formal apologies and reparations. My sense is that no government—at least not now or in the near-to-medium-term future—will agree to financial reparations, because historians, philosophers, and politicians are increasingly pushing back on such a solution, questioning why UK taxpayers (already under huge strain) should fork out huge sums for the wrongs committed by some of their ancestors more than two centuries ago.

What would Queen Elizabeth II make of this? She saw the Commonwealth as her father’s legacy and her second family.

I think she would probably be relatively relaxed, recognizing that times change and institutions have to evolve. Let’s not forget that as queen she oversaw many key alterations in the way both the monarchy and Commonwealth functioned through her long reign, as was required by shifts in politics, economics, culture, and social norms. While the Commonwealth was of emotional importance to her—not least for the way it connected her back to her father and predecessors—by the end of her reign it was already a shadow of what it once had been and she would have known that it was likely to continue on a trajectory of decline. William has decided that given the challenges and changes of the mid-20th century the monarchy and royal family’s future is likely to be stronger without the post-imperial baggage of the Commonwealth. I think his grandmother would have respected the way he is putting the family firm first in this instance.

#3550. 15 Years Ago Today: Henry Cavill Starred In An Epic Fantasy Movie Before Superman

With now-former DC Studios heads James Gunn and Peter Safran's version of the DC Universe coming to a premature end, it's times like these when we would do well to look back at what has worked, and what hasn't worked, when it comes to DC's films. One thing that kinda worked was Henry Cavill, a great Superman who never got a great Superman movie during his run in the DC Extended Universe. Without doubt, the actor had both the charisma and physicality to make you believe a man can fly.

And yet, just two years before debuting as Superman in "Man of Steel," Cavill made audiences believe a man could battle gods with a sword. It was November 11, 2011, and Indian director Tarsem Singh Dhandwar had just released his film "Immortals," an epic fantasy movie inspired by Greek mythology.

In the film, Henry Cavill plays Theseus, a humble stonemason with the physique of a Kryptonian who is chosen by Zeus himself (Luke Evans) to lead humanity in their resistance against Hyperion (Mickey Rourke), a tyrant king wreaking havoc on Greece in search of a mythical bow that would allow him to free the Titans and overthrow the gods of Olympus. No, this movie isn't really based on any particular myth. Rather, it borrows from a number of legends and blends them together in a nonsensical yet very cool tale full of superhero-like action, incredible costumes, and some of the most stunning imagery in any fantasy movie out there.

Back in its day, critics generally praised "Immortals" for its stunning visuals while admitting its story left a lot to be desired. Nowadays, though, the movie represents an underrated entry in Cavill's body of work, as it showed he was ready to be a star and lead a franchise (or two).

"Immortals" is, admittedly, not a well-written movie. And yet, Tarsem Singh Dhandwar went about crafting this movie like it was going to mark the last time he ever set foot on a film set, leaving it all on the screen. Case in point, he tapped Eiko Ishioka ("Bram Stoker's Dracula") to design the movie's impossibly flamboyant costumes, which make the human characters look so extravagant that they almost overshadow the literal gods around them.

Then there's the film's visual style, which Singh once described as "Caravaggio meets 'Fight Club.'" He wanted to make a hardcore action flick in the manner of a Renaissance painting, and it shows, resulting in a movie that blends the desaturated colors and slow motion of something like "300" with a striking painterly aesthetic. When it comes to its spectacle, "Immortals" similarly combines gods with mythical weapons that tear down city walls and intimate, grounded sword clashes, making its violence feel huge in its scope and scale. Indeed, the first scenes involving gods are especially stunning, as they move at full speed while the humans they're reducing to smithereens are slowed way down. It's a great way to illustrate the awesome powers of these deities.

Speaking of awesome powers, "Immortals" is further bolstered by Henry Cavill, who very much proves his ability to carry a big-budget movie ihere. To be sure, his performance matches the wild tone of everything else around him, all while bringing some needed humanity to Theseus. It's enough to make you more than a little excited for Cavill's return to the realm of outlandish fantasy movie adventures with his upcoming "Highlander" reboot.

#3549. Eight 'Winter Arc' Rules That Will Actually Deliver Results

There are a lot of terrible social media trends out there aimed at self-improvement, yet even though everybody has been making fun of the "Winter Arc" craze, I actually think it’s a good one. During your Winter Arc, you promise yourself you’ll stick to your fitness and self-care routines during (and despite) the end-of-year chaos. It's a good goal, with one caveat: Make sure you choose rules that will actually improve your life and deliver results.

Think of the “arc” in the sense of a “story arc.” The Winter Arc is a self-improvement journey that unfolds over the last few months of the calendar year. The most hardcore #gymtok-ers will tell you the Winter Arc officially begins on Oct. 1, but others start in early November, or whenever they get around to it. The "when" isn't critical, though—whenever you read this is a fine time to start. The close of the Winter Arc is fixed, however: It ends Jan. 1, just as everybody who is less dedicated than you is waking from their holiday food comas and resolving to get in shape.

You get to choose your own terms for your Winter Arc. The general vibe is one of locking in, committing to your goals, and actually doing the things you’re always saying you’ll do. TikToker @carlyupgraded has said that her own mental image of someone nailing their Winter Arc is “hood up, headphones on, getting ready to go for a run in the rain at 5 a.m.”

It turns out I’ve accidentally been Winter-Arc-ing for years; I just didn’t know it had a catchy name. Why save your gym routine for New Year’s when you’ll have the place to yourself all December? We’re even gifted with an extra hour in the mornings to fill with something productive.

I really love the mindset shift involved. Commonly, people are active in the summer (great time for outdoor fun), may or may not stick with their routines in the fall, and let everything fall apart as the holidays approach. Who has time to go to the gym when you’re planning Thanksgiving, attending holiday parties, studying for final exams, or whatever else the end of the year throws in front of you?

But that’s the exact reason why this time of year is the best to start (or restart) a fitness routine, or really any kind of routine. When you start a routine during a busy time of year, you’ll be forced to make it sustainable. The gym routine you can stick with amid the chaos isn’t going to be one you drop after a few months. You’re already training yourself to work around obstacles as they come up, which is a key component of self-efficacy. And when the chaos clears on Jan. 1, your routine will be even easier to stick to.

Of course, there are ways to lean in too hard: Choosing unsustainable habits, falling for bad diet advice, mistaking not masturbating for some kind of health hack, the usual suspects. There’s also the pitfall of focusing too much on the vibes and too little on what you’re actually going to do or how you’ll benefit.

And then there’s the framing: You were working on yourself all year, but you’re in danger of letting up on the gas, but you’re committed to locking in so that you’re a step ahead of everybody who takes this time to slack off. I really don’t love this tack. Self-improvement is not a competition. There’s a difference between being consistent in your training and healthy eating (good) and seeing the pursuit of health and fitness as something where you always have to work harder because you’re at risk of getting left behind.

I also don’t love how gendered the Winter Arc TikToks tend to be. When you search for Winter Arc content, the first few suggestions include “winter arc for women” and “winter arc for men.” When I first started looking at the Winter Arc trend a few years ago, the women’s versions were more likely to include restrictive dieting or to focus on how the Winter Arc will finally (sigh) snatch your waist. These days, the focus is more on personal goal setting: Lots of the girlies filming their Winter Arc rules are doing so in a notebook and talking about journaling exercises that will help you identify what you need to work on to get to your "best self." Sometimes this is all monetized; training plans and journaling prompts can, of course, be purchased at the link in bio.

I do like that many of the women’s versions emphasize sustainability and setting your own goals rather than copying somebody else's. I don't love the enormity of the mental burden you're supposed to shoulder before even beginning. Should I really have to file an in-depth written report with myself before revamping every area of my life with a 100% commitment to multiple goals?

The men’s versions tend to go off the rails in another direction, with rules like “no girls” or “go ghost.” No distractions! Here, I've seen a shift over the years as well: at first there was overly serious content, followed quickly by satire (yelling at the viewer to get divorced and go work out in the dark). Now the men's videos tend to be more vibes-based, featuring images of pre-dawn workouts and plates full of salad with motivational quotes playing in the background. When the men give their rules, they tend to be simpler than the women's—no journaling exercises—but they often boil down to the same overly strict routines. (And then, of course, they'll offer to sell you a 90-day or 60-day plan.)

If you’re going to do a Winter Arc (or if you’re already doing one), make sure to structure it in a way that benefits you. Choosing 10 overly ambitious goals and setting yourself up for failure is not a healthy way to approach self-improvement, OK? Pick goals that are meaningful, achievable without divine intervention, and trackable with tools you already have at hand (for example, tracking your steps with a Fitbit or your running mileage with a Garmin watch).

It’s also helpful to think of developing yourself over this arc, rather than taking it as a three-month (or two-month) challenge where you have to do everything right all the time. If you currently wake up at 8 a.m. and want to wake up at 5 a.m., you don’t have to set your alarm for 5 a.m. tomorrow. It’s OK to aim for 7:30 a.m., make that a habit, then try for 7:00 a.m., and so on.

With that in mind, here are some "rules" I've seen from creators that I'm actually on board with (so long as you don't overwhelm yourself with them):

Wake up earlier. A great goal, especially if you take advantage of the time change to make things easier on your body.

Get to bed on time. Never a bad idea. Cultivating good sleep habits in general is always worthwhile.

Get your steps in. Be thoughtful about what your target is: 10,000 is not for everybody. Better to choose a number that would be a modest improvement on what you already do.

Exercise X times per week. Pick a number that works for you, and get into it. Be realistic about your goal, and for the best results, be consistent even if you’re sore at first.

Eat healthy. This is a great goal, with the major caveat that there are a lot of ways to eat healthy. You don’t need to cut out sugar or pretend that there’s something evil about seed oils. Do get more protein and veggies.

Be more thoughtful about using social media. I’m not going to tell you to delete all your apps (“except TikTok,” as the TikTokers say). But it’s fair to consider whether you might want to delete a few apps, turn off some notifications, or put your phone on Do Not Disturb for more hours of the day.

Journal or read more. Journaling can be great for working through your feelings or cultivating a creative habit. Reading can be entertainment or a great way to learn. Choose whichever you need most.

Learn a new skill. I’ve mostly seen this one in the men’s TikToks, and I love it. They’re often thinking of “skills” that will help in some kind of entrepreneurship grift they’re about to sell you, but there are tons of skills that will come in handy in life, or that are at least fun to learn. Practice a language, get better at cooking, make some art. Skills are, as I’ve noted, a multi-layered exercise for your brain. And they may come in handy someday.

This year I've slacked off on my fitness routine as I've gotten more involved in other hobbies, but I'm actually looking forward to being more consistent. My winter goals include exercising early in the day when possible and reading 20 minutes each day. (I'm even tracking the second one with a sticker chart.)

#3548. 10 Funniest 'Far Side' Comics About Penguins That Prove Gary Larson Is Unbeatable

Everybody agrees that penguins are funny. They walk funny. They sound funny. They all look like they’re wearing tiny little tuxedos. They’re birds, but they can’t fly — that’s very funny. They live in utterly ridiculous places, and they fall down all the time.

It almost seems as though nature designed penguins purely for our amusement, which is why these clownish creatures have been comedy staples forever, including in The Far Side.

While penguins weren’t a top-tier Gary Larson fixation like cows and dinosaurs were, they were a semi-recurring source of comedy in his daily comic strip, which ran from 1980 until 1995. And, because penguins are such funny little guys, here are the 10 best penguin-oriented Far Side comics.

Penguins are such ridiculous creatures that if your town was being terrorized by a giant one, it’d be more embarrassing than anything else. Even with other funny animals, I don’t think this is the case. Monkeys are funny, but King Kong is one of the greatest monsters ever. Goats are funny, but I’m pretty sure a giant goat head-butting buildings would be horrifying. A giant penguin, though? There’s just no way to take that threat seriously, especially since these creatures presumably have a complete inability to stomp.

Okay, hamsters are funny, and I’m pretty sure they’d be funny as giants, but still not funnier than penguins.

This is just a great example of a simple, silly gag which is kind of the opposite of the previous one. The idea of penguins as an animal you can get an infestation of is really ridiculous.

I just love this idea that these two penguins are waiting for just the right person to come by while they’re isolated on an ice float.

Sometimes Gary Larson would find a particular thing about a subject that he just fixated on, and he’d essentially come back to the same funny idea over and over again, like a great running joke. For example, he loved to depict scientists as childish idiots — the contrast there was ripe for comedy. Larson had also decided that the worst musical instruments ever were banjos and accordions, so he leveled insult after insult at those instruments and the ones who play them.

For penguins, the running gag was that they all look identical.

This is a great example of that, where a penguin is saying, “Say … you’re not Bob! … You look like him, but you're certainly not him!”

The idea that even penguins can’t tell penguins apart is especially good.

This is another “all penguins look the same” gag, with the joke being that the singing penguin is desperate not to be like the rest.

Another “penguins all look the same” gag, with a murder-mystery twist.

This is the best example of the “all penguins look the same” joke, as it's one of those panels where Larson made you work for the punchline. It's an especially nice use of his wide Sunday panels because it provides all the more penguins you have to inspect until you figure out what the joke is.

This kind of seems like a variation of the penguins looking alike thing, but the punchline here is more about ridiculously bad disguises and penguins being little dummies — which, I’ll admit, I don’t know if penguins are stupid or not, but they feel like they are.

This is just a fantastic joke. It’s the kind of unique perspective to an age-old subject that Larson specialized in.

Finally, this is Larson’s best-ever penguin comic, bar none. Capitalizing on a penguin’s clumsy habit of falling over, it depicts a lone penguin on a sheet of ice having slipped on a random banana peel. It’s a remarkably simple comic, yet each element builds upon the other. Banana peels are slippery, ice is slippery, and penguins can barely stand upright. It’s a comedic perfect storm that is then further enhanced by the thought, “How did the banana peel get there?”
