News broke a few days ago that Universal Orlando’s beloved mascot Earl the Squirrel would be hitting a big milestone this year. He’s headed to the 100th Annual Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade, and if you plan to watch on NBC or with your Peacock subscription, you’ll be able to see him getting his own giant balloon. It’s a big anniversary for the Thanksgiving parade, but it’s also a solid one for Earl, who turns 5 this year. Let’s talk out what we know.

Here at CinemaBlend, we’ve been big fans of Earl The Squirrel for a while. The story behind Earl goes that Earl the Squirrel was a real mammal who burrowed in Universal Studios’ giant Christmas tree in Orlando in the early aughts. One of the best parts of being at Universal Studios around the holidays is the lighting of the Christmas tree, and the original Earl liked to chew on the aforementioned lights.

Someone on the team jokingly put a stuffed squirrel in the Christmas tree in homage, and then in 2021, someone had the bright idea to bring Earl into the parks officially.

Now, he’s the mascot, and most definitely one of the cool Easter egg found throughout the parks. I visited during the holidays last year and saw him cutely burrowing in the big Christmas tree. I’ve also caught Earl in the Tribute store in the past, and a life-size version of Earl does meet-and-greets throughout the holiday season. Finding him on the tree is still a sort of yearly scavenger hunt.

However, I get the sneaking suspicion anyone watching the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade won’t have any trouble spotting Earl. That’s because he’s going to be 30.4 feet tall and 14.5 feet wide. Literally, you won’t be able to miss him.

I haven’t been to the real-life Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York, but Universal Orlando already offers the next best thing: The Holiday Parade Featuring Macys. The theme park actually has had ties to the Macy’s Parade for years, and even if you aren’t normally a parade person, bringing the giant balloons into the theme park is real feat, and impressive to see. A visit around the holiday season is worth it for the parade alone.

The holiday season kicks off this weekend at Universal Orlando, starting on Saturday, November 14th, and Earle will join The Holiday Parade lineup in early December. For now, you can catch The Grinch in action, or check out the Red Coconut Club's alpine makeover. This year, Universal is also once again upping its food game, and you can try out one of the many new cabin-style holiday food kiosks featuring items like Christmas Tree waffles, red-nose reindeer donuts, oh and Earl gets a shoutout there too with Earl The Squirrel’s hazelnut dot cake.

I’m not even getting into the hot chocolate options, which are usually my personal favorite snack this time of year. (Well, as long as it’s not 90 degrees out.)

All in all, there’s a lot to look forward to if you’re planning a trip to the parks, and there are special tickets being offered this holiday season. You can find out more on the Universal Orlando site.

#3546. The Lord Of The Rings: The Rings Of Power Season 3 Confirms A Popular Fan Theory

Meat's back on the menu, but so are spoilers for "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" Season 3, Episodes 1-4.

One of the biggest joys of "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" is getting to see mythical J.R.R. Tolkien characters like Gil-Galad (Benjamin Walker) and Elendil (Lloyd Owen) finally appear on screen for more than five seconds. Similarly, getting to watch the Dark Lord Sauron himself (Charlie Vickers) deceive Celebrimbor (Charles Edwards) throughout Season 2 by calling himself an envoy of the Valar is hilarious (as is Sauron being haunted by Celebrimbor's ghost in the Season 3 premiere).

That said, there are plenty of engaging new additions on "The Rings of Power" as well, with Adar (Joseph Mawle and Sam Hazeldine) – the elf-turned-orc who just wants to create a safe place for his kin — being indubitably the best. Others, however, are not nearly as successful, with possibly the worst of them being Theo (Tyroe Muhafidin). The character, who lived in what is now Mordor with his mother Bronwyn (Nazanin Boniadi) in Season 1, has the unfortunate job of serving as the annoying kid whose seemingly only purpose is to ruin everyone's fun, act racist towards elves, whine every five minutes, and make horrible decisions that end up causing a volcano eruption that engulfs the Southlands in darkness for millennia.

(Okay, that last one's not entirely on Theo, but still...)

What makes this all especially frustrating is how overtly "The Rings of Power" has foreshadowed Theo becoming someone important and evil down the line. As such, he has inspired a variety of fan theories about his true identity, like him being the King of the Dead. Now, Season 3 has confirmed that Theo is none other than one of Sauron's Ringwraiths.

In the premiere episodes of "The Rings of Power" Season 3, we see Sauron recruiting allies, luring men with the promise of Rings of Power that will turn them into his Nazgnagôl (proto-Nazgûl or Ringwraiths). This includes Theo, who arrives at Mordor in order to compete for one of the rings that would give him the power to fight back against the Númenórean overlords that have been abusing the Southland refugees in Pelargir. It's clear Theo isn't really loyal to Sauron, he just wants to use him to gain power for himself.

Well, things get worse when Sauron lures Theo with talk of his ancestry, revealing that Theo comes from a long line of royalty in the Southlands and even communicating with Theo's long-dead father, Fäldred. According to the Dark Lord, Theo belongs to the "sworn stewards of Mordor", which explains why Theo was drawn to the broken sword in Season 1. Sauron then claims that Bronwyn murdered his father when she discovered the truth of his lineage, then kept it all hidden from her son.

Granted, this is Sauron, a notorious liar and expert manipulator. At the same time, it wouldn't make much sense for Sauron to casually hand Theo a ring unless there actually is something special about him. Regardless, the Dark Lord appeals to the kid's greed and ambition, saying he has it in him to be a conqueror, a sorcerer, and a king.

Unfortunately, it appears that "The Rings of Power" is setting up Theo to become the Witch-King of Angmar, as evidenced by him donning the familiar Nazgûl armor in Season 3's third episode.

While Theo's feelings about sand have yet to be revealed, we do know he's easily manipulated. Indeed, with the benefit of hindsight, we can see just how much his story has echoed Anakin Skywalker's fall to the dark side in the "Star Wars" prequel trilogy. After all, he's never known his father, used to live with his mother, and would do anything to protect those he loves, yet he has an undeniable sense of ambition and hunger for power (which Sauron recognizes, just as Darth Sidious/Palpatine did with Anakin).

Except, Theo doesn't turn to darkness while trying to save someone, so he's nowhere near as tragic as Anakin. It's his fear of being abandoned, combined with his desire for power, that make Theo an ideal candidate to become the latest victim of Sauron's lies. First, it was Galadriel (Morfydd Clark), whose thirst for vengeance made her susceptible to Sauron's trickery back when he was going by Halbrand in Season 1. Then, in Season 2, it was Celebrimbor, whose aspiration to become better and more famous allowed Sauron (passing himself off as Annatar) to gaslight him into crafting the rings of dwarves and people. Now, Theo is playing right into Sauron's hands and allowing himself to be enslaved by the Dark Lord.

It remains to be seen whether Theo is capable of coming back from this. He does seem hesitant to carry out all of Sauron's wicked biddings, yet he does it anyway. Is he beyond redemption? And most importantly, is Theo actually the Witch-King? Or will he die and get replaced by one of the Nine we know from "Lord of the Rings?" We'll see what happens as "The Rings of Power" continues.

#3544. Loose Lips Sink Chips: Silicon Valley Reacts to the (Alleged) Spy Who Shagged Jensen Huang

I remember asking my parents when I was a child why it was such a big deal for a politician to have an affair. They explained to me the many layers of possible compromise beyond the simple breach of morals and propriety. Extramarital affairs, my parents explained, could expose politicians to blackmail, undue influence, and the temptation to give up vital state secrets over pillow talk.

Maybe someone should have that explain-it-to-me-like-I’m-five conversation with investors like Shaun Maguire and Bill Ackman, who rushed to the defense of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang this weekend following his shocking confession that he’d been involved in an affair with Megaspeed executive and alleged Chinese intelligence asset Alice Huang. (A Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson has called the spy allegation “unsubstantiated” and “nothing but smears against China.”)

Sure, Jensen Huang is not a head of state. But he’s arguably someone even more powerful. He’s the man in command of the world’s largest company—and its most coveted technological infrastructure: high-performance GPUs required to train artificial intelligence systems.

For years, tech-world observers scratched their head when he insisted again and again that his company should have the right to supply those elite chips to China—even as Americans were told that letting our most formidable adversary gain any advantage in the AI race would spell doom for the Western world. When Huang took the number four spot on our New Establishment list this fall, I wrote that his commitment to fighting these export controls could become his Achilles’ heel. And boy, has it. Nvidia has now launched an independent investigation into his affair, while the government continues to assess the blast radius of the scandal.

There are “three big national security implications from this,” Ryan Fedasiuk, a senior fellow at the Foundation for American Innovation, told me this week. “The first question is whether Chinese intelligence has succeeded in obtaining any sensitive nonpublic information about Nvidia, about its products or—I think what’s being overlooked—its customers of massive quantities of GPUs, like large AI labs.” The second, he said, “is whether Chinese intelligence may have succeeded in indirectly obtaining information about President Trump or people close to him,” given Huang’s unusually close relationship with the president. And third is “the question of whether Mr. Huang’s personal relationship with his customer might have motivated the company’s decision to sell large numbers of computer chips to Megaspeed, a company that has been under investigation by the Commerce Department for violations of American law.” (A Megaspeed rep told The New York Times that the company was “conducting an internal investigation into allegations of chip diversion,” the subject of the US probe, and that it had “repeatedly offered to cooperate with the US government.”)

According to the Times, the US government has been aware of Huang’s relationship since at least 2025, prompting many more questions about why this knowledge was not made public until it was uncovered piece by piece by the killer investigative team at the Times—notably, right after the midterm elections.

“Someone in the national security establishment clearly decided that they were sick and tired of the president playing this game with Jensen,” said Dennis Wilder, a former senior intelligence official who now teaches at Georgetown’s School of Foreign Service.

Of course, investors have plenty of reasons to turn a blind eye to Huang’s misdeeds. His company has also played a keystone role in keeping the entire economy afloat, taking many investors’ portfolios along for the ride on its seemingly never-ending bull run since 2023. Many are wondering if dethroning him from the company he built from the ground up could also send our entire economy over the edge.

Fedasiuk thinks the decision is worthy of a bit more nuance. “I think investors and the American people have to remember that there is actually a distinction between the personal interests of Mr. Huang and the corporate interests of Nvidia, a $4 trillion company that is the backbone of the intelligence revolution,” he said.

Mentioned in this issue: Dario Amodei, Sherrod Brown, Whoop, Culper Research, Daniela Amodei, Holden Karnofsky, Brian Chesky, Ramp, Sean Parker, Tilt, Kalshi, Modal Labs, Lina Khan, Bernie Sanders, and Elizabeth Warren.

Buried in The New York Times’ excellent deep dive into the ideologies that influence Anthropic cofounder Dario Amodei was a link to the archived wedding website of his sister, Anthropic cofounder Daniela Amodei, and Anthropic staffer Holden Karnofsky. However weird you expect it to be, triple that.

I’ve always felt a kind of kinship with short sellers—would-be investigative journalists who’ve decided to use their skill set to make real money. Kudos to the investment-research firm Culper Research for publishing a brief back in May detailing its short position on Nvidia, taken, in part, due to Jensen Huang’s “uncomfortably close relationship with Megaspeed’s Alice Huang.”

Next time you log your weekend party habits, remember that Whoop sees you, and it’s judging you. “LSD and ketamine use were associated with bedtimes over an hour later and Recovery scores about 9 points lower. Psilocybin showed smaller changes: 33 minutes later and 2.9 points lower,” the company posted over the weekend. Tsk tsk.

Let the road show begin. Anthropic has proposed pricing its IPO shares at $70–$78 a pop, seeking a $1.3 trillion valuation for the AI company. The offering is expected to start trading on November 19.

Just the other day, a source was venting to me about how Silicon Valley billionaires have failed to use their wealth to improve their own surroundings. #3543. Your Android Can Get Hacked Without You Doing Anything at All

You probably know that clicking suspicious links online or opening attachments from strangers in an email or text is a recipe for hacking. It's a dangerous world out there online, so it's always important to be vigilant. However, the danger doesn't always involve something you do. There are ways to hack your devices without requiring any intervention on your part whatsoever—and one such example is likely plaguing your Android device right now.

As reported by The Hacker News, there is a critical Android security flaw that could enable remote code execution on your device. In other words, bad actors could use the flaw to run their own code on your phone, effectively taking over the device for their own gain. The flaw, identified as CVE-2026-58868, isn't universal, but it is widespread: It currently affects Android 14 through Android 17, the latest version of Google's OS. If your phone runs Android 12 or Android 13, it may be unaffected, as Google doesn't identify these versions in its security bulletin, but it doesn't explicitly rule them out, either.

There are two silver linings here, however. One, Google hasn't confirmed any active exploits for this security flaw. While that isn't a guarantee that bad actors have missed this exploit so far, it at least opens that possibility. As such, there may be time for users to patch their devices before hackers truly take advantage of the flaw. Second, Google does have a patch for the flaw. The patch may not be available to you right away, however, as it's up to both the manufacturer of your phone and your carrier to issue these updates. Still, a patch is, at the very least, on its way.

This flaw is perhaps the most important to fix, but it's not the only serious issue. In all, Google's latest bulletin highlights 216 vulnerabilities, and, of those, 23 are "critical." As The Hacker News explains, two other of those critical flaws could also allow remote code execution when exploited.

To see whether the patch is installed on your end, open the Settings app on your phone, tap "About phone" or "About tablet," then choose the Android version on-screen. Look for a date of "2026-11-01" or later. All security patches from Nov. 1 and on will fix this issue. If not, you'll ned to wait for the patch.

#3542. How To Rob A Bank Producer Explains How The Movie Reinvents The Heist Genre [Exclusive]

It's easy for novices to make the mistake that if you've seen one heist film, you've seen them all. As the genre junkies among us know, it takes a little more effort than most to make these sorts of movies stand out from the crowd. Steven Soderbergh found lightning in a bottle with his "Ocean's Eleven" remake in 2001, while Christopher Nolan added a mind-bending spin with "Inception" less than 10 years later. Classic cinema is rife with examples of how to craft memorable heist movies, from Michael Mann's "Thief" to Sidney Lumet's "Dog Day Afternoon" to Stanley Kubrick's "The Killing."

So when David Leitch came across writer Mark Bianculli's script for "How to Rob a Bank" and chose this as his next directorial effort after "The Fall Guy," it quickly became apparent how this could become a heist flick like nothing we've ever seen before. As the title implies, the unconventional heroes of this story are a group of social media influencers who've become viral sensations — not just for pulling off bank robberies like they were born to do it, but for creating a YouTube channel teaching others how to stick it to the man and perform heists of their own.

Not long ago, I had the chance to talk to the creative team of Leitch and "Violent Night" producer Kelly McCormick (who happens to be Leitch's longtime producing partner at 87North, as well as his wife) during the "How to Rob a Bank" press junket about what drew them to the script. According to McCormick:

"In this case, it's like, 'How do you turn a heist movie on its head — not your daddy's heist movie?' And it's the [idea of] thieves hiding in plain sight, as opposed to not wanting to be seen."

It's a staple of practically every heist story ever told, from "The Italian Job" to "Heat" and everything in between: In order to pull off the perfect caper, our protagonists must cover their tracks, don some clever disguises to maintain a low profile, and escape the scene of the crime without anyone being the wiser. It's definitely not advised for robbers to film themselves while on a job, edit and upload those tutorials to YouTube, and revel in the viral fame that comes with being the most well-known crew the internet has ever seen. It's all about avoiding detection — not seeking it out.

But "How to Rob a Bank" isn't exactly interested in the conventional approach. With Nicholas Hoult's Ryan as the ringleader, this motley group of Robin Hood-like revolutionaries have figured out how to successfully weaponize simmering anti-capitalist sentiments among a generation fed up with living under a broken system. They just happen to do so with a GoPro strapped to their masks and a knack for live-streaming their crimes to an eager audience. According to director David Leitch, this was the main appeal behind taking the screenplay by Mark Bianculli and bringing it to life:

"That's what we saw in it and that's why we really wanted to do this material. It had all of those elements where you could create something fun, but yet also with a bigger message. That was one of the things we haven't gotten to do: maybe have something that has a little bit more of a commentary. There's usually a moral tale [in heist movies], but this has a little bit of ... it's asking you big questions about where we are in the world right now."

Where studios like A24 and Blumhouse deserve credit for establishing themselves as high-minded horror destinations, 87North has cornered the market with the most exciting action films. Upon seeing David Leitch's name attached to any given film, audiences can safely expect more visceral set pieces, an emphasis on practical effects, and a certain, undefinable je ne sais quoi when it comes to mixing and matching genres. After "Atomic Blonde," "Deadpool 2," and "Bullet Train," "How to Rob a Bank" seamlessly fits into Leitch's ongoing interests.

Or, as Kelly McCormick aptly puts it in our conversation, "I believe one of David's pillars is that he always is doing a little bit something different with the genre every time out, and wants to and enjoys changing genres and the subgenres within action and really wanting to tell a lot of different tales." It's one thing to identify that branding, however, and another to actually put it into action. As she went on to explain:

"So then, how can you make that Leitchian? How can you make that atonal? And ['How to Rob a Bank'] had all the things, with regards to the drama versus the social media content and all those kinds of aspects. And then, I think the extra unique part is being able to have a bigger message, more front-and-center than what we do a lot of times out with our commercial propositions."

That "bigger message" may hit particularly hard at a time when working-class struggles remain at the forefront of the national conversation as the rich only get richer. "How to Rob a Bank" hits theaters on November 13, 2026.

The latest episode of NCIS was a special one for Katrina Law, as the Jessica Knight actress co-starred in it with her daughter. Law told CinemaBlend her kid knocked it out of the park, but she was ready from the moment it was suggested to shut it down if she wasn't ready.

I had a chance to speak to the actress ahead of the episode's airing on the 2026 TV schedule. Law explained that her daughter, Kinley Andreen, actually pitched the idea of coming on the show, so when an opportunity came up, she was asked about having her on. While she was thrilled to give her daughter a chance to be on the series, the actress explained she wanted her kid to earn it through an audition:

There was a part of me going, like, if she's not really good, I'm not going to make [them cast her], I'm not going to, like, put everybody through this experience. She nailed that audition within 20 minutes.

Things went well, and Andreen booked her debut acting appearance as Chloe in NCIS. I was, frankly, a bit surprised to learn it was her first time acting, because I would've assumed she'd been doing it a while based on her performance. However, she'd never done traditional acting outside of school play performances. Did we all just witness the beginning of a future A-lister's career in television?

Due to that lack of experience, Katrina Law said she wanted to have her daughter go through the audition process to see if she's up for the challenge, but told us she couldn't be prouder of how she did:

It was a four-page audition...she picked up all the beats, she had props, she was doing different notes, there was an emotional arc, she memorized all the lines, was completely off book, and I'm like, there are adults who have to spend two days doing this just to prep for this moment, and you got it in 20 minutes. It was amazing.

Law and her daughter also got to display their fluency in Mandarin after the agents were shocked to find the little girl they found was bilingual. It was quite an acting debut, which makes me all the more thankful she pulled it off.

Jessica Knight's run in Season 24 of NCIS is off to a slow start, but the seeds are being planted for her to have a larger role later this season. Her constant monitoring of Tony DiNozzo for Ziva screams that a future team-up is in the works, which I'm very excited to see.

As for what's next for her daughter, who knows where we'll see Kinley Andreen show up next? There's nothing wrong with being a nepo baby when it comes to Hollywood, especially if you have the talent to back it up. Maybe if NCIS can stay on the air another 20+ years, we'll see Andreen come back and play an agent on the series!

For now, I'm just content we have a solid block of NCIS to enjoy on Tuesday nights. Tune in to CBS on those nights for a healthy dose of nostalgia, as the lineup is loaded with classic NCIS actors.

#3540. Lord of the Rings Officially Reveals Gollum’s Replacement

Rachel Leishman is a writer, interviewer, and self-appointed "professional" fangirl. She has an encyclopedic knowledge of all things movie and television and loves all things comedy. Part of her coverage includes her deep love of Spider-Man, Interview with the Vampire, and more. She is also the self-appointed "unofficial" Leslie Knope.

The Lord of the Rings has a lot going for it right now. Next year, The Lord of the Rings: The Hunt for Gollum is set to release from director Andy Serkis, who brought Gollum to life in Peter Jackson's The Lord of the Rings trilogy as well as the trilogy for The Hobbit. He is, in many ways, the most iconic character in the franchise and is easily the most quoted. You can't talk about Lord of the Rings without someone saying "My precious." Now though, a new character has taken the place of Gollum within the franchise. Meaning a new creature being dragged into things with our main characters.

Season 3 of The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power began releasing on Prime Video on November 11 and a new character has captured the hearts of fans in the first four episodes. The series, much like the films before it, use the orcs as Sauron's (Charlie Vickers) soldiers. The first two seasons had Adar (played by Joseph Mawle in Season 1 and Sam Hazeldine in Season 2) that fans were obsessed with and now a new orc has taken over as the new chosen one. Marnûkh (Adam Young) embarks on a quest with Galadriel (Morfydd Clark) and Arondir (Ismael Cruz Córdova) and the rest was television history.

Part of what makes Marnûkh such a wonderful addition to The Lord of the Rings and the lore of the orcs is that he's so incredibly funny. As Galadriel and Arondir are trying to follow Marnûkh and what he's willing to tell them about Sauron's quest to create the one ring to rule them all. Marnûkh's quest is to help Galadriel and Arondir infiltrate the orc army at Gundabad but it leads to a lot of exploration for both Galadriel and Arondir, who have to learn how to trust an orc as elves after everything in them is telling them to distrust Marnûkh. Luckily, they go along with what the orc is trying to tell them and it leads to one of the best dynamics on all three seasons of The Rings of Power.

Part of why fans loved watching Samwise Gamgee (Sean Astin) and Frodo Baggins (Elijah Wood) with Gollum was that the two hobbits knew and understood each other and then they were forced to deal with a creature that thought differently from themselves. In many ways, that's the dynamic we're seeing with Marnûkh as he leads Arondir and Galadriel to Sauron. Even if it doesn't end on the best of terms for Arondir by the end of this quest. But what really makes the inclusion of Marnûkh so special is that it gives us a new way to look at the orcs rather than just seeing a group of beings who are almost blindly following Sauron into battle, as has been the case within the franchise prior to Season 3.

Often, the orcs are depicted as the evil, dark-side of elves. In Jackson's films, they are monstrous beings that don't really have any real depth to them. The Rings of Power showrunners, J.D. Payne and Patrick McKay, have been using the orcs to show more dimension in the other creatures of Middle Earth that often get the short end of the stick when we're exploring J.R.R Tolkien's beautiful story. A character like Marnûkh helps change the idea of what an orc is supposed to be because he's compassionate, poetic, and someone who is just trying to do what he thinks is right instead of giving his blind faith to Sauron, like other orcs.

So yes, on paper, Marnûkh is the new Gollum. He is taking the spot of "creature people are forced to trust" like Gollum was with Frodo and Sam but to take it one step further, Marnûkh is also a character that forces you to have compassion for a being you thought you understood. The orcs are just trying to find a place to belong and Marnûkh realized that the war was not the way to do that and took matters into his own hands and that's why he's kind of the best.

#3539. Netflix’s ‘The Body’ Explores Queer Girlhood, Catholic Guilt, and the Teenage Search for Faith

“Confess!” yells a teen as she stares into a pack of wide-eyed Catholic schoolgirls.

“I made out with Katie’s dad,” one reveals. “I masturbate to Daddy Franklin!” another cries, a black cross still smudged on her forehead.

Welcome to The Body, a new Netflix series that recalls a holy trinity of inspirations: Carrie, Jennifer’s Body, and Heavenly Creatures. But while all three were reference points for the show’s star, Geena Meszaros, she also wants her character to stand alone. “I really wanted her to be her own thing,” she told VF in October.

“It was kismet,” Meszaros says of landing the role of Lisbeth. “I feel like she was my dream character to play before I even realized it.”

The Body is set in a Catholic girls school circa the early 2000s—complete with Juicy Couture pajamas, Yahoo! Messenger, teenage devilry, secret lesbian relationships, and plenty of Catholic guilt. Meszaros plays Lisbeth, a gawky reject whose desperation to join the dance team leads her to some fairly sinful decisions. On Halloween night, mutually pining co-captains Anya (Kristina Bogic) and Elise (Sara Boustany) stage a team initiation that goes wildly wrong—and maybe accidentally summons the devil.

Amid the chaos of their drunken houseparty, Lisbeth takes one for the team and buries a body—literally. Before long, high school devolves into Crucible-style mania as the girls start seeing visions.

Though showrunner Quinn Shephard has described The Body as a love letter to the female-centered horror of the early 2000s, and it arrives amid a similarly themed Carrie remake and the Nov. 20 return of Yellowjackets; the series might be less of a Y2K echo than something entirely new: a snapshot of Gen Z’s faith in 2026.

“There's a sense of faith in each other, that you need to have, that you just don't get if you're not part of a team,” Meszaros says about connecting with her costars.

Meszaros calls the show a mix of horror, comedy, and grittiness, all smushed together. There’s also a bit of romance overseen by Chala Hunter, the same intimacy coordinator who worked on Heated Rivalry. Meanwhile, a very pregnant Gabby Windey makes her acting debut as the team’s coach. (“I don’t know if I’ve met anyone who’s just so themselves all the time,” Meszaros says of her costar.).

Like Meszaros, almost everyone else in the cast is an up-and-comer: Kristina Bogic, who plays the popular high school sweetheart Anya; Sara Boustany, who plays her wicked best friend (and secret lover) Elise; Sofia Wylie, the doomed preacher’s niece; and Nnamdi Asomugha, an NFL cornerback turned actor who plays that very preacher (and the school’s principal): Father (Daddy) Franklin.

“I'm more of a spiritual person, but I think having faith in anything outside of yourself, whether that's God or whether that's something else, I think that's important,” Meszaros says.

In the months before filming, the team bonded just like their characters do: through dance team training, which sometimes lasted seven hours a day. “There was no pretending with the friendships on the show,” Meszaros says, even if the rehearsals were so intense that they cost her two toenails.

Unlike the other girls, though, Meszaros was playing a pariah. “I love a flawed human,” she says. “I love kind of being able to dive into the psyche of someone that maybe some people find awful.”

It wasn’t hard for Meszaros to feel empathy for Lisbeth. Her character has roots in a rural West Virginia congregation famed for their serpent handling rituals, where worshippers handle live snakes to prove their faith. Lisbeth’s Stephen King-esque arc kicks off when her dad dies and she and her mentally ill mother move to a new town to start over. Their bad luck follows.

On some level, Meszaros could relate. “My parents divorced when I was a baby, and so at my dad’s house, I was raised Christian, and at my mom’s house, she was just more spiritual,” she says. “I went through a dark period where I didn’t [believe]. I just kind of abandoned it all, which is very Lisbeth.” Her own experienced gave her a bit of a blueprint for the character: “I [kept] that feeling of like a hole left over from her world being turned upside down after her dad died, and just what it does to someone when you don't have some sort of faith, and you don’t really believe in anything. That desperation.”

Gen Z shares that desperation. Research shows that young people are plagued by mental health crises at higher rates than any previous generation. And although experts today differ on whether there’s an actual religious revival among Gen Z, there’s no denying that the way young people approach religion is rapidly evolving.

Meszaros’s feed is divided about the show, even before its premiere: “People are gonna love it or hate it,” she says, laughing. But she’s mostly just excited for people to see it, even though it’s coming out too late to inspire Body-themed Halloween costumes.

“I kind of wish people could be Lisbeth,” she says with a sigh. “But maybe next year.”

#3538. 'Ocarina of Time' for Switch 2 Might Already Have a Weird Glitch

Thursday is a big day for Zelda fans. That's when the remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time officially launches on Switch 2, marking the first major linear (i.e., non-open-world) 3D Zelda game since the 2016 Twilight Princess remake on Wii U. I, for one, have been waiting for this day for years. I loved the N64 original and the 3DS remake, so to have the chance to play a modern take on the definitive Zelda is so exciting—that is, if it actually runs as it should.

I stumbled upon this interesting post on X from Austin John Plays, a YouTuber with a host of Zelda coverage. According to Austin John Plays, Ocarina of Time already ships with a weird glitch that won't necessarily break your experience, but which may slow it down for a while, and perhaps even confuse players into thinking something is wrong with their game or their console.

As his post explains, if you're playing the physical copy of Ocarina of Time, and it's the first game you've ever played on your Switch 2—maybe you got one of those fancy new Zelda anniversary consoles and want to break it in properly?—you may run into glaring performance issues: The game may freeze, your controller may stop working, and the FPS may drop to single digits.

Luckily, Austin John Plays says the fix is easy: just wait. Eventually, your game will boot back to the title screen. When it does, don't try to play right away. Instead, close the game, restart your Switch 2, then try relaunching Ocarina of Time. Austin John Plays advises you may need to repeat this process two or three times, but after that, you shouldn't continue to run into issues. I wouldn't be surprised if Nintendo releases a patch right away for this glitch if it turns out to be as widespread as this post implies.

However, seeing as the game doesn't come out until tomorrow, there's something you can do to prevent it. Austin John Plays thinks the bug only impacts Switch 2 consoles that haven't run other games before. If you've had your console a while, you're likely set. But if you just bought the 40th anniversary Zelda edition of the Switch 2, you might not have had a chance to run a game on it yet. As such, download a game from the e-shop—even a free demo—just to get the system running. Hopefully, that will be enough to circumvent the glitch, and prevent issues when Ocarina of Time launches tomorrow.

Awards Season will be here before we know it, and there are already a few projects getting early buzz. One of them is the new A24 movie Club Kid, which stars Jordan Firstman, who also wrote and directed the acclaimed dramedy. Club Kid is my favorite movie of the year, largely thanks to its heart and the authentic representation of queer nightlife. I had to ask him about bringing those sequences together, and he got honest about why the club scenes (especially in the darkroom) went so hard.

Club Kid is a new LGBTQ+ movie, and as a gay man myself I was immediately take by how real those club scenes felt. As you can see in the video above, I asked Firstman about how he brought those sequences together, especially the scene where his character Peter has sex with a woman in a club darkroom. He told me:

I got in like a fight with someone because they're like 'Darkrooms like didn't come until like 2019.' And I was like, 'They definitely came in 2016.' I like remember like at least they were popping up in New York, but I remember going to like a sex party in 2015 or 16. But I say like the Berlin-ification of New York, mama, in the movie. But I do feel like, you know, Chris Cruse started this party Spotlight in LA, which was kind of like our first like LA introduction into darkrooms. It was a cool moment for queer people because we like weren't like doing that publicly before really in my generation. So yeah, it was important for me to like show that and show what goes down at the club

For those unfamiliar, darkrooms have a long history in queer history. They're typically pitch black rooms in bars where patrons can engage in anonymous sexual activity. They were shown in the media dating back to Harvey Fierstein's Torch Song Trilogy back in 1988, and Jordan Firstman's movie brings them back to the big screen in a more modern context.

In a drug-fueled haze Peter has sex with a woman early in Club Kid in a darkroom, and that unknowingly gets her pregnant. That's how his son Arlo ends up dropped at his door over a decade later, with the party promoter suddenly forced to become a parent to a child he never knew existed.

There's been a ton of chatter lately about LGBTQ+ movies actually starring queer actors, and Jordan Firstman was able to bring a very real, niche experience to the mainstream as the director, writer, and star of Club Kid. Later in our conversation he spoke more about the way the darkroom scene was shot, telling me:

But I think also showing it in a elegant way, like I really love how that scene is shot. I think it's like very classy. And it's not, it's like, I don't know. It just it's like beautiful, but still it does, a dark room does feel that way.

He's not wrong. The darkroom scene isn't a sexually explicit scene, despite the setting. Instead it uses light in a fascinating way that's immersive, but not overly graphic. The audience sees Peter decide to have sex with a woman at the behest of a guy he's interested in, and it's that union that serves as the catalyst for the movie's primary story.

The authentic way the darkroom is shown, as well as the unique chaos of the nightlife as a whole, instantly brings Club Kid into a specific time and place. The movie shows what the club scene is like for LGBTQ+ folks, warts and all. While it's a world not all moviegoers might understand, the specificity of Firstman's work ends up making the story universal.

Club Kid is in select theaters now as part of the 2026 movie release list, and will be getting more screenings as the month goes on. I laughed, I cried, and I loved how real the movie felt as a member of the queer community.

What if you could take the same movie that swept up the entire globe in hype and watch it all over again ... but, this time, with a little extra #brandsynergy? That was the (admittedly cynical) gimmick behind "Avengers Endgame: Encore," the buzzy re-release that ruled the box office again earlier this year and will no doubt do so on the streaming charts in the days and weeks ahead. The blockbuster, at one time considered the capstone to the grand Marvel Cinematic Universe experiment, now comes with a whopping four minutes of new footage meant to tie things together with the upcoming "Avengers: Doomsday." That includes a noticeably altered ending and new post-credits scenes, all of which will serve as a bridge to the multiverse-focused chaos to come.

That means you can expect to get your Infinity Vision on (no, we're still not quite sure what that means) with just a snap of your fingers, now with added scenes and new color grading.

Party like it's 2019, folks, because everything old is (slightly) new again. Back then, we had no inkling of a certain novel virus making its way across the globe, we had not yet had the privilege of seeing Palpatine somehow return in "Star Wars: The Rise of Skywalker," and we certainly didn't think the MCU could ever top its grand finale of Earth's Mightiest Heroes assembling against the Mad Titan Thanos. Less than a decade later, Marvel Studios is hoping to keep the hype train going on the road to "Doomsday" with "Avengers Endgame: Encore."

In short, it's a good time to be a Disney fan ... and a Disney stockholder, for that matter. For those looking for an excuse to revel in some nostalgia, "Endgame: Encore" fits the bill. "Avengers: Doomsday" will finally arrive in theaters on December 18, 2026.

#3535. Meghan Markle’s Mother, Doria Ragland, Helped the FBI Investigate Thomas Markle, Meghan’s Father

New details have emerged regarding the arrest of Thomas Markle, Meghan Markle’s father, on charges of possessing child pornography. According to People magazine, Doria Ragland, mother of the Duchess of Sussex, assisted the FBI and played a key role in identifying her ex-husband, leading to his arrest in Florida on November 6. (Thomas Markle has previously denied any possession of child sex abuse material.)

The Sun also reports that she played a central role, one that, as the outlet writes, involved reviewing a series of photographs obtained by federal agents. Ragland was reportedly shown a series of blurred images depicting alleged sexual abuse of minors, and she identified the man in the photographs as her ex-husband. Markle, now 82, was reportedly between 30 and 40 years old at the time the photos were taken, during a period when he may not have even been married to Ragland yet (they were married from 1979 to 1987, while Meghan was born in 1981). Markle was also reportedly recognized by another person, whose name has not been disclosed. This person is said to be a witness who spent a great deal of time with him around the time the photos were allegedly taken.

The photographs in question were found among the material seized from a storage unit that Markle rented in Los Angeles. According to statements from the Department of Justice, this was a space where the man allegedly stored “child sexual abuse material, including photographs depicting himself with minor girls.” The FBI took action following the suspicious discovery of alleged child pornography at Markle’s home in Cebu, Philippines, where he lived for a year—until last May—before returning to the United States due to health issues. After a court appearance in Tampa following his arrest, he was released on the condition that he remain at the Maravida Senior Living nursing home in Lakeland, Florida—the same facility from which he had been taken into custody.

The investigation was initiated by Thomas Markle Jr., whom Meghan’s father had with his first wife, Roslyn Loveless, along with another daughter, Samantha. The man told police that he had found a great deal of compromising material among the family mementos, which was why he had filed a complaint against his father. Markle Jr. was initially considered a person of interest by investigators, with Juanito Victor Remulla, secretary of the Philippine Department of the Interior, saying, “There are signs that point that the son is involved in the crime as well.” However, the Philippine police have since publicly apologized to Markle Jr. after interviews with his fiancée and others in his circle reportedly exonerated him.

Meanwhile, following Ragland’s intervention, Meghan is also reportedly willing to cooperate with the FBI in the investigation into her father, a source told The Sunday Times. The Duchess of Sussex no longer has any relationship with her father, and—as was revealed when the story about the alleged child pornography surfaced—it is precisely for this reason. “I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father, and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them,” Meghan said in a statement on the matter. “I trusted that the authorities were doing the same for other families.” She continued: “Although the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine, my sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children.” This is a story with many unresolved issues. More will be known after the first hearing, the date of which has not yet been set.

#3534. 10 Shows Like 'Phony' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

What if you knew your mom wasn't really your mom, but no one believed you? That's the improbable but entertaining premise of Hulu's Phony, which stars Sam Nivola as a teenager who wakes up from a car accident and quickly comes to believe that his mother (Friday Night Lights' Connie Britton) is an imposter. Of course, no one believes him. I'm not sure I believe him, but it'll be pretty boring if it turns out that he just had a really bad concussion the whole time.

It's a coming-of-age drama and a surreal mystery with hints of comedy, and though it borrows elements from other shows, it stands apart for the skill with which it blends everything together. While you wait to see how the story plays out, here are 10 more twisted mysteries to stream now.

A twisty-turny (and well-reviewed) bit of fake identity folderol, Apple Cider Vinegar stars Kaitlyn Dever as Belle Gibson, a real-life Australian cancer survivor (except not really!) With a cheeky sense of humor and a willingness to distort reality, the show follows the wellness influencer as she fakes multiple cancer diagnoses in order to better market her alternative, MAHA-esque app and remedies to the unwitting. As her livelihood comes under threat, her lies grow more elaborate. Stream Apple Cider Vinegar on Netflix.

Alia Shawkat stars here as Dory Sief, an aimless millennial who decides, after seeing a missing-person poster for a college acquaintance, that she's going to make it her purpose to track her down—with the extremely begrudging support of her friends. But neither Chantal nor her disappearance are anything like what Dory expects. The show shifts focus from season to season. Initially a darkly comic take on a Nancy Drew-style mystery, it later finds the gang desperate to cover up a mostly unintentional murder, and getting in deeper each season. It's a funny, smart, and weird and shares talent with Phony in the form of writer/producer Anthony King, who serves as co-showrunner on the new series. Stream Search Party on Netflix.

This one's largely about adults, so it skips the coming-of-age angle central to Phony, but it has a quirky mystery, gaslighting, and a protagonist whose sanity is questioned by just about everyone all the same. This fun and very loose adaptation of the 1989 Tom Hanks film finds Keke Palmer's Samira and Jack Whitehall's Rob moving back to his impossibly safe and tidy hometown. Their house happens to be across the street from a dilapidated Victorian eyesore that may or may not have been the location of a murder a couple of decades before—a murder of a girl who made the mistake of trying to get away. As Samira adjusts to new motherhood and life on the cul-de-sac, she learns that even the nicest of her neighbors have secrets, and comes to suspect that her husband knows more about the missing girl than he's letting on. Stream The 'Burbs on Peacock.

When pretty, popular girl Kate Wallis (Olivia Holt) goes missing without a trace in 1993, awkward Jeanette Turner (Chiara Aurelia) steps in to fill the gap, modeling herself after Kate, working her way into the missing girl's social circle, and getting close with her boyfriend. That's all going great until Kate reappears two years later, accusing Jeanette of having witnessed the events around her disappearance and keeping quiet. Whoops. There's even more going on, as the show shifts back and forth between 1993, 1994, and 1995 to slowly reveal the missing pieces. Stream Cruel Summer on Hulu.

Based on a Harlan Coben novel, Fool Me Once is a bit more of a political thriller than a coming-of-age thing, but we're still in "what the hell is up with my family?" territory: Michelle Keegan plays Maya Stern, a former special ops pilot dealing with the murder of her husband, whom she then impossibly catches playing with their daughter on a nanny cam. The resulting mystery ties into the earlier death of her sister and leads to a web of conspiracy involving her husband's family and a shady pharmaceutical company. Stream Fool Me Once on Netflix.

A vibe match more than anything else, this dark and twisty mystery with a slightly surreal sense of humor also features a single mom who is definitely not what she appears to be. Kim Mo-mi (Lee Han-byeol, initially), the Mask Girl of the title, is a uniquely complicated woman; she always wanted to be a K-Pop idol, but it was always made clear to her that she's not nearly pretty enough for that kind of stardom. So, in order to fill that void, she's got a side hustle. On top of her boring office job, she puts on a blonde wig and a mask to perform as a camgirl for anonymous men. It's a means to express herself creatively and sexually with a level of control—until a mistake causes her to lose that control, a co-worker discovers her secret life, and desperation leads to murder. The show shifts perspectives continually, feeling most like Phony when it focuses on Mo-mi's daughter. Stream Mask Girl on Netflix.

Flipping things around a bit, albeit in a similar "am I just being paranoid?" vein, The Girlfriend deals with a mom who may or may not be freaking out for no reason. Starring Robin Wright as Laura Sanderson, a wealthy art gallery owner in London whose son (Laurie Davidson) brings home a new, working-class girlfriend, Cherry Laine (Olivia Cooke)—immediately strikes Laura as not-our-kind. But is there more to it? Can someone with the name "Cherry Laine" truly be trusted? There's definitely something off, and we're kept guessing as to whether or not this is the story of a dangerous con artist or an overbearing mom—or maybe a little of each. Stream The Girlfriend on Prime Video.

Coming from Irish playwright and Derry Girls creator Lisa McGee, this show eschews the relatively subtle dark comedy of Phony for something much more gloriously surreal. Three high school friends from Belfast reunite after learning that an estranged bestie has died unexpectedly—except that maybe she didn't; a mixed blessing given that they all have secrets that they were hoping would be buried with the maybe departed. Now they're off to investigate the mystery of the murder(?), which turns into a hunt for the friend that they only thought they knew, while inadvertently revealing plenty of secrets of their own. The tone is all over the place in a way that somehow works, with flashes of sincerity balancing out the comedy. Stream How to Get to Heaven From Belfast on Netflix.

Shin Hye-sun offers up a phenomenal performance as Sarah Kim (well: sort of), a wealthy businesswoman who is discovered, at the series' opening, under a sewer grate. The police detective charged to investigate quickly finds inconsistencies in the woman's identity, and after interviewing Sarah's friend and business associate, comes to feel that neither woman is exactly (or anything, like she seems. Though it takes itself more seriously than Phony, it's still an addictively twisty mystery built around a constructed identity. Stream The Art of Sarah on Netflix.

There's a lot going on in this steamy, telenovela-esque drama. Camila Román (Carolina Miranda) finally meets Fernando Castell (Rodolfo Salas), a Tinder match, in Las Vegas, and things get very hot very quickly—he's everything he seemed to be and then some. If anything, she's the sketchy one: a dancer, not a nurse as she said, and with a possessive ex following her around. Still, it's all going great until she decides to surprise Fernando after he flies back to Colombia (which: never do that), and gets a totally different dude when she asks for him at his work. And that's just the beginning! Stream Fake Profile on Netflix.

Spoilers for Season 3 of Nobody Wants This are ahead! Read at your own risk, and stream the series with a Netflix subscription.

Season 3 of Nobody Wants This was all about Joanne and Noah getting engaged and eventually married amid Joanne converting to Judaism. However, I’d argue that Sasha and Morgan’s story, and specifically Sasha’s whole situation with her and Esther, played an equally important and big role in this installment that dropped on the 2026 TV schedule. Now, as the series prepares to go into Season 4, two of the stars joked about Timothy Simons, who plays Sasha, taking over as the lead. However, here’s the thing: I actually think that should happen.

Now, I’ll admit it, my worst Nobody Wants This fear had to do with Sasha and Morgan getting together. However, when it happened in Season 3, I couldn’t deny how entertaining their arc was. Specifically, their episode in New York is a standout of the season, and that’s what began this conversation that led to a joke about Simons leading the show. Here’s what Joanne actress Kristen Bell had to say about Morgan and Sasha's trip to the Big Apple during an FYC event in LA (via THR):

The whole New York episode I think is one of the best episodes of television that has ever been made. I was standing up watching the cut.

Bell also said that her “body was aching for them to be together.” Meanwhile, Justine Lupe, who plays Morgan, said she was “live texting” Timothy Simons about “how hot” he was in the episode. That’s how we get to this idea of making Sasha the lead of Nobody Wants This, because the Frozen actress said:

I was like, ‘You guys, Tim is a romantic lead.’ I said it, everyone’s gonna know it. We’re gonna need security on set next year. He’s the lead of the show now — somebody’s gotta tell Adam [Brody].

Again, while I don’t really want Morgan and Sasha to be endgame, and I often have weird feelings about their romantic relationship, I see the potential here. Their chemistry is undeniable, they are so funny together, and their friendship is genuinely so special. Meanwhile, Sasha’s whole situation with Esther, especially now that she knows about what happened in New York, ups the drama exponentially. To me, the story writes itself, and it’d make perfect sense if Sasha’s love life became the focal point of Nobody Wants This.

Plus, Joanne and Noah are married. Their origin story is done. They’re an established couple, and while I always want to see them, their romance feels like it won’t (and probably shouldn’t) feature the drama it did in earlier seasons. So, by making Sasha the lead, they can stay a happy couple, while he dives into the drama of figuring out his marriage with Esther and his relationship with Morgan.

So, now that we know Season 4 of Nobody Wants This is coming, I hope this dream becomes a reality. Sasha is such a wonderful character, he’s in quite the mess with Morgan and Esther, and I’m certain that his love life would make for a brilliant season of TV. So, let’s make it happen.

#3532. One Of 2025's Biggest TV Shows Is Now A Box Office Success As Well

One of the biggest breakout TV shows of 2025 has now found success at the box office. The "Heated Rivalry" Season 1 finale ended last year with a barnburner and the show's popularity has only continued to grow since then. While fans eagerly await Season 2, Regal Cinemas partnered with HBO Max and Crave to bring the first season to theaters. Fans turned up to see Shane and Ilya on the silver screen.

As "Godzilla Minus Zero" ruled the box office with a $30.5 million opening, much further down on the weekend's chart, "Heated Rivalry" pulled in a respectable $1.4 million on just over 1,000 screens, making for a solid $1,409 per-screen average. That's certainly not bad for a show that anyone could stream right now from the comfort of home with the price of a subscription they likely already pay for. But this speaks to the rabid fanbase that has developed around the romantic hockey show.

"Heated Rivalry" focuses on two rival hockey stars at the top of their game who develop feelings for each other, complicating their careers and the sport's expectations. It's based on the book series by Rachel Reid. Hudson Williams and Connor Storrie lead the cast as Shane Hollander and Ilya Rozanov, respectively.

To say that the show took off in a way that surprised people would be a bit of an understatement. It dominated HBO Max's charts and became a downright cultural sensation. So much so that a former NHL player hopes "Heated Rivalry" can change pro hockey culture. It made a real impact.

For Regal, Crave, and all involved, the millions the show makes in its theatrical release is a cherry on top of the sundae. Regal is charging $9.99 for two episode blocks of the series, which fans can watch in order if they choose to go three times to watch all six episodes.

This is just the latest example of an already successful TV show finding success on the big screen. Netflix's "Stranger Things" finale was a huge hit for theaters even if it didn't impact the box office, as those tickets were for "concessions vouchers" and not actual tickets. But lots of people still turned up nonetheless. "Doctor Who" has also had multiple theatrical events for various episodes over the years, sticking in the sci-fi realm.

More recently, an unlikely savior emerged at the box office in 2024, with two very different shows doing meaningful business. "Demon Slayer: Kimetsu no Yaiba — To the Hashira Training," which is just several episodes of the TV show fashioned into a feature, helped establish anime as a true, blue way to sell a lot of tickets. At the same time, the faith-based series "The Chosen" was finding lots of success by screening episodes in theaters. All together, those episodes have grossed more than $100 million worldwide.

Not every show is a good fit for this sort of thing but the right show at the right time can certainly benefit from catering to more hardcore fans. Meanwhile, "Heated Rivalry" Season 2 is in the works, but that's just the tip of the iceberg. Deadline recently reported that Season 3 is also being filmed, along with a movie. So there's much for fans to look forward to.

#3531. 7 Greatest Live-Service Games Killed Before Their Time, Ranked

At one point or another, most of us have enjoyed a live-service game. Likewise, many of us have been burned when a game publisher decided the revenue no longer justified the ongoing expenses of maintaining an always-on experience. Suddenly, we had nothing to show for our time except memories. It was a bit like paying for tickets to a ballgame, watching the athletes do their thing, and then leaving with a smile. Except with the live-service game, we knew that was the end. We could never go back next year.

Plenty of games reach that point after giving off warning signs. Maybe they never got big enough to last. Maybe they became huge, but then they faded away rapidly as audiences lost interest. Some live-service games were killed before their time, however. They deserved better, and we’re here to remember them.

The extended Final Fantasy franchise has included a number of live-service games. Despite the brand recognition, those efforts haven’t always fared well, even when they should have. For me, Mobius Final Fantasy is the best example of unmet potential.

First launched in Japan on June 4, 2015, the game lasted just shy of five years in that region and less than four in North America. It was originally a mobile-only title, noteworthy in part because of the involvement of producer Yoshinori Kitase and scenario supervisor Kazushige Nojima. The two Final Fantasy veterans helped assemble a compelling new take on the classic original Final Fantasy, featuring Garland and blank-slate Warrior of Light characters, among others.

The game reached Steam in November 2016 in Japan, and arrived in North America the following February. Not a lot needed to change for that port, because the game had always been beautiful and deep, despite the gacha system humming away at its core. Unfortunately, Square Enix didn’t see the return on investment that it wanted. Things took a sad turn when a controversial job class (named after Tidus, hero of Final Fantasy 10) alienated free-to-play people like me, who enjoyed seeing how far we could get without spending actual money.

Mobius Final Fantasy delivered two full acts packed full of content that I would be happy to enjoy today. But when the servers went down, so did the possibility of playing the game in any form.

The team at Wildlight Entertainment, consisting of veterans who previously worked on Titanfall and Apex Legends, built something special with Highguard. In its first week, it had nearly 100,000 players battling at once. However, those numbers fell off sharply, enough so that studio backer Tencent pulled funding, according to a Bloomberg report. The studio experienced layoffs and servers shut down within weeks of launch.

Built on Unreal Engine 5, Highguard blended a variety of genres, including first-person shooting, base destruction, tactical combat, resource gathering, and gear upgrading. As Wardens, players had to balance all of those activities to thrive in a world that memorably blended high fantasy elements with modern weaponry.

Highguard quickly shed players for numerous reasons we may never fully understand, but a few of the more apparent ones were lackluster progression, limited voice communication, and unforgiving multiplayer matches that required team cohesion from players who were still learning the ropes. A final patch, released shortly before the game’s demise, fixed many of the issues with progression. By then, however, the die was already cast.

Sony has a full stable of all-star characters it might profitably rely on to drive interest in a live-service release. Something like 2012’s PlayStation All-Stars Battle Royale, a PlayStation-flavored riff on the Smash Bros. formula, proves it. But when the publisher released a vehicular arena brawler, it ditched that heritage and went with something fresh. The gamble ultimately seems to have failed.

Destruction AllStars featured 16 human racers who drove wild cars through unique environments. Instead of staying behind the wheel the entire time, drivers could abandon their rides and use parkour moves to navigate the arena while collecting items. They could even hijack rival cars when they were ready to drive again.

Players appreciated the satisfying driving elements, which were designed by individuals who previously worked at Bizarre Creations (best known over the years for driving games like Project Gotham Racing and Blur). However, players didn’t love running around on foot, nor did they appreciate the repetition and the microtransactions, a frequent point of contention with live-service games.

Technically, Destruction AllStars is still operating at the moment, but the game has already been removed from digital storefronts and the trickle of remaining server support will halt on Nov. 25, 2026. Get that game a coffin.

Square Enix has sometimes struggled to keep its live-service games afloat, though it keeps trying and continues to produce experiences that reward the efforts, such as Final Fantasy 14 and Final Fantasy Record Keeper. Sadly, Marvel’s Avengers was not one of those successes.

When the time came to build a live-service game around the white-hot superhero IP, Square Enix had then-internal studios Crystal Dynamics and Eidos handle the honors. The teams built a spectacular single-player campaign focused on Ms. Marvel as she reassembled the team of powerful heroes. For that side of things, the developers knocked it out of the park.

The multiplayer component fared poorly in comparison. Players found themselves completing repetitive tasks for minor enhancements that yielded minimal results. Microtransactions and cosmetic outfits didn’t delight anyone, especially when added on top of a retail package that already cost as much as other blockbuster games. Marvel’s Avengers also had the misfortune of releasing around the time of the COVID-19 pandemic, when bugs that prevented it from working as intended were more difficult to address. It was a perfect storm that led to a highly imperfect game. Square Enix lost millions on the project and sold its North American development studios shortly thereafter.

Paragon’s death hurts more than most because it didn’t do anything wrong.

Launched in 2016, Paragon was a 3D MOBA with a dedicated, engaged community. It sported gorgeous 3D visuals in line with third-person action games, despite its multiplayer online focus. Elevation played a significant role, allowing players to stage surprising ambushes in vertical spaces. And the heroes were memorable, with flashy moves that gave the game a personality all its own. Its dedicated community loved it.

Unfortunately, players at large didn’t respond as meaningfully to Paragon as they did to a separate project from the same publisher, a little game called Fortnite. As that other title began raking in revenue, Epic reassigned its development talent to the project that had already proven it had the ability to smash through revenue projections. With internal competition like that, Paragon never really stood a chance.

A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

We owe Turtle Rock Studios gratitude for its work as a co-developer on the original Left 4 Dead, one of the most memorable zombie games ever made. It worked closely with Valve on that game, and even became part of the company for a period. Eventually, though, the two companies separated. The next project from the team was Evolve, and expectations were high.

In Evolve, rather than facing off against zombie hordes, players hunted one powerful monster, controlled by a separate human. The asymmetrical design felt fresh, and publisher 2K Games shipped millions of copies. But while players were enthusiastic about the premise, they didn’t love the title’s monetization. Getting everything available to buy at launch increased the price by more than $130, on top of $60 for the base game.

It’s a shame executives focused so heavily on microtransactions, because the core gameplay held a lot of promise. That said, matches could grow repetitive, especially if the player controlling the monster proved too capable of hiding until its strength matured. Even so, ongoing balance tweaks might have easily salvaged the less exciting aspects of the design and allowed Evolve to, well, evolve. Turtle Rock and 2K relaunched the game as a free-to-play experience in 2016 before dedicated servers finally folded in 2018. A 2022 attempt to revive it with fresh server support went nowhere, and there have been no signs of life since July 2023.

At launch, Gotham City Impostors offered a fantastic shooting experience. Developed by Monolith Productions (the studio behind Middle-earth: Shadow of Mordor), the lively shooter cast players as the Bats and the Jokerz. The rival street gangs sped through outdoor arenas on skates, used grappling hooks to reach vantage points, glided between buildings, and more.

Combat was fast and frenzied, with knockoff versions of two beloved DC characters that had more than enough personality to carry a game. I had a lot of fun with it, even if I wasn’t especially good at it, and a lot of other players shared that experience.

Unfortunately, the game not only ended before its time, but launched ahead of its time and with bad infrastructure in place. Players likely would have responded more favorably if it had arrived in the middle of the superhero craze, or if matches weren’t so difficult to arrange, and it might also have endured if the GameSpy servers it relied on didn’t go away in 2014. That’s a lot of bad luck for a game that otherwise might still be around today.

On the positive side, Gotham City Impostors fans have found ways to continue playing online, with a dedicated group chat on Discord to organize events. But for most potential players, the game is just mostly dead.

Every big publisher was chasing forever games, until reality set in

For many of us, web browsing involves juggling dozens of tabs at once, and it's easy for important pages to get lost in the chaos. Now, Firefox has introduced something I think could help us multi-taskers: a "Mini Window." As highlighted by ZDNET's Jack Wallen, this new Firefox feature works like picture-in-picture overlays for videos—only here, that PiP displays a website.

"[Mini Window] lets you move a tab, or a selected section of a page, into a compact window that stays on top of your other windows while you browse," runs Mozilla's official blurb. "It's useful when you're multitasking and need to keep a few sources of information in view at once: Reference docs, a chat, a video call, a form you're filling out." As such, Mini Window doesn't necessarily replace running tabs side-by-side; rather, you can prioritize one tab in a full-size window, while keeping another page in view at all times.

This is a feature that's still in its early stages, and right now you can only get it in the "Nightly" version of Firefox, a very early beta version of the browser. Mozilla says it will push the feature to the full version of the browser later this month.

If you want to try this out as soon as possible, first install Firefox Nightly on your Mac or PC. Once up and running, you can launch Mini Window by right-clicking on a tab header and choosing Move Tab > Move to Mini Window. The tab shrinks and drops down to the lower right corner by default, staying on top of all other windows (not just Firefox). You can then scroll through the page and follow links as normal in the Mini Window—any links set to open in a new tab (manually or automatically) will launch in the main Firefox view, not the window overlay.

By dragging the title bar around, you can put your Mini Window anywhere you want on screen, and you can change its size by dragging the edges of the window too—so it doesn't necessarily have to be all that "mini." Firefox hides all buttons by default—including forward, backward, and refresh buttons, together with the address bar and buttons for closing the window or putting it back as a normal tab—though they appear when you hover over the Mini Window.

I'm finding the feature most useful when writing up articles where I need to refer to something else already on the web (so almost all of them), but there are a host of ways this can be used. It's particularly handy on a small laptop, where you don't necessarily have the screen space to put two tabs side by side, or when running a lower-priority window (like checking a social media site while reading an important document). No doubt, Firefox will continue to refine and improve the feature as it makes its way to the stable version of the browser, and it feels like something other browsers (looking at you, Google Chrome) might adopt as well in the near future. Eventually, using Mini Windows might become as common as opening up a long row of tabs.

#3529. Jensen Huang Did: Have an Ill-Advised Affair. He Did Not: Wear Vintage Saint Laurent.

Jensen Huang, the president, cofounder, and CEO of Nvidia is making headlines this week. Not for developments in AI technology—for all the wrong reasons.

On Sunday, Nvidia said it had opened an investigation into Huang regarding his relationship with a woman whom intelligence agencies have said is a Chinese spy. (The Chinese government has denied that the woman is a spy.) That same day, Huang sent an email to the company’s employees apologizing for being unfaithful to his wife and for “hurting” her and their children with the affair. He also apologized to his colleagues and the company’s board and shareholders. “My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility,” he wrote. “I am fully committed to Nvidia and will work to earn back your confidence.” He said he’d cooperate with the investigation opened by Nvidia’s board of directors. “I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America’s national security,” he wrote. “I am proud and grateful to be an American.”

The news of Huang’s affair filled X with memes about Chinese spies and mistresses in a variety of configurations. By Monday evening, Huang had reached the fashion world’s stylish netizens: The Instagram account @hidden.ny, an anonymous digital mood board and cultural platform, posted a series of images of Huang in a studded leather jacket. The caption read, “NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang in Hedi Slimane SLP Studded Leather Jacket after admitting to affair with alleged Chinese spy.”

It’s well-known that Huang is a leather-jacket enthusiast, and he is seldom seen in public without one. In July Sotheby’s auctioned one of his pre-worn jackets, this one by Tom Ford. The auction house originally estimated its sale price between $40,000 and $60,000, but it sold for a whooping $960,000.

Despite Huang’s penchant for a black-leather moment, it appears that he was, in fact, not wearing the Saint Laurent jacket as previously shared by Hidden and a variety of other accounts on both Instagram and X. A quick run through an AI image detector debunked Huang’s being a “Slimaniac”—what Slimane’s fervent fans often call themselves—at least in this particular case. SynthID, the detector created by Google DeepMind to identify AI-generated or enhanced media by OpenAI, Google, Kakao, and, of course, Nvidia, detected that the images posted by Hidden and other users online had been generated or edited with OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT. To burst the bubble even further, it appears that the images used as the base for this particular edit weren’t taken following the disclosure of Huang’s affair, but from a trip to South Korea in June. (He was wearing a Dior jacket by Jonathan Anderson then.)

Just last week, a Free Press reporter went viral on X for posting an image she had not disclosed as enhanced by AI as part of her election-night reporting, which was also debunked by VF. It’s not necessarily fun being the AI fashion police, and the stakes of netizens giving Huang the fashion-meme treatment versus a reporter using AI to illustrate a point are not the same. But as the use of AI becomes harder to detect, disclosure has become paramount.

Apologies to the menswear crowd for ruining the fantasy—but did you all really want Huang to be a certified “Hedi boy” after this news? As one comment under the original post read, Huang might be the “first person in history to have negative aura wearing archive Hedi.”

#3528. The Rings Of Power Season 3 Finally Solves A Major Lord Of The Rings Lore Mystery

Spoilers are never late (nor are they early; they arrive precisely when they mean to), so don't read ahead without first watching the Season 3 premiere episodes for "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power."

"The Rings of Power" Season 3 is here, and it finally feels like the series we were promised from the start (i.e. the one that showrunners J. D. Payne and Patrick McKay wanted to make all along). At this point, the introductions are done and the show's characters, lore, and locations have all been established. Most importantly, the very silly mysteries around the identity of certain characters all disappear in the first four episodes of Season 3. Because of this, we now know that Gandalf (Daniel Weyman) and Sauron (Charlie Vickers) are a big part of the story, that the insufferable kid Theo (Tyroe Muhafidin) is actually a Ringwraith, and the truth about Ciarán Hinds' Dark Wizard.

As you might recall, the reveal that Weyman's "The Stranger" is actually Gandalf didn't mean all that much in Season 2, given how Gandalf-coded the character was from the get-go. By comparison, the Dark Wizard has been quite Saruman-coded from the start, be it the color of his beard or the way he calls Gandalf an old friend. Yet, the notion of him being Saruman has never made much sense, given how blatantly evil he is. After all, it's meant to be a huge shock when Saruman aligns with Sauron in "The Lord of the Rings," so the idea that he was known as the "Dark Wizard" for centuries would seem to undermine that.

Thankfully, "The Rings of Power" has now confirmed that the Dark Wizard is really Pallando the Blue Wizard, not Saruman.

While Sauron is very much the focus of "The Rings of Power" Season 3 (something that's been praised in early reactions to the show's latest batch of episodes), Pallando is an important part of the story. Except, Pallando doesn't exactly ally himself with Sauron out of greed, ambition, or evil the way that Saruman does in "The Lord of the Rings" (nor does he seem all that afraid of the Dark Lord). Instead, he's already murdered his fellow Blue Wizard and Istar companion Alatar prior to his first appearance on the series.

Pallando's betrayal, it turns out, was an act so malevolent that it turned the once-green realm of Rhûn into a desolated wasteland. The wizard isn't entirely repentant by the time "The Rings of Power" takes place, but he does acknowledge that it's his fault the region has turned to desert, and he seeks specifically to fix it. Hence, his submission to Sauron and the power of Mordor represents a desperate last attempt at correcting his greatest mistake.

All we know from J.R.R. Tolkien's source material is that the Blue Wizards failed their mission and their fates are unknown when "The Lord of the Rings" begins (although they're presumed dead). In other words, "The Rings of Power" can resolve a major "Lord of the Rings" mystery by revealing what ultimately became of Pallando in particular. This should also make Gandalf's mission in Season 3 all the more interesting, as he might yet have a chance at saving the Blue Wizard. Either way, there's much we've yet to learn about the character.

"The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" is currently streaming on Prime Video.
