When you’re lucky enough to have the kind of successful career that Daniel Radcliffe has had, adoring fans come with the territory. Of course, the 37-year-old will always be the original Harry Potter (even though the new series is coming quickly on the 2026 TV schedule), and he’ll always have people quoting the Harry Potter movies and books to him. The actor was just asked about that experience, and his answer lines up with Keira Knightley’s take on it.

Radcliffe was just asked if there’s a quote from one of his movies that’s recited to him the most during an interview with People. Here’s what he had to say:

Unless you’re doing a very obvious one to me now, it will go over my head. You do a deep cut Harry Potter line to me, I’ll probably look at you very blankly right now, because it’s been a long time.

So, if you’re hoping to impress Radcliffe by quoting something from one of his roles, as he says, it probably will go past him very easily. And to be fair, much of his most famous work was filmed when he was growing up. It’d be like asking someone to remember what you said in class in fifth grade once. Here’s what Keira Knightley said to Heart on the same topic just the other day:

I have not watched Love Actually since the premiere, which was when I was 18. So, I think I’m the person that knows it the least of anybody. I know that people have a particular look on their face and then they say things to me and I know that means they’re quoting Love Actually, but I don’t really know what it is. It means nothing to me.

Wild, right? It’s like everyone knows their most famous work except for them. In Knightley’s defense, she also said she was on the set of Love Actually for a week. And now it’s considered one of the best Christmas movies.

Hey, I wouldn’t rewatch my 18-year-old self either! But it’s still pretty crazy that she has managed to only see it once, considering its widespread popularity. It’s funny that she can tell when people are probably quoting something at her, but she doesn’t quite know what to do or what movie or TV show they are talking about.

While Daniel Radcliffe isn’t going to get most of the Harry Potter quotes you might throw his way, he did point out one he’ll probably get. In his words:

But, I suppose it would be, ‘You’re a wizard, Harry.’ But like, no one’s said that for a long time to be honest. So yeah, I don’t know, but that’s a classic. That one I would be like, ‘That’s from Harry Potter. I recognize that.’

That’s a softball one, for sure. I mean, if he didn’t get that one, I would be a little bit worried about the guy to be honest.

Anyways, it’s definitely an understandable take from both of them, considering they've been working since they were kids and have both dealt with mass fame for most of their lives. It wouldn’t be healthy if they knew every line of their projects either, would it?

These days, Daniel Radcliffe has his own comedy series in The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins and is one of the leading voice stars of Netflix’s new animated movie, Steps, coming out on November 20. Whereas Keira Knightley has just returned to her well-reviewed thriller series, Black Doves for Season 2, which is streaming on Netflix now. I guess you know what to do if you happen to cross paths with them… maybe don’t confuse them with deep-cut quotes you've memorized.

#3526. These Signature Sony Headphones Are Under $200 Ahead of Black Friday

The Sony WH-1000XM6 headphones are the most recent entry in Sony's 1000X series, which has been around since 2016. They're the best over-ear headphones in terms of audio quality currently on the market—but not everyone can (or needs to) drop nearly half a grand on headphones.

The WH-1000XM5 are a generation older and were at the top of their class until they were supplanted by the XM6. On the plus side, by virtue of being older, they're currently discounted to $198 (down from the original $399.99) during Amazon's early Black Friday sale. That 50% off brings it down to the lowest price they've ever reached, according to price-tracking tools, a good deal for premium headphones that still sound incredible, even in 2026.

I have been a loyal customer of the 1000X line for many years; they're my go-to headphones for most activities. The WH-1000XM5 received an "outstanding" review from PCMag for their top-notch audio quality and exceptional audio when using the best-in-class active noise cancellation. The headphones are also well-designed to be comfortable for long listening sessions. The ear controls use tapping and swiping, which isn't my favorite, but it's what all modern headphones are moving toward. There's a companion app that lets you adjust your EQ settings to your liking, including what the swiping and tapping functions do.

These headphones also have a stereo 3.5mm connection, which is perfect for those who want to use a cable and not worry about battery life. And speaking of battery life, Sony says you can expect about 30 hours, but it will vary depending on your use of ANC. They are compatible with AAC, LDAC, and SBC codecs and have multipoint connection, meaning you can pair them with more than one device at the same time.

Personally, I think the value for the money you get with the XM5 for $198 is better than paying full price for the XM6. If you're looking to get ahead of the Black Friday chaos and secure an amazing deal on great headphones, this is it.

#3525. CD Projekt Red Will Use AI to Bring Back Geralt’s Original Voice

Geralt will sound the same 12 years later

In 2019, Jacek Rozenek, the Polish voice actor for Geralt of Rivia in The Witcher games, suffered a stroke that greatly affected his speech. He underwent extensive training to recuperate and regain his ability to act. However, the changes in his voice were still noticeable. To keep the same voice actor in the upcoming DLC Songs of the Past, CD Projekt Red decided to use AI to match his current voice to the original and create the best possible replica.

If you played the English version of The Witcher 3, Doug Cockle will immediately spring to mind when you think of Geralt of Rivia. However, in the game's original version, Geralt is played by Jacek Rozenek, a renowned voice actor with 30 years of experience. CD Projekt has hired Rozenek to play Geralt of Rivia since the original The Witcher game in 2007, and the Polish studio wants him to continue in the role for Songs of the Past. Unfortunately, the actor suffered a stroke in 2019, that, according to Game File, left him unable to speak for months.

After extensive rehabilitation, Rozenek was able to speak again, but his voice was not the same. Stephen Totilo wrote, "it was lower, gruffer," after an interview with the actor. CDPR concluded that while this voice change might work well for an older Geralt in The Witcher 4, it wouldn't blend well with the voice you hear in The Witcher 3. Coming out next year, the Songs of the Past DLC is set in the same era as the main game, and the two are closely connected. This means that fans will hear newly recorded lines and older lines in close succession. To solve this problem, CDPR is working with AI voice cloning company Respeecher.

Respeecher will analyze the 10,000 voice lines recorded for The Witcher 3's base game. It's important to specify that Rozenek will still record all of the lines for Songs of Past, and AI technology will make the changes required to match his original voice. The actor feels very confident in his ability to continue playing Geralt of Rivia and sees this as a good thing. “I can play this role. Of course, it’s very good that this voice will be matched,” he told Game File.

While AI isn't always well received in the world of video games, this might be one of the few cases in which fans will be happy with the developers' decision to use it. Rather than changing voice actors or modifying Geralt's voice altogether, the team found a solution that works for them as well as the original actor. CDPR Localization producer, Mikołaj Szwed, believes that “this is one of those ways where you can use AI ethically, with consent and also to do something good.”

CDPR went from a small Polish studio to a global powerhouse producing games loved by millions of people. Still, the studio cleary does not forget about its origins and its first fans in Poland, who helped CDPR make it to where they are now. With Rozenek's extensive training and rehabilitation, plus the AI assistance, Geralt's voice will sound as close as possible to what it did when The Witcher launched almost twenty years ago.

#3524. Model Alex Consani on Starring in American Horror Story and Pursuing a Career as an Actress

Alex Consani, a mainstay of the runways and one of the most emblematic supermodels of her generation, was notably absent from the spring-summer 2027 shows in September and October, bar a few exceptions. That’s because the California native, 23, has been busy broadening her horizons: Consani is following in the footsteps of many supers before her—including Cindy Crawford, Gisele Bündchen, and Tyra Banks—and trading the runway for the silver screen to pursue a career as an actress. She’s currently starring in American Horror Story: 13, the latest installment of Ryan Murphy’s stylish horror anthology series. Up next, Consani will appear in Molly Gordon’s Peaked and Janicza Bravo’s Preppy.

On Saturday night, Consani joined Demna and his Gucci crew at the 15th annual LACMA Art + Film Gala, where she says she had to do a “Hannah Montana”–style wardrobe change so that her voluminous gown could make it to the step-and-repeat before changing again to “pump it in a side-slit” in the look she wore on the runway in September. Yesterday, the model and newly minted actress Zoomed in after touching back down in New York to break down her film ambitions.

Alex Consani at the 2026 LACMA Art + Film gala.

José Criales-Unzueta: I’m not going to lie, I miss you on the runway. But you’re busy and otherwise occupied!

Alex Consani: I miss being on the runway. I’ve been busy. I’ve been doing a lot of cool projects. You might not see me on the runway, but you’ll definitely see me on the silver screen.

I mean, American Horror Story, all the episodes just came out. I don’t know if you watched, but that was obviously super fun. I also have two projects that are coming out next year, Preppy and Peaked. I’m just really excited. I’m in this era now where I’m kind of shifting into a different space, and it’s exciting to be able to do it specifically with people that understand that. For fashion and film, there are many places where both come together in such a natural way, and I think the LACMA [gala] really is that.

I worked with Sarah Paulson for American Horror Story, and then I sat next to her at LACMA, and we’re both wearing witchy outfits. Sarah and I were looking at Demna and he was like, “Look at my witches,” [laughs]. I love that the fashion world and the film world come together in such a fun way. I think Demna specifically is really big into characters—it’s not just the clothes, but it’s the woman in the clothes.

Did you always intend to go into acting, or was it something that unfolded as you went into fashion?

It’s something that I’ve always been interested in. And I think, in a way, fashion for me has always been acting. I mean, what I enjoy most about fashion is being able to become the character, being able to ask the designer, who is the woman that’s wearing this? It gives me the most gratification when I’m able to build the world around the clothing. [Acting] came naturally, but obviously it was in the back of my head. When I was a kid, I did classes and stuff. With fashion, the time constraints or the time needed to be in fashion is a lot. So I think it was just difficult. I’m blessed to be at a point in my fashion career and also in the [acting] projects that are coming to me, that it isn’t impossible to do both.

I’m putting work into being a better actress. It’s a really exciting endeavor for me, especially considering all the projects that I’ve done that are coming out. There’s a lot of diversity within the projects. I did American Horror Story, which is obviously a horror TV show, and then I have a comedy movie coming out, and then I also have a period piece coming out. It’s fun to be able to bounce around those. And fashion-wise, fab, honestly, the fashion in the films that I’ve done is quite fun. It’s nice because then I get to give my insight as someone in fashion to all the teams, and it feels like a real collaboration, which is my favorite part of any creative job.

Alex Consani with Sarah Paulson (left) and Leslie Grossman (right) in the sixth episode of American Horror Story: 13.

You and I are from the generations that grew up on Ryan Murphy shows.

Coven, for me, is my favorite American Horror Story season by far. What was it like to join the project? Did you audition? Did you get a call?

I’m signed with a really incredible agency that manages that facet of my career, and they expressed that Ryan had some interest in seeing me. I sent in an audition and it fell into place in that way. I definitely was auditioning and going through that script a lot before I got to filming. It was really important for me to really understand the character. And so when I got there, it was obviously super exciting, but I was also a little bit nervous considering the fact that I’m with some of the most seasoned actors in the industry. It was so gratifying and comforting hearing how supportive these women were. My biggest takeaway from this experience is that the reason that those women and those people in Coven are so acclaimed, on top of being incredibly talented, they’re kind and they’re open arms to anyone that wants and that puts in the effort into the acting industry.

What I find so exciting about it is that it doesn’t feel as exclusive as fashion does, in a way. It opens up the conversation to anyone that’s willing to work for it. Fashion is being the right person in the right place at the right time. I think that acting is being the right person, yes, but putting the right energy and the right time into the job. It was just such an incredible experience. Jessica Lange, Emma Roberts, Sarah Paulson, Gabourey Sidibe… it was fab. It was fab! I have so many iconic memories made on that set that I’m going to have forever. I got so much knowledge from these women. I think that it was just really reassuring to see how kind and open-minded these people were, especially Billie Lourd. She’s an icon of mine, but then I got to work with her, and she was just so open and honest about how she’s felt in her first roles. It’s just really gratifying to hear this stuff.

There’s a long legacy of supermodels trying to crack into the silver screen. A lot of models have done it, some very successfully, some have done it once and then moved on. Do you feel any sort of pressure for this to work?

I think I was really ready to just lock in and have fun, but for me, what I was most excited about was being able to be ugly. I see this a lot in models and actresses, where it becomes difficult when you’re so aware of the camera, and you grow up being so aware of the camera to then unlearn that awareness. It was so exciting to be able to go into a space where I was able to get into the character without there being the perception of others there. Obviously there’s a camera, but it’s not a fashion show where you hear like, yeah, work! [laughs] It was a real experience that I worked on within myself.

I was reading The Artist’s Way, which, not to be all corny, I think I realized that the feeling of gratification and the feeling of completing something is only as good as that feeling. I think that perception, especially now with social media and [giving] a numeric value to art, it’s really important to be able to feel like you did the best you could and that’s enough. I think for me, that was really where it kind of progressed. I was able to lock down away from the facet of just being pretty. I didn’t get the touch-ups before set, I didn’t get the lighting right. I wasn’t asking to see the playback, which, as a model—I know you’ve been on many sets where you see the girls and with every single shot we’re looking at the screen, there’s a mirror behind the photographer— it’s very not that. I do the day, and I don’t know if I did a good job. I felt like I did a good job, and that’s enough for me. I’m excited to see it in seven months when it comes out. But that really took a lot of the pressure away. I was just enjoying the experience and doing my best. I think that that’s the beauty of it and that’s the beautiful difference between fashion and film.

I love a lot of animated characters. I was watching Rio yesterday. Did you know Anne Hathaway is the love interest? That’s my dream. Honestly, I would love to do some really fab, cool animation because I think that in itself is a challenge. It’s nice to be able to build a character with just your voice.

Fundamentally, I would really love to have a role that really personifies someone different for me. I also watched Catwoman yesterday with Halle Berry. I think powerful women roles are obviously exciting for any female actress. Having the opportunity to do that would be incredible. I’m very “divine timing” when it comes to this stuff, so I believe everything will happen and run its course in the way it should. But there’s also a lot of really interesting biopics that I would love to see. Maybe I write them, maybe I act. Who knows?

Consani arriving at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art.

A polaroid of the final glam for the night.

So you want to get into writing too, or have you been writing?

Yeah, I actually have. I have been in the background of my mind thinking about this and maybe moving into that space as well. I think it’s quite exciting. In my whole career, it’s always been if you’re not given the opportunity, you make it yourself. I think of other actresses, and the behind-the-camera work that goes into the shows that they do.

That’s a really good point. A lot of the actors that we grew up with—Nicole Kidman, Reese Witherspoon—have really gone into production, or are part of the writing process. Do you have a dream director to work with? Do you have a bucket list?

Totally. Wes Anderson is a really big one... I love Wes Anderson. I think he’s an incredible director. But on top of that, I just worked with Janicza Bravo, and I’m such a big fan. She’s so incredible with the way that she thinks. Lena Dunham [is another]. There’s so many incredible people, but I think I like the way that each different director works. My favorite part about working with Janicza was just the youth in her perspective. I’ve worked with multi-generations of directors at this point, and to see the difference between how Ryan works versus how Janicza works versus how Molly Gordon works, it’s just quite interesting. There’s a lot of directors that I’m a big fan of, people who are obviously focused on cinematography, but also understand how to have fun.

#3523. The Lord Of The Rings: The Rings Of Power Season 3's Two Big Character Deaths Explained

The land of Mordor is where the shadows lie, and this article is where major spoilers lie. Read no further if you haven't watched the Season 3 premiere episodes of "The Rings of Power."

"The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" has one thing in common with the TV phenomenon that was "Game of Thrones" — they're both exercises in enduring misery. After all, the show is all about watching stupid sexy Sauron (Charlie Vickers) make everyone in Middle-earth suffer season after season. And sure, the series is willing to kill beloved characters, but it really excels at killing hordes of people and turning entire kingdoms into desolated volcanic wastelands where the sun never shines.

Things are even worse at the start of Season 3, between Sauron trying to forge the One Ring, Mordor's Ringwraiths spreading across Middle-earth, and a Dark Wizard (Ciarán Hinds) ruling Rhûn. Elsewhere, when it comes to the civil war plaguing Númenor, the realm's only hope is Eärien (Ema Horvath), who was responsible for the King's Men usurping the Númenórean throne in the first place. In fact, Eärien is an unexpected main character early in Season 3, acting as a faithful servant and the head torturer for the usurper Ar-Pharazôn (Trystan Gravelle) while at the same time operating as a double agent for her brother Isildur (Maxim Baldry) and father Elendil (Lloyd Owen) as they try to restore Queen Míriel (Cynthia Addai-Robinson) to power.

Unsurprisingly, things don't go well, as "The Rings of Power" Season 3 kills off two original characters made for the show in its first four episodes. First, Eärien dies in the second episode, followed by the wood elf Arondir (Ismael Cruz Córdova) being tragically betrayed and murdered in Episode 4.

Let's start with Eärien. The character has always felt out of place on "The Rings of Power," with her scenes slowing down the pace and taking away from other, better storylines. Frustratingly, the show simply doesn't have time to cover all the ground it wants to, with the limited number of episodes per season forcing it to jump around too quickly. That being said, Eärien aiding the rise of the King's Men in the secluded and isolated island of Númenor due to her mistakenly believing that following Queen Míriel had gotten Isildur killed was interesting, as was her becoming a double agent once she learned the truth.

Unfortunately, Eärien's double age storyline — her best so far — doesn't last long. By Episode 2, she's already been discovered. So, rather than be subjected to torture and forced to become truly loyal to the King's Men, she dies by suicide by jumping off a balcony.

Likewise, when he was first introduced, Arondir was a great character. Sure, he didn't actually do much, with much of his screen time being dedicated to an attempt at a romance between him and the now-deceased Bronwyn (Nazanin Boniadi). And yet, Ismael Cruz Córdova has always played his role with great gusto, giving Arondir a strong personality that makes him feel like more than just a Legolas knock-off. But that just makes his departure all the more upsetting.

Indeed, Arondir gets little more to do in Season 3 than worry about Bronwyn's annoying son Theo (Tyroe Muhafidin). This all leads to a confrontation in Episode 4 when Sauron orders Theo — now a Ringwraith — to murder the elf. A tragic end, sure, but with little buildup.

With Arondir and Eären's deaths, "The Rings of Power" is quickly getting rid of its original characters. After all, the show had already killed off one of its best brand-new additions in Adar (Sam Hazeldine and Joseph Mawle), while the Harfoots that were so essential in Seasons 1 and 2 are nowhere to be found in Season 3 so far. Granted, Theo's still around, but he's likely to be killed soon as well (due to that whole being a Ringwraith thing). That just leaves Kemen (Leon Wadham), the tiring nepo baby at the center of the Númenor story.

Instead, it's clear "The Rings of Power" is currently more focused on bringing in previously missing characters from J.R.R. Tolkien's source material, like Isildur's brother Anárion (Andrew Richardson) and Middle-earth's own Odysseus, i.e. Celeborn (Jamie Campbell Bower), who's married to Morfydd Clark's elfish warrior Galadriel. It makes sense for the show's writers to be doing this right now, too, as we're getting closer and closer to the end of the series' reported five-season plan. But that means "The Rings of Power" will also have less and less time to explore any of its original characters from this point on.

Another problem is the show's condensed timeline, as "The Rings of Power" is trying to tell a story that spans thousands of years in Tolkien's literature over a much, much shorter period. That means we still have a lot of major "Lord of the Rings"-related developments to get through, be it Elendil and his sons founding the kingdom of Gondor or Celeborn creating Lothlórien with Galadriel. Will all that and more to cover, there's just no more room for the likes of Arondir the wood elf.

#3522. Five Hacks Every Una Watch User Should Know

The Una watch is pretty much made to be hackable, with its interchangeable parts and open development environment. But it’s also pretty barebones at launch, without many features available yet. However, here are five things I’ve discovered I can do with it—and I hope to expand this list quite a bit as the device and its community mature.

Because the Una watch has a regular USB-C port, you don’t need to remember any specific cable, dongle, or adapter to charge it. I knew that, but it didn’t occur to me until recently that I didn’t need a computer or a wall outlet to plug into the other end. I was able to take a USB-C to USB-C cable—the same kind I might carry around to charge my phone—and plug one end into my watch and the other into my phone. It charged!

(You can also charge some other devices from a phone, including an Apple Watch, but you’d need to carry around that specific adapter, which is why nobody bothers.)

The Una watch doesn’t have any built-in sleep tracking, but a few community-built apps aim to provide it. The Slumber app, for example, will let you know how long you slept and compare your most recent bedtime with when you usually get to bed. There are no sleep stages (honestly: refreshing, since watches are rarely good at this anyway), and the analysis is done on the watch itself.

But if what you’re really hoping for is a recovery score or an overnight HRV reading, the HabitLab app combines that with habit tracking. Every evening, the watch will buzz and ask you to check off which habits or factors played into your day: Alcohol and late meals are among the options, and the watch will automatically detect morning or evening workouts to add them to the list. In the morning, the watch asks you how you slept, and then it gives you a score based on your resting heart rate, HRV, and your subjective rating.

The app is supposed to be able to put together trends and insights from this data, but I haven’t managed to get it to do this. Maybe it’s waiting for more data (I’ve been using it a little over a week), or maybe it’s just buggy.

By contrast, the barcode app worked even better than I expected it to. It’s meant for a parkrun barcode; each participant in the free weekly 5K has a number that you can use to check your results online. But it works just as well for other barcodes.

I installed the Barcode app and entered the number for my library card. Perhaps because of the watch’s MIP screen, I found this barcode scanned more reliably than any barcodes I’ve previously tried to use on a watch. The library scanner picked it up just fine on the first try, and a phone-based scanner also had no problem with it. You can store up to six barcodes, so I’ve also entered a few others, like my grocery discount card.

The app supports QR codes as well as regular barcodes, and to enter a QR code, you just type in a shortened URL. (It needs to be 22 characters or less.) This means that the Barcode app is also a QR code creator, a nifty feature indeed.

Seeing how soon the sun sets is a bit of a downer as we leave daylight saving time and get into the dark winter months, but it’s also helpful in planning. The Sun & Moon Face puts a graphic on your wrist that shows how far along the sun is in its trajectory across the sky for the day. When evening is approaching, you’ll see just how little time you have left.

The app grabs your GPS location once a day, which means that for the first few hours I wore it, the sunrise and sunset times were incorrectly listed as 6 a.m. and 6 p.m. But as long as you aren’t flying to a drastically new location every day, the app does the job just fine. As a bonus, it changes the color of the screen’s sky to show daylight, nighttime, or sunrise/sunset colors.

If you want to hack this hackable watch, you might as well take the plunge and try to build something yourself. Instructions are here to download the development tools for Windows, Mac, or Linux, and there are tutorials for different features you might want to use and implement. There are also about a dozen example apps you can build on, including activity trackers, watch faces, and glances. I'm not much of a coder myself, but this is the friendliest setup I've seen for someone to get into building their own apps for a watch.

#3521. Everyone Is Talking About Wicker's Sexy Parts, But I Was Caught Off Guard By Its Emotional Depth

The romance is great, but the emotional depth is better.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Wicker has been advertised as an extremely sexually charged movie with a hot man made of wicker. The film doesn’t shy away from sex and sexuality. It has a few very fun sex scenes that a lot of hard work went into. I wasn’t sure what to expect going into Wicker beyond some raunchiness.

I was delighted to discover it's far more complex than it's promoted. It touches upon topics of self-esteem in really haunting and interesting ways.

Warning: Wicker spoilers are ahead. Proceed with caution.

Fisherwoman (Olivia Colman) has always been an outcast in her town. They tease and treat her as if her only purpose is to sell them fish. She has no real friends and not much of a romantic prospect. This led the Fisherwoman to accept a lonely life. She finally decides to change that, but the scars remain from being told that she doesn’t deserve good things, especially a man who loves her.

The Fisherwoman has a lot of trauma and self-esteem issues from years of being told by society that she’s not worthy of happiness. However, she isn’t the only one with society-based scars. All the women in town have them. This is why the Wicker Husband (Alexander Skarsgård) is so attractive to many women. He doesn’t operate with the same rules of this society.

He loves deeply and purely, without constraining how his wife should live. Sadly, this nonconforming spirit also makes the Fisherwoman doubt his love and fidelity. She has seen the men of this society. She finds it hard to believe that she has one who respects and loves her.

I left Wicker very annoyed with the Fisherwoman. She almost killed her husband because of a lie. Additionally, she refused to believe him, even though he has only ever been honest. It’s also clear that he only exists for her. I was shouting, “Be reasonable, woman!” as she behaved in unreasonable ways.

However, then I had to think about how many women and men let their lack of self-esteem or past trauma ruin good things in their lives. Many relationships have been destroyed because one or both people in them let their insecurities grow and create bigger problems. The Fisherwoman is frustrating, but she’s very human.

I really enjoyed the Wicker ending because everyone got what they deserved. The townsfolk got scammed and traumatized. The Butcher (Phil Daniels ) got murdered, as the worst husband of them all, and the Fisherwoman and Wicker Husband left with a new child.

It was only after the Fisherwoman could let go of her insecurities and her awful town that she could have a happy ending. Wicker is about letting love into your life, even when you don’t think you deserve it.

The Fisherwoman creates a husband who loves her completely, but she also learns to love herself in the process. That’s the real message. Find love within yourself, and the right person may find you, or you will at least love yourself enough to feel fulfilled with or without a partner. Wicker is definitely worth seeing in a theater full of women, or alone, where you can meditate on its messages.

Either way, come for the sexy parts, stay for the self-love.

#3520. Warby Parker and Gentle Monster Are Launching Smart Glasses. Does Anyone Want Them?

This is the November 11, 2026 edition of Fit Check, your front row seat to the power players, peacocks, and deep pockets of fashion—and how they influence the rest of the world.

It’s been a meme-worthy news week: the new Met Gala theme launched endless online discourse, Jensen Huang ignited the internet with news of his affair with an alleged Chinese spy, then fashion netizens had a time memeifying him as a Hedi-boy, and Maybelline changed its slogan with some very confusing punctuation.

IRL, Gentle Monster and Warby Parker are getting into the smart glasses space. Like Meta, they’re working hard to get fashion’s co-sign in order to have tastemakers influence everyone else to wear them, though I have yet to find a fashion person happy to wear these without a check involved. And this week, Alex Consani video-called me to discuss her acting ambitions after her debut in American Horror Story: 13. She’s already filmed two movies coming next year.

Mentioned in this issue: Iron Man, Robert Downey Jr., Kylie Jenner, Timothée Chalamet’s security guard, Steven Meisel, Martine Rose discourse, Luca de Meo, Woke 3.0, Hedi Slimane, Slimaniacs, Sarah Paulson, Ryan Murphy, and many more.

Amelia Gray at the Gentle Monster launch dinner.

Last night Warby Parker and Gentle Monster celebrated the launches of their “intelligent eyewear” lines (not to be confused with Meta’s “smart glasses”), both developed with Google and Samsung. Warby Parker hosted a literary activation with Vogue, and Gentle Monster held a “preview experience” and dinner attended by Alex Consani, Anok Yai, Charles Melton, Joaquin Phoenix, and more.

Snap also tapped Robert Downey Jr. to star in videos showcasing its technology, Iron Man–style. Phoenix appeared in Gentle Monster’s launch campaign in a callback to his role in Her, in which he plays a man who falls in love with an AI voiced by Scarlett Johansson. (In 2024, she had a dispute with OpenAI after learning the company had created a voice that sounded similar to hers for its AI, which she had declined to license for ChatGPT. Sam Altman denied any intentional imitation.) Leveraging two movie stars who’ve been the face of this kind of technology in film to bring their products to the masses is a cunning move from Google and Samsung. Yet it’s possible that no co-sign can combat the anxiety around AI and its surrounding gadgets. There is a budding battle in the smart glasses space—but does anyone actually want them?

Martine Rose is officially taking over from Pierpaolo Piccioli at Balenciaga. I still think he could have been right for the brand, but he came at the wrong time. Balenciaga is essentially Kering’s youth vehicle after a decade under Demna, and Piccioli just wasn’t the designer to fulfill that brief. That his collections seemed to try to honor both Demna’s casualwear range and his own couture-like sensibility only muddled the brand’s remit further. But Rose, who worked with Demna on his Balenciaga menswear early on, is a much better fit in this context, and she has the industry’s goodwill—fans have been advocating her ascent to a role like this one for years.

Rose is the first official hire under Luca de Meo’s tenure as Kering’s CEO, and she is walking into a brave new world. De Meo believes Kering has been overly dependent on its creative directors, and is looking to streamline operations with a new strategy dubbed “ReconKering.” If reports are confirmed that Chemena Kamali will head to Saint Laurent and Virginia Burlina to McQueen, four out of five creative directors at Kering will soon be women. Along with Rose and Louise Trotter at Bottega Veneta, these are designers who are better known as prolific workhorses rather than buzzy household names. De Meo is evidently looking to grow beyond the star creative director strategy that defined fashion in the 2010s, with Demna as an exception. What this means for Rose and Balenciaga, and for Saint Laurent and McQueen, which have historically depended on the persona of their creative leads, remains to be seen.

Balenciaga is back in the news this week with the opening of the first of several activations around the 25th anniversary of its Le City bag, arguably the most enduring of It bags after the Birkin. Damien Hirst has hand-painted 25 bags for the occasion, and Nicole Richie is fronting the campaign in a callback to the aughts. This was planned prior to Piccioli’s exit, yet it’s taking place in between creative directors speaks to an undeniable fact that plays right into ReconKering: These brands are bigger than their designers, despite how important these appointments are to industry insiders and fanatics.

A look from Jun Takahashi’s fall-winter 2024 collection for Undercover, which will be included in the upcoming Met Costume Institute exhibition.

In case you missed it: The Met announced on Thursday the replacement exhibition for the John Galliano blockbuster postponed earlier this year. “ExtraORDINARY: Fashion and the Poetics of the Everyday” will focus on how designers have explored familiar, ordinary garments: jeans, T-shirts, workwear, and more. It sounds like both an ode to normcore and to the ingenuity with which designers like Matthieu Blazy, Demna, Jun Takahashi, and more have reimagined the most simple of clothing. Andrew Bolton, the curator in charge of the Costume Institute, told Vogue he “didn’t have a plan B” after Galliano and that he wanted the replacement show to be “challenging and provocative.” The announcement drew both positive and negative reactions. Its main criticism is its simplicity, especially when compared to Galliano’s extravagance. Bolton has a singular way of placing fashion in larger cultural contexts to underscore its historic importance—I’m curious to see what he’ll do when the fashion he’s dealing with already exists in an atmosphere that requires little explanation.

Maybelline has updated its famous slogan, “Maybe she’s born with it. Maybe it’s Maybelline,” which was first introduced in 1991, to a more democratic, inclusive riff: “Maybe. We’re born with it. Maybe. It’s Maybelline.” Confusing punctuation aside, the change feels like it belongs to the late 2010s era of DEI marketing. It’s true that binary pronouns have fallen out of style, particularly at the makeup counter, even if brands shied away from this kind of revamp in the Trump era. But then again, after last week’s blue wave in the midterm elections, maybe Maybelline is just in time.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang waves to the media as he arrives at Gimpo airport in Seoul on June 5, 2026 wearing a Dior jacket. Images from this same outing were modified with AI by fashion netizens.

The news of Jensen Huang’s affair filled X with memes about Chinese spies and mistresses in a variety of configurations. By Monday evening, Huang had reached the fashion world’s stylish netizens: the Instagram account @hidden.ny, an anonymous digital mood board and cultural platform, posted a series of images of Huang in a studded leather jacket. The caption read: “NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang in Hedi Slimane SLP Studded Leather Jacket after admitting to affair with alleged Chinese spy.”

It’s well-known that Huang is a leather jacket enthusiast. But despite Huang’s penchant for a black leather moment, it appears he was not, in fact, wearing the Saint Laurent jacket. A quick run through an AI image detector debunked Huang being a “Slimaniac,” at least in this particular case. SynthID detected that the images posted by Hidden and other users online were generated or edited with OpenAI. To burst the bubble even further, it appears the images used as the base for this edit weren’t taken after the disclosure of Huang’s affair, but during a trip to South Korea in June. Apologies to the menswear crowd for ruining the fantasy.

#3519. These Bose QuietComfort Headphones Are $160 Off Ahead of Black Friday

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

Bose’s second-generation QuietComfort Headphones in Dewdrop Mint, Eucalyptus Green, and Hazelnut Taupe are down to $199 from $359 ahead of Black Friday, saving you $160 and bringing them to their lowest price yet, according to price trackers. Weighing around 8.1 ounces, they’re among the lightest premium noise-canceling headphones, with generously padded earcups and a cushioned headband that spreads pressure without gripping too tightly, making them comfortable to wear for extended periods. They’re also easy to pack for travel, as the earcups fold and swivel for storage in the included hard-shell carrying case. The removable earpads are another welcome touch, since you can replace them as they wear down without having to retire the entire pair.

Comfort aside, noise cancellation is another area where these headphones deliver, doing a particularly good job of reducing lower-frequency rumble and background chatter, though some higher-pitched voices can still come through, notes this PCMag review. As for their sound profile, it leans warm and bass-forward, with deep lows that suit bass-heavy genres, while the companion app adds Bose Immersive Audio for spatial sound and lets you create customized listening profiles—the three-band EQ is fairly basic, though, so anyone who likes fine-tuning their sound may find the adjustment options limiting.

Connectivity, too, brings some useful upgrades over the previous generation, including Bluetooth 5.4, multipoint pairing for two devices, Google Fast Pair, and lossless audio over USB-C. That same USB-C port lets you charge the headphones while you listen, and the included USB-C-to-3.5mm cable covers standard headphone jacks, including the ones on in-flight entertainment systems. That said, battery life is less impressive, topping out at 24 hours with ANC enabled, although a 15-minute charge adds around 2.5 hours of playback. Wireless audio is also limited to the standard AAC and SBC codecs, with no support for the higher-quality aptX Adaptive—a feature available on Bose’s QuietComfort Ultra Headphones.

#3518. The Best Ways For Star Trek Fans To Play Magic's New Set: A Guide For Beginner Players

When I sat down at my friendly local game store to participate in a pre-release drafting event for Magic: The Gathering's new "Star Trek" set, several players saw the Enterprise tattoo on my forearm and asked me the same question. If a longtime Magic player wanted to sample "Star Trek," what was the best place for them to start?

Ironically, I was there to ask the Mirror Universe version of that same question: If a longtime "Star Trek" fan wanted to sample the new Magic set, what's the best place for them to start?

I am new to Magic, having only picked up the game a few months ago to prime myself for the new "Trek" release. And one thing Magic and "Star Trek" have in common is that they're both absolutely daunting at first blush. One is a collectible card game with over 30 years of history and dozens of ways to play. The other is a sci-fi universe with nearly 1,000 episodes of television and 13 movies, with dozens of possible entry points.

I can answer one question immediately. "Trek" newbies should start with "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds," with its glossy production values and modern streaming sensibilities, before backtracking and sampling the various other shows and finding the one that connects with their tastes. (This is a sometimes controversial opinion, but I stick by it.)

But the other question involved some legwork, a lot of time spent at a gaming table, a great deal more time sorting through cards, and even a question proposed to the lead designers of the set itself. So, what is the best way for a "Star Trek" fan to sample the new Magic: The Gathering set? Here's what I learned.

One thing I will not do here is explain the rules of Magic: The Gathering, which are intuitive and easy to learn, but challenging to master. There are countless online resources to learn before you try anything I recommend below. I'm writing this piece under the assumption you intend to seek those out on your own.

The best way to truly dive in headfirst is to visit your local gaming shop and participate in a sealed or drafting event. Naturally, this is dependent on your location and whether your local gaming shop is an inviting and safe space (shout out to Mothership Games in Austin, Texas for playing host to my first sealed event). If such a place exists for you, check the calendar and see what's on offer. The good news is that the "Star Trek" set is brand new and there should be plenty of opportunities.

At events like these, players are organized into one-on-one matches and construct their decks from scratch, tearing open booster packs, examine their cards, and trying to build the most effective strategy possible around a 40-card deck. While experienced players will have an edge, they can't bring finely honed and powerful decks from home to immediately wipe the floor with you. Everyone starts at square one. And "Star Trek" fans should take very easily to this format, since the characters you'd expect to be powerful tend to have cards that are powerful. It also leads to some amusing team-ups, like how my winning deck involved an unlikely alliance between Deanna Troi and Gul Dukat.

In a friendly shop with a friendly crowd, this is Magic at its purest: a direct, competitive game where tactics at the table are as important as the strategy behind your deck construction. And the mechanics in the "Trek" set are intuitive and mesh well, meaning that creating a deck that functions as needed is fairly straightforward, and going with your gut choices (i.e., building around characters you like) often leads to strong results.

I can hear your next question: You don't have access to a local shop, or you don't feel comfortable going to one, so what's the best way to play at home? Once again, there are options.

You and a friend (or more) could always buy booster packs, tearing them open and building personal collections and constructing 60-card decks for standard play. However, I would recommend booster packs being the start of your collection, and once you have bought a few, track down single cards to complete your strategy rather than buying more and blindly hoping for strong pulls.

Another option is for you and a friend to buy a pre-release kit, as there are always plenty leftover after the initial week of special event. Use these to construct imperfect but fun starter decks to learn the game, and then grow and expand those decks as you see fit, doubling down on the characters and strategies you're enjoying.

However, the best at-home experience would be to pick up one of the set's Draft Night boxes, which are pricy but offer bang for your buck: enough cards for four friends to craft decks and go head-to-head for an evening, leaving everyone with enough cards to build upon in the future.

However, all of these options require tinkering, and suggest that you'll enjoy the process of building a deck as much as playing one. These options require additional legwork, additional financial investment, and even a bit of luck (although that can be mitigated by buying single cards from reputable online and brick-and-mortar shops). If you want to truly just dive into the game itself and skip the rest of the process, there is another way.

When I had a chance to speak to the key designers behind Magic: The Gathering's "Star Trek" set during a launch event in Los Angeles, I asked if the new set was friendly for "Star Trek" fans with no gaming experience, and if they had a recommendation on where to start.

First, they noted that the set was designed with new players in mind and puts narrative first. A card will generally behave like its counterpart in the "Star Trek" universe, so a fan knows that a Captain Kirk card will be a bit more headstrong and aggressive while Spock will allow for more wily, thoughtful strategy. This means a "Trek" fan should be able to grasp the new cards fairly quickly, using their existing knowledge as a crutch.

Second, they highlighted their recommendation for the best way to sample the game: the "Star Trek" commander decks.

Commander is the most popular format in Magic, where players utilize 100 card decks in four-player games that are slowly paced, socially driven, and generally take an entire evening to play. Think of them as more of a board game experience — or a nerd poker night — than a standard Magic set. Many Magic sets are accompanied by a few pre-constructed commander decks, which players can purchase, open, and play immediately without any prep. The "Star Trek" set has four of them: Federation Fleet, We Are the Borg, Klingon Fury, and Landing Party.

Specifically, the designers recommended the Federation Fleet commander deck as their choice for a "Star Trek" fan hoping to play the game.

Naturally, the next step was to test the designers' suggestion. I rounded up three friends and assigned them each a different Star Trek commander deck, taking Federation Fleet for myself. It's easy to see why this one was recommended: With Picard on the cover and a deck full of '90s "Trek" staples, it's the most popular era of the franchise in one 100-card deck.

Our four-player game took over three hours, and frankly, it was some of the best Magic I've ever played, with all four decks interacting in surprising and wild ways that left everyone at the table screaming and laughing. The "Trek" fans were impressed by the thematic touches, and how the mechanics relate to character personalities and motives, while the Magic players simply relished in the new design elements. I squeaked out a win, but only after the Borg player staged a comeback that essentially wiped out the table. My victory told a story in of itself: Dr. Bashir threw himself at the Borg player, perishing, but in the process, activated his ability to resurrect Ro Laren from the dead, activating her ability and ending the Borg threat once and for all.

After seeing the commander decks in action, I'm inclined to agree with the designers' recommendation. The Borg deck is scary and powerful, but makes them an immediate threat the other players will team up against to defeat. The Klingon deck is pure aggression, which may work against a new player's inherent shyness. The Landing Part deck, with its focus on Original Series characters, is fairly straightforward, but has a lot of moving pieces to consider. The mechanical simplicity of the Federation Fleet deck, and its arsenal of beloved characters, makes it easy to grasp and understand quickly.

Much like with "Star Trek" itself, there are countless ways to get into Magic: The Gathering, and no incorrect way. Ultimately, I agree with the designers: the pre-constructed commander decks, and specifically the Federation Fleet deck, are the best point of entry. Ideally, you'd buy all four and learn with friends for the best possible experience.

But like with "Star Trek" itself, you should be warned: once Magic has sucked you in, be prepared to be sucked in for the long haul.

#3517. 47 Years Later, the Best 'Peanuts' Quote About Life and Death Still Hits Just as Hard

You can track the evolution of the American comic strip through its typical depiction of childhood. Early 20th century strips like Ernie Bushmiller's Nancy (1933) show kids' lives as relatively prosaic, particularly given the culture and publication standards of the time. While their child protagonists might have faced some incidental frustrations, the comics page was mostly about gentle humor. Yes, Sluggo is a homeless orphan, but no, that isn't a source of angst or conflict.

Charles Schulz's Peanuts has become a sort of cultural shorthand for safe, family-friendly entertainment, but for its first decade, it was a genuinely daring comic. Schulz's kids were frustrated, unlucky, and often pointlessly cruel to one another, in a more realistic approach to kids' behavior than most comic strips risked showing at the time. Even if you don't have any particular use for Peanuts itself, you can see it as a necessary stepping stone towards the edgier mainstream comics of the 1980s and '90s, like The Boondocks or even Calvin and Hobbes.

Even at his most potentially controversial, Schulz was never interested in "very special episodes." No one in the Peanuts gang usually had to deal with anything more serious than academic underachievement. That's part of why some other comics' big swerves, like the death of Andy Lippincott in Doonesbury or the raccoon cub storyline in Calvin and Hobbes, hit as hard as they did at the time. You didn't often see the funny pages get anywhere near topics like death or mortality.

As far as Peanuts is concerned, there are two real exceptions. One is part of a weird series of comics that involve Snoopy's brothers, while the other is a month-long storyline from 1979.

In the daily Peanuts strip for July 2, 1979, Charlie Brown started to feel woozy during a baseball game and decided to just go home. This was the start of a surprisingly long plot arc, particularly for Peanuts, in which ol' Chuck landed in the hospital.

No one ever says what's wrong with Charlie Brown. He feels "woozy," then goes to the hospital for treatment, at which point he's admitted. Charlie Brown winds up staying in the hospital until July 29, at which point he's released and fully recovered. This leads into one of the high points of Peanuts' running football gags at the start of August 1979.

More importantly, Charlie Brown's illness has a strong ripple effect throughout the Peanuts gang. Sally immediately tries to steal his bedroom, Snoopy is only vaguely aware Charlie Brown's gone at all, and both Peppermint Patty and Marcie make a point of supporting him as best they can.

The character who's the most affected, however, is also the one that you might least expect. Lucy, who spends most of her panel time with Charlie Brown tearing him down, is worried for him to the point where she can't eat, sleep, or even harass Schroeder. She actually goes so far as to cry over Charlie Brown (and then wipe her tears off on Schroeder's piano).

Lucy's emotions on the subject hit their apex in the Peanuts strip for July 26, 1979. When Linus tells her that Charlie Brown doesn't appear to be getting any better, Lucy loses it.

"He's not any better? That's crazy! He's got to get better!" Lucy yells at Linus. "What's wrong with a world where someone like Charlie Brown can get sick, and then not get any better?! I need somebody to hit!"

That leads into Lucy's promise, in the next two days' strips, to actually abandon the football gag for once. It's an uncommon amount of empathy for Lucy and it gets abandoned almost as soon as it arrives, but it's also one of the most emotional moments in the daily strip. The July 26 comic doesn't even have a punchline as such. Instead, it's an understandable outburst that can resonate with anyone who's ever been in a situation where they can't do anything but wait.

Given how much of Charles Schulz's real life made it into Peanuts, it's enough to raise the question of whether Schulz himself had a relative in the hospital at some point in 1979. This particular Peanuts arc ends up as a strange outlier in the comic's history, as well as an oddly resonant brush with mortality.

Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s documentary from A24 about Elizabeth Holmes, You Can See Everything, is all about the truth. The central question that we, as the audience, are asking the entire time, who is telling the truth, who is lying, and just what is the truth. Even though Fielder spent weeks living with Holmes and her partner just prior to the former Theranos founder reporting to prison in 2023, even he still doesn’t have a grasp of how much Holmes is deceiving people, or what she actually believes. He talked about it in a recent interview, and it both makes things clearer and more opaque at the same time, just like the movie.

In the documentary, Fielder dances around how he feels about Holmes’ statements, like being incredulous when she claims that she’s never lied about anything at all in her life. By design, he rarely calls Holmes on her lies (with a couple of exceptions). He also doesn’t get into the definition of the truth. He leaves that up to us as the audience. Specifically, he doesn’t address whether Holmes even knows if she is lying or not. He addressed this with Wired recently, saying:

It almost feels, at times, that it’s not so black-and-white what’s going on in her head. A lie, a classic lie, is someone who’s like, ‘OK, I am saying something that I’m consciously knowing is not true in this moment.’ But it’s not just the words, it’s the design of every aspect of her life that feels like a part of what is going on.

He also doesn’t quite have his head around just how much of her whole life is wrapped up in the deceit? He adds:

What’s interesting about her to me, I think, just goes beyond that in any given moment … I can’t piece it together. She makes these claims that are like—how could anyone believe this or say they’ve never done this? Is it a lie in that moment? Is it a lie if she believes it to be true?

This is something that has long been discussed and pontificated upon when it comes to the truth and people who spend their loves deceiving people. Do dishonest people like Holmes either know they are lying, or are they so calculating that almost everything becomes a lie, or at minimum a tall tale? Fielder doesn’t seem to have any answers, even after spending all that time with Holmes, as she told him those stories.

One of the most impressive things about You Can See Everything, which is still tearing up the box office on the 2026 movie schedule. is that the movie lives on in the viewers' brains for days or weeks after seeing it. I mean, I saw this movie a month ago, and I still think about it and want to talk about it all the time. Like lies, when you have to peel layers off of them like an onion to get to the truth, this film is much the same way. To mix metaphors, every thread you tug on pulls out more layers to peel back.

#3515. This TP-Link Wi-Fi 7 Travel Router Is 27% Off for This Early Black Friday Deal

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

A novel solution for connecting to the internet on the go, the TP-Link Roam 7 travel router is now down to $87.99 from $119.99 in an early Black Friday deal—marking its lowest price to date, according to price trackers. This is not a full-size home router but, as the name suggests, a compact travel companion that measures roughly the size of a paperback book, with foldable antennas so it slips easily into a bag.

More about convenience than chasing top speeds, you can use the Roam 7 as a standard router, connect it to public wifi to create a private network, or share your phone's internet through USB tethering. It also supports Ethernet input and USB modems, along with range extender and wireless client modes. That flexibility is particularly useful when you’re juggling a laptop, phone, and maybe a tablet and would prefer not to sign each one into a shaky network separately. Setup is straightforward through the TP-Link Tether app: scan a QR code, choose your connection type, and you’re online in a few minutes.

Once it’s running, the hardware covers the basics, with a 2.5 Gbps port for a wired connection like a hotel’s Ethernet jack, a 1 Gbps port for a wired device, and a USB 3.0 port for a storage drive or phone tethering. And since it draws power over USB-C (5V/3A), a basic power bank can keep it going through a long layover or a camping trip. As handy as it is on the road, though, it’s not meant to replace a full-size home router—even with its 5 GHz band and Wi-Fi 7 support—which will generally offer better coverage and more consistent speeds. Real-world performance also depends heavily on your connection and setup. USB tethering, for example, can feel slower than using your phone directly. It also leaves out features like automatic band steering, so you may end up managing networks yourself. Still, if you travel often or need a portable network hub for multiple devices, you’ll find it holds up pretty well.

#3514. Henry Cavill Comments On Superman Return After James Gunn's DC Studios Exit

Henry Cavill was a great Superman who never got a great Superman movie, and that should have been the end of it. But it's now 2026, and we're still talking about whether Cavill will return as the Man of Steel. With James Gunn and Peter Safran "stepping down" as DC Studios co-heads, DC's cinematic future is very much up in the air, and now Cavill is saying he'd always be open to returning as Supes.

During an Inverse interview, the actor was asked if he'd ever play the DC hero again and seemed open to the idea. "Look, there's lots of fantastic storylines," he replied. "There's always a lot of opportunity. As the pigeon sang to Fievel in 'An American Tail,' "never say never." And I buy into that." It's hardly surprising, given that Cavill and his former DC Extended Universe colleague Dwayne Johnson once launched a pretty bizarre attempt to remain in the cinematic universe, most pointedly with 2022's immediately forgettable "Black Adam." At the time, Cavill proudly announced his return as Superman in a social media post following the film's release, but it never actually amounted to anything more than that and left Gunn deeply (and understandably) confused about what was even happening.

Since then, Gunn has introduced us to an all-new Man of Steel in David Corenswet, who made his debut in the charming crowd pleaser that was 2025's "Superman" and is set to return in the 2027 follow-up "Man of Steel." But with Gunn out at DC Studios it remains to be seen where the Corenswet version of the character and his story will go from there. Meanwhile, we've got Cavill telling Inverse he "had such a wonderful time playing Superman in the past" and "would never say never now." It's a bit tiresome, no?

Directly after the extremely perplexing return of Henry Cavill's Superman in "Black Adam," the DCEU collapsed with back to back flops in 2023. Meanwhile, James Gunn was gearing up to launch his DC Universe, which is why the whole situation left him baffled – especially since he was already actively preparing his DC reboot at the time. He wasn't the only one, either. Audiences thought they'd seen the last of the so-called Snyderverse after 2023, but Gunn chose to soft reboot DC with a new cinematic universe that retained elements of the old one. What's more, calls to reinstate the DCEU persist even today.

Now that Gunn and Peter Safran have been removed (er, "stepped down") from DC Studios, it looks as though Skydance CEO David Ellison — who's running the newly-merged Warner Bros. and Paramount — is planning to pretty much dismantle everything Gunn built at DC to prepare for yet another reboot.

Whatever Ellison and his new president and chief creative officer of DC Studios, Jeremy Latcham, have planned for the brand, I think it's safe to say we really don't need more talk of Cavill suiting back up. Had the actor left this character alone following 2017's "Justice League," it might have been a thrill to hear of his possible return a decade later. As it stands, like calls to restore the Snyderverse, this seems to be the discussion that never dies. Perhaps it's that lingering feeling that Cavill never got the movie he deserved, or the fact that Superman remains his best-known character. But for now it would be nice to go a few years without hearing about anything from the Snyderverse era coming back.

#3513. Chris Harrison on Launching The Vow, His Faith-Based Reality Show, and Leaving The Bachelor

“It really has very little to do with being on The Bachelor,” Chris Harrison, the series’s former host, tells me over breakfast at Manhattan’s Whitby Hotel in mid-October. Harrison orders avocado toast with poached eggs on top, then gently redirects the conversation to The Vow, his new faith-based dating series that premieres November 11 on Fox Nation. “It’s what we noticed, reading articles about this revival of young people going to church more than ever,” he says, turning to his wife and fellow executive producer on the show, Lauren Zima, who is seated beside him. “Here in New York, there are youth nights at the Catholic Church, at the temple, that are selling out thousands of kids. Clearly, this generation is searching for something solid—salvation, foundation.”

The six-episode series airs on the conservative-associated Fox Nation, Harrison says The Vow isn’t meant to have a political slant. “We’re not telling you to believe this or follow this path,” says Harrison. “Good shows look into a niche, this one’s about faith-driven people trying to find love. The hookup culture was a big deal and settling down became a cocktail joke. This generation’s really pushing back the other way.”

Faith-based dating shows aimed at Gen Z audiences have begun to infiltrate the reality TV landscape in recent years, from The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives to Hulu’s Ring by Spring Break, an upcoming series “that drops single Christian college students into a steamy spring break in Cabo, where finding ‘The One’ isn’t a dream…it’s a deadline.” But mixing romance and religion can be tricky business, as evidenced by the indeterminate future of the Mormon Wives and a ready-to-release season of The Bachelorette put on pause following allegations made against Taylor Frankie Paul, who leads both shows.

On The Vow, Jace Cates is a 30-year-old devout Christian mortgage-loan officer from Canby, Oregon that 10 similarly faith-driven women compete to marry. The goal is that, “Jace finds love,” says Harrison. “If it leads to marriage and children, we don’t have enough time for all that to happen on the show, but I want to help try and create the real article on TV. And if we don’t, that has to be real as well because this show is not predicated on the fact that it’s guaranteed to work.” But it’s hard to imagine any contenders stand a chance against Sierra, a virgin who lives 20 minutes away from Jace and attends his same Portland church. Her frontrunner status is cemented with a night-one kiss, the filming of which happened to coincide with Sierra’s 26th birthday. “We cast her before we cast Jace,” says Harrison, which feels as telling a reveal as any about producers’ ability to set themselves up for a successful outcome.

In February, before Fox Nation’s public involvement, Harrison shared a casting call for The Vow on Instagram, seeking single men and women aged 21 and older “who want a traditional, marriage-minded partnership built on commitment and shared values.” The description sparked early backlash on social media, but an initially surprised Harrison says he now understands the reaction. “Because in this day and age, we all have our guard up when we hear something that might be controversial,” he explains. “I’m not going to shy away from the fact that [the show] is about faith-based people saying, ‘I really do want to get married. I really do want to have babies’ Even those that might think it’s polarizing, I hope you watch,” Harrison adds. “You might be pleasantly surprised at how unbiased and uncontroversial it really is.”

The 55-year-old Harrison and Zima, who is 16 years his junior, are themselves “on different stages of faith,” she says as her egg-white frittata arrives. “Not drastically, but a bit. He’s probably more traditionally spiritual than I am.” Harrison was raised by a Jewish mother and grandparents, but grew up in a Protestant household during adolescence in the Bible belt of Dallas, Texas. After getting baptized as a Christian in his twenties, Harrison now says he identifies as “a religious mutt.”

“What matters most in our relationship,” the Chicago-born Zima continues, “[are] our values—family, loyalty, wanting to be good to people—those conversations [about] core things that drive you were what we really wanted people to have on the show.” Seeking “a really diverse spectrum of faith” meant casting Christians who ranged from the recently baptized to a first-generation American from Ghana. And the term “tradwife” means something different to everyone—Audrey aspires to be “a woman who makes her own money” as a penile implant sales rep fromin Wisconsin, while California native Mya is a second-grade teacher who one day wants to “do my husband for a living and have a big family.”

“We are always wanting to bring people together,” Zima continues. “And part of the way you bring people together is conversation—giving them dynamic, interesting, layered things to unpack together.”

The couple is open to devoting future seasons to different religions outside Christianity. “The important thing is finding really good, authentic people who have faith in their heart—whatever that faith is—but then really want to get married,” says Harrison. As “one of the rare few that was there on day one back in 2001 when we were inventing what The Bachelor was,” he adds, “it was rough and raw. We shot tons of silly things that never made air because you’re not exactly sure. So there will be some of that on The Vow. As veteran as I am, we’re still asking people to watch our art and accept it.”

The stakes are high for Harrison, who parted ways with The Bachelor franchise following a controversial Extra interview in February 2021, during which he excused racist behavior from one of the show’s contestants. He later issued an apology acknowledging that “by excusing historical racism, I defended it.” After announcing he would be “stepping aside for a period of time” from the series, Harrison also attempted a poorly received daytime TV mea culpa on Good Morning America that anchor Michael Strahan called “a surface response.,” Harrison promptly announced that he would be “stepping aside for a period of time” from the series. He permanently departed the show in June 2021 and reportedly received a “mid-range eight-figure settlement” from ABC, according to Deadline. A follow-up report by Variety adjusted that figure, revealing he received roughly $10 million. Vanity Fair has reached out to Harrison for comment about the payout.

Harrison’s comeback project has already ruffled feathers at his former workplace. In mid-September, Warner Bros, owner of the Bachelor franchise, sent a cease and desist letter against Harrison and Fox Nation, regarding what they viewed as an IP violation on the teaser for The Vow released on September 16. “Sadly, I wasn’t surprised. It’s par for the course. I don’t know why, because in my opinion, you can’t put a cease and desist on finding love,” says Harrison. “So it was unfortunate that’s where they wanted to go in this breakup. I feel a bit like a lover they can’t let go.”

For better or worse, Harrison and Zima’s real-life love story will forever be linked to his time spent hosting The Bachelor. “Oh, the other show?” Zima quips. “All of that, I look back [at it] as a blessing. And blessings don’t always come wrapped in this cute box under the tree,” Harrison says. “Sometimes it’s a humbling and traumatic experience.”

Zima met Harrison while covering The Bachelor franchise as a red-carpet reporter for Entertainment Tonight before things turned romantic in August 2018. “Obviously, what I loved most about her in the beginning was that she was a great interviewer,” says Harrison.

“This is so weird for me. I have to clock myself as being interviewed right now,” says Zima, who brings a bubbly, over-caffeinated energy to Harrison’s politely warm, but largely stoic presence. “By the way, I’m going to shut up. This is his interview,” she says a few times during breakfast, each of them subtly, but noticeably aware that a fellow journalist is meant to be observing their dynamic. They seem more at ease and physically affectionate as the interview wraps up; indeed, it’s only when my recorder stops that Zima dispenses her juiciest morsel of reality TV gossip—a blind item involving Harrison and a certain Real Housewife.

Zima, who earned thousands of views on weekly recaps of the show, credits Harrison’s level of care for those who came on The Bachelor with “how Bachelor Nation was created,” says Zima. “Speaking as someone who watched and reviewed it before we were ever together—he created that energy. What we have together is such a deep understanding of each other’s fields that really adds a passion and joy to our relationship and takes away what could be, in other scenarios, resentment or confusion about a very demanding job.”

Harrison and Zima were both previously married, and he saw two kids off to college in the early years of their relationship. “Maybe it just took the right person, but when she knocked me upside the head with those feelings that I had, that made me want to stop,” Harrison says of his hosting duties on The Bachelor, which often required extended amounts of international travel. “For the first time, I didn’t want to hop on a plane and go to Asia for the next season.”

Coincidentally, his post-COVID epiphany overlapped with Harrison’s exit from his day job. “I’d been on the road for a long time and I felt like something special was happening here with Lauren,” says Harrison, before asking for a reheat of his tea. “I’m just going to hit the pause button and be selfish, fall in love. It allowed me to fall in love and get married. I don’t think she was going to wait around and pine for me while I was on the road shooting another show.” ABC later enlisted former Bachelor, NFL quarterback, and sports commentator Jesse Palmer to replace Harrison as host.

As they celebrate their third wedding anniversary, the Austin-based couple say they’ve come to a peaceful place about “the other show.” Says Harrison, “What a weird thing that I was hosting this show about love and that it allowed me to find love myself. So how can I begrudge that completely?”

As Hollywood weathered hardships of its own, Harrison was happy to employ some of his former Bachelor colleagues, including casting director Lindsay Liles, executive producer Louis Caric, co-EP Deb Read, and director Michael Shea for The Vow. “It’ll probably end up being one of those silly reality TV show drinking games, drink every time someone says ‘intentional’,” says Zima, “but there’s so much meaning behind it and that’s why it gets repeated so much. When we’re kids we read about fairytales and hope to find our love. This guy’s literally bought a house and is filling his savings account for the family he hopes to have one day.”

The show’s dates are grounded in real life. “It’s not too hard to fall in love on a beach in Bora Bora,” says Zima, borrowing a line from Harrison. And there are no elimination rituals where the show’s lead can “hide behind a flower,” says the host. Instead, breakups happen face-to-face and at any time. “It’s what real relationships require,” Harrison tells the participants in the show’s premiere, the only episode provided in advance of our interview. “And honestly, it’s what a gentleman would do.”

That isn’t the only element of The Vow that directly invokes Harrison’s time on The Bachelor. One of the contestants vying for Jace’s heart is Kylee, a 28-year-old who appeared in a post-Harrison season of The Bachelor and now declares herself “on fire for Jesus” following her recent baptism. “There were others. We had a lot of people reach out to us,” from his former franchise, says Harrison. “Kylie was somebody that we were very thoughtful about.”

The showman in Harrison says “it’s fun to poke the bear” with references to his former gig. “It’s reality TV. I’m a TV host. There’s always a side of you that wants to promote the show.” Plus, it’s easier for Harrison to claim his victory in the breakup, given that The Bachelor franchise hasn’t aired a season of its product since March 2025. “And as far as I know, they’re not going to be on the air anytime soon,” says Harrison with a shrug. “So I would just say worry about cleaning up your own mess. Don’t worry about mine.” Roughly two weeks after our mid-October conversation, and just five days before Harrison’s return to TV, ABC announced the official return of The Bachelor in March 2027. No casting has been confirmed.

The search for love is a sensitive one, even for someone as seasoned as Harrison. “I’m not bitter and angry about The Bachelor because I don’t take for granted that I’ve been to the Super Bowl,” he says with a polished kind of sincerity. “I am opening my heart and bearing my soul to everybody, hoping that we could be together again. I do miss that connection and I hope it’s still there. But it’s a very vulnerable thing to do. That’s why I’m not out banging my chest or beating the drum. I’m a producer like anybody else hoping to produce a great television show. My guard is up,” he admits as our plates get cleared away. “Like I was for 20 years before, I will be in front of everybody taking the bullets, and I told [the participants] I will be standing beside you and [we will] do the best we can.”

Behind the scenes, Harrison and Zima often had to convince their young participants that the show wasn’t part of a larger gimmick. “There’s no gotcha—this is really just about you guys finding love,” Harrison recalled. “It was shocking at how low the bar has been set. I don’t mean dating shows, I just mean dating in general. I told the women, ‘I apologize to you on behalf of all men.’ Maybe too arrogant of me and maybe too lofty of a goal, but my hope is that, of all things, maybe we raise the level of debate of what women deserve and what men need to be.”

Zima remembers what it was like to see Harrison return to his element, getting visibly emotional just before our goodbyes. “That first night in the control room, when I saw him on screen, I teared up like I’m tearing up now,” she says with a slightly embarrassed laugh. Harrison reaches over to grab her hand. “It means the world to me that as his wife, more than seeing him on screen, when people stop him in the street and say, ‘Man, you were the thing I could watch with my grandma every week,’” says Zima, “and please come back and do a show because I miss that connection with my family.’ What a meaningful thing to have done in this life, to bring people together.”

Anthony Mackie just went on Entertainment Tonight and blurted out the previously unannounced involvement of Paul Bettany in "Avengers: Doomsday." Yep, Vision will re-assemble with Earth's Mightiest Heroes on December 18, 2026, and Mackie probably received a not-entirely-pleasant phone call from Marvel Studios' head honcho Kevin Feige.

Mackie was in the middle of describing the "Avengers" movies as a summer camp experience. It's one of those things where you just catch up with everybody," said Mackie. Marvel Studios makes it very plain to talent and their assistants as to what must not, under any circumstances, be mentioned ahead of time. But let Mackie off the hook here.
