The man has more important things on his mind than trying to keep straight what he can say pre-release and what's meant to be a surprise in the movie (which will get spoiled in headlines the second it's released anyway).

But now that we know Vision is in the movie, let's guess at his role in the narrative. If you haven't finished "VisionQuest," you should duck out now because I'm going to spoil the final episode's post-credits scene.

At the end of "VisionQuest," we're treated to a replay of the "Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness" finale, where Elizabeth Olsen's Wanda Maximoff/Scarlet Witch sacrifices herself to rid the multiverse of the Darkhold. We know from "Avengers Endgame: Encore" that Doctor Doom has also kidnapped the Hulk, so he's amassing some serious power to wreak a heapin' helpin' of havoc. Since its debut in the mid-'90s, Friends has permeated various parts of pop culture and is still considered one of the best sitcoms of all time. Between the hilarious one-liners and memorable storylines, there is a lot to love. In fact, it made such an impact that women flocked to hair salons to get “The Rachel” haircut to mirror Jennifer Aniston’s beloved character. It seems like the ‘do is making a comeback, and while I don’t know how to feel about it, Aniston shared some thoughts.

Rachel Green’s iconic haircut, dubbed “The Rachel,” is a shoulder-length bouncy bob with layers. And even though it may seem like a lot, essentially every woman in the ‘90s wanted to have that same haircut. While the term "viral" wasn't really a thing at that point, that's now the best way to describe the craze. The haircut has now made its way to the 21st Century, as Gen Z has apparently found a love for it. Now, with a modern version of The Rachel making the rounds, with longer and softer layers, Aniston opened up to Elle about its return:

I love that people are still inspired by it. The modern versions feel a little more relaxed and lived-in, which I love.

I have mixed feelings on this. At this point, it feels kind of late for The Rachel to be going viral. It’s a ‘90s haircut, and it should stay in the ‘90s, even if there's a modern version. On the other hand, I do love that Aniston is all for the comeback and appreciates that the younger generation is jumping on the bandwagon. Of course, there have been plenty of ‘90s outfits and trends that have come back, so it probably shouldn't be too surprising that this 'do is one of them.

That being said, despite the look’s longevity for the past 30 years, Aniston was not exactly a fan of it back in the day. Rachel’s haircut may have seemed effortless and amazing, but the actress recalled that getting it together was easier said than done:

I remember how much work that original haircut was!

Considering how great Rachel’s hair looked throughout all seasons of Friends, I’m not surprised to know that it took some time to get it looking the way it did. Still, given the fact that The Rachel has been a consistent favorite over the years, it seems people don’t mind putting in the work to keep it up. It's funny to think about how nostalgia can influence different parts of our daily lives.

At present, what I wonder is whether 30 years from now, The Rachel will still be a hit. It’s hard to predict what fashion will look like in three decades or even in one, to be honest. However, if Friends continues to remain in the zeitgeist, which I’m sure will be the case, I wouldn’t be surprised if another version of the hairstyle comes along and fits with the times. For now, fans can see the look in all its glory by streaming Friends with an HBO Max subscription.

#3510. There's a New Way to Automatically Back Up Your Android Photos for Free

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you're an Android user looking for a way to save your photos and videos without maxing out your cloud storage space, your device may soon be able to back up automatically to your PC. As spotted by Android Authority, Google included automatic backups from Android to Windows via Quick Share in its release notes for Google Play services v26.43.

Quick Share is a wireless file-sharing feature for Android that allows users to send photos, videos, and documents to nearby devices, including Windows computers and iPhones with AirDrop. The new automatic backup feature, which is likely to roll out gradually, uses Quick Share's functionality to transfer copies of photos and videos on your phone to your PC when nearby.

Since these backups happen locally, you don't need to rely solely on cloud storage in your Google account, nor do you need to remember to initiate transfers of photos and videos between devices. Plus, this is all free and doesn't require a separate cloud service subscription. While you can back up your media to Google Photos, as of earlier this year, more data from your Android backups count toward your Google Account storage cap unless you exclude specific types. Alternatively, you can also cobble together a decent amount of cloud storage from other providers at no extra cost, but automatic backups between Android and Windows minimize the likelihood that you'll forget to save data, and your PC provides plenty of space for free.

Once the feature is available on your device, you'll be able to initiate backups in the Quick Share for Windows app. Your Android and Windows devices must be in close proximity and signed into the same Google Account. You can toggle Automatic backups on and change the settings for what gets backed up and to where. The transfers will then occur wirelessly in the background.

As Android Authority reports, early hints at this feature suggested that Samsung phones and PCs would be excluded from automatic backups, but the release notes don't specify any further details.

#3509. Dua Lipa Talks About Her Book Club, and Her Favorite Authors Join Her for a Photo

It’s the 41st week of this year, and Dua Lipa has already read 22 books. Next up is Sufiyaan Salam’s novel, Wimmy Road Boyz, a coming of age story about a British Pakistani friend group. But fresh on her mind is Careless People: A Cautionary Tale of Power, Greed, and Lost Idealism by Sarah Wynn-Williams, which Lipa has just finished, logging the accomplishment in the Notes app on her orange iPhone.

“Do you know about it?” she asks me, eager to recommend the whistleblower’s memoir. “She’s getting censored because she started working at Facebook very early on and she dishes it all out.”

PAGE TURNERS Lipa at Albertine Books in October with seven of her hand-selected Service95 book club monthly reads. Shirt by Gucci; jewelry by Bulgari.

It should come as no surprise that Lipa, the internet’s favorite hardworking “vacanza queen,” gets most of her reading done while traveling. “I can read in cars. I don’t get sick. It’s kind of a flex,” she says. When we meet in New York in early October, Lipa has just returned from a trip to Madrid, where she performed with Shakira, doing what she humbly refers to as her “day job,” and Paris, for a Chanel show. No matter the destination, for work or play, Lipa will always toss a book—no e-readers—in her bag. “I love the feeling of a book. I love when all the pages get all fucked up a little bit,” she says.

Dressed in an off-duty uniform of blue jeans, a black Chanel sweater, leather boots, and a black Gucci purse big enough to stash a hardcover or two, Lipa, the 31-year-old British Albanian singer who has emerged as a leading literacy advocate, is gearing up for the London Literature Festival, which she guest-curated this year.

Her reading habit is impressive. Not just because she is a jet-set Grammy Award–winning pop star and half of a newlywed power couple (she and husband Callum Turner famously bonded over finishing the same chapter of Hernan Diaz’s novel, Trust) whose Instagram suggests that she exists in a perpetual state of glamour, but because, according to a recent statistic, more than half of American adults read approximately zero books in a year. “Sad,” Lipa says when I give her this stat.

Since 2021, Lipa has been using her spare time to run Service95—a website, newsletter, book club, and podcast—described as a “cultural concierge.” Through the platform, Lipa offers bespoke recommendations and publishes writing on a wide range of topics from style, travel, and wellness to politics and activism. It’s also where, since Service95’s inception, she has hosted in-depth conversations with authors from around the world and across genres. With dozens of podcast episodes under her belt so far, she’s quickly learned what it’s like to be on the other side of an interview. “I’ve done so many interviews myself and I’ve had to answer the same question over and over again. I’m quite sensitive to the fact that I don’t want to put the author in the same position of having to repeat themselves,” she says. “It’s one of my favorite things that I do. I feel like I get so much out of the conversations.”

Today, at the Villa Albertine, a French cultural institution on the Upper East Side, she’s brought her bookshelf to life, gathering seven of her favorite writers—memoirists, novelists, journalists, a National Book Award and Booker Prize winner—for a class photo. Standing together in one room, beneath a mural of a constellation, the stars align: Douglas Stuart, Brit Bennett, Patti Smith, Roxane Gay, Jennifer Clement, Patrick Radden Keefe, Min Jin Lee, and Lipa, all looking like the English department of your wildest dreams. Sitting next to Smith, the author of Just Kids, Lipa, one of the biggest celebrities in the world, appears to be starstruck. In a rare role reversal, Lipa is the fangirl, whipping out her phone to commemorate the occasion with a group selfie.

Here, her impact in the literary world is undeniable—and so is her range.

Between takes, Smith inquires about how many languages Lipa speaks—English, Albanian, some Spanish, and she’s learning French and Italian, she says. The Just Kids author quips that she only knows how to ask where the “biblioteca” is. “That’s kind of all you need,” jokes Keefe, author of Say Nothing, who tells me he often encounters young readers who were introduced to his work via Service95.

READ THE ROOM Dua Lipa and authors take a selfie at Albertine Books. Lipa’s shoes by Prada; jewelry by Bulgari.

Watching all of these literary titans in conversation with each other, it’s impressive to see them all embrace Lipa as an advocate of their work. “I’m sure that there are lots of other things she could be doing with her time that would be far more profitable than championing books,” says Bennett, author of The Vanishing Half. “It’s amazing that she does this out of a genuine love for reading.”

“It’s fun work. It’s good work,” insists Lipa, who is happy to disprove naysayers who think she just “holidays all the time.” “I’m having a good time, and I get all my work done, and I do what I want to do, and then I go on holiday, and I’m happy with that.” It’s what keeps her motivated: “Sometimes being underestimated gives me extra fire in my belly.”

In 2023, when Lipa launched her book club, which has racked up nearly 1 million Instagram followers, she joined the likes of Oprah Winfrey, Reese Witherspoon, Kaia Gerber, Dakota Johnson, Emma Roberts, and Jenna Bush Hager. But the saturation of the celebrity book club market gave her no hesitation. “If people feel a little bit inclined to just go and pick up a book and read something, we’re all doing our job,” she says. “I don’t care if someone’s going to go to this book club or the next one. As long as they’re reading, I’m happy.”

But Clement, author of Widow Basquiat, considers Service95 to be in a league of its own. “It is not simply curating individual titles; it is curating perspective,” she says. “Almost as if, taken together, the books themselves are forming an arc, a larger story unfolding through the choices.”

Lipa works closely with her book club director, Maria Padget, to select her monthly reads, guided not by what’s trending but instead, as Lee, the author of Pachinko who calls Lipa an “exemplary literary citizen,” puts it, by honoring “her intellectual curiosity,” often highlighting marginalized voices, and not absorbing literature through a strictly Western lens.

“When she looks at her readers, she doesn’t think what would be easiest for you to enjoy, or what would comfort you or challenge you the least,” says Stuart, author of Shuggie Bain. “Instead she signals, go on, you can read this, you should read this; read this challenging book, read this banned book, and see what they want to deny you, see what you can achieve and have access to what would make you more powerful!”

In the face of a burgeoning literacy crisis, global book bans, rampant censorship, and the rise of artificial intelligence, Service95 is a venue for Lipa to educate herself and her readers on global issues—encouraging an open dialogue and discourse. “I don’t shy away from it. I also like the fact that I do it on my own terms,” says Lipa, who calls activism an “important pillar” of Service95.

As a result, she’s spoken to Margaret Atwood about the fight for female reproductive rights and discussed sexual violence and intersectional feminism with Gay, author of Bad Feminist. “The book had already been out for more than a decade, so it was quite a thrill to see her introducing the work to a new audience,” the essayist says. Lipa has also pondered the impacts of AI with Nobel Prize laureate Kazuo Ishiguro and provided required reading on Israel and the war in Gaza. She’s even joined a reading group at a women’s prison in Surrey and opened the Manifesto Library—stocking banned books inside the Livraria Lello in Portugal.

“The whole goal was to get people to take a breather, learn about the thing that’s happening, and not to be afraid to ask questions or not be right all the time,” she says.

Lipa, who admits to using the Opal app, which limits her to an hour a day on social media to post her famous photo dumps, is hopeful Service95 can also serve as an antidote to doomscrolling and AI. “Not only are we declining in reading and not picking up a book, but the fact that you can have these cheat codes that completely bypass the whole point of the learning or the ingesting of information,” she says. “It’s just going to make us stupider as people.”

She credits her mother, Anesa, for her love of reading, reminiscing on their weekends spent at a London bookshop. “I basically would just sit there and read for hours and hours and hours. I loved it,” she says, rattling off the names of authors from her childhood, like Jacqueline Wilson and Malorie Blackman and the Mr. Men and Mary-Kate and Ashley Olsen series. Reading is formative to who she is as an artist; it makes her a better songwriter, as she tells me, but it is also fundamental to who she is as a person. “I feel like we get a better understanding of ourselves, of our friends, of our family members, of the people around us, what they might be going through, what’s happening in their life by just picking up a book,” says Lipa.

When I bring up the recent claim from influencer Alix Earle that she had never read a book (apart from maybe Dr. Seuss), Lipa considers the topic thoughtfully and speaks without passing any judgment, generously suggesting the possibility that maybe, as a public figure, Earle said this as a protective measure, to shield her from further prodding and criticism. “Books are so personal, I think people also get intimidated,” she says. “Books should just be enjoyable. No one’s expecting anything from the person reading it. You don’t have to overanalyze it. It’s just supposed to make you feel something.”

And true to form, she offers a book recommendation: “I love The Girls by Emma Cline. I think that’s a cool gateway drug book.”

For Lipa, it all harkens back to searching for that feeling. She returns to her recent interview with Ishiguro, the Klara and the Sun author, who drew parallels between pop music and literature and their ability to foster connection. “He said the heart has so many rooms, so many things that make us, and AI can’t do that,” she says. “There is something really encouraging about that, that some things can't be replicated. Our real humanness and the love we feel, the loneliness even, it can make us feel even more alive and more human.” Perhaps Lipa’s book club is an act of resistance, but it’s also, to borrow a line from her last album, an act of radical optimism.

#3508. Windows Laptops Just Closed a Major Gap With the MacBook Neo

To say the MacBook Neo disrupted the laptop market would be an understatement. When the Neo dropped, former Apple CEO Tim Cook said Apple had its best-ever launch week for first-time Mac customers, and the company is reportedly planning on doubling the MacBook's sales for 2027. It's not hard to see why the MacBook Neo is such a hit: Apple is offering the essential Mac experience at a fantastic price point. You no longer need to spend $1,000 or more for a MacBook, so long as you're okay making some sacrifices to get there—which, it seems, many customers are.

While the MacBook Neo has been a boon for Apple and Apple fans alike, I can only imagine the stress it brought to PC manufacturers—especially those with budget or midrange machines. Windows PCs have long won the price war against Apple. While MacBooks have their passionate customers, buyers looking for the best value have had to weigh expensive Apple laptops against many far cheaper options from companies like Dell, HP, ASUS, and Lenovo. But with the Neo, suddenly a MacBook was competing in this space, and well.

Part of the issue for PC manufacturers was Apple's control over its own ecosystem. Unlike most PC makers, which only produce the hardware for each machine, Apple makes both the hardware and the software for its MacBook lineup. As such, the company has the advantage of optimizing that hardware. It can design macOS to run more efficiently on weaker hardware, in a way that companies like Dell or ASUS can't. You might be comparing the MacBook Neo against a Windows laptop with similar specs, or even better specs, but because Microsoft makes Windows, not the laptop manufacturer, it's possible the Neo ends up with the better overall experience. While that might still be the case, Microsoft may have just closed that gap in a meaningful way.

This week, Microsoft announced key upgrades to memory-management efficiency, particularly for machines with 8GB of RAM. This is the amount of memory the MacBook Neo has, as well as many budget and midrange Windows laptops. That's not much memory for 2026, regardless of platform, but Apple seems to have squeezed a lot out of it for the Neo. Now, Microsoft may have just done the same for PCs, as Windows is reportedly 20% more responsive, with 40% faster multitasking.

In its blog post, Microsoft highlighted improvements that users with 8 GB of RAM can expect from Windows going forward. First, Microsoft says it focused on better utilizing the RAM your machine already has. The company compares its memory management to a desk: Anything on the "desk" is stored in RAM; anything in your "drawer" is stored in your drive. As you use your PC, Windows used to move more of your apps and tabs to your drawer to free up more RAM for other things, meaning you'd need to reload those items whenever you returned to them. Going forward, the company says that Windows can keep up to 2GB more of your active data in RAM instead of moving it to slower storage elsewhere. That means apps and tabs should refresh less frequently when you leave and return to them.

Microsoft also says that small actions should be faster across the board. When you open the Start menu, search across your PC, right-click, open Settings, launch the Snipping Tool, and open File Explorer, those actions may be up to 20% faster than they were in January. Microsoft Edge may open up to 33% faster, while Teams can enable Efficiency Mode by default on 8 GB machines, which means it can launch up to 20% faster too. Microsoft put together an interesting stress test to compare multitasking performance between today and January. It opened 20 tabs in Edge, a 4K video, large Word, PowerPoint, and Excel files, then Outlook and File Explorer, all without closing any windows. That experience was 40% faster following this latest update.

Microsoft says it also improved the memory efficiency in its apps: The company claims it reduced committed-memory growth by up to 900 MB, and saved up to 360 MB in RAM across Word, PowerPoint, Excel, and Outlook. That extends to third-party apps as well: Microsoft says that WhatsApp has double-digit memory improvement now. Widgets also only load when you open the app, which saves 200 MB of RAM when the app is closed, while Edge tabs go inactive after 15 minutes instead of two hours.

Microsoft isn't making these upgrades in a vacuum. Hardware costs, particularly for RAM, have skyrocketed in the age of AI. Microsoft knows that people are likely going to hold onto existing hardware for longer than they usually do, or that they'll opt for less-expensive configurations, including, perhaps, machines with 8 GB of RAM.

PCMag's Chris Hoffman was adamant before this latest Windows update that buyers should steer clear of PCs with 8 GB of RAM. Now, he's pulling back a bit. In his testing, Hoffman noticed improvements when multitasking on an 8 GB PC when compared to similar tests from months ago. He could run multiple Chrome tabs, a Microsoft Word window, and Spotify without bogging down the computer much. Hoffman isn't a lightweight user, so he still wouldn't personally choose an 8 GB machine, but he admits, "If I were an average PC buyer looking for a reasonable desktop experience and could save hundreds of dollars by opting for 8GB of RAM, I might be happy with the performance."

To that point, I think this new Windows update makes 8 GB PCs competitive, especially against the MacBook Neo. We'll still need direct comparisons to know how well this new Windows experience holds up across the board, but these updates are promising. Users with 8 GB machines just got a free, valuable update overnight; new customers can opt for a more affordable PC without feeling like performance will take a nosedive just because they opened one too many Edge tabs.

As Hoffman says, 8 GB of RAM is not ideal for any user looking for serious multitasking or professional workflows, regardless of whether they choose a Mac or PC. But for the average computer customer looking for a solid machine without breaking the bank, I no longer see the Neo as necessarily the default choice. After all, Apple has slowly raised its price, too, from $599 to $699. If you're platform-agnostic, or even prefer Windows to macOS, these updates from Microsoft are quite promising. If you're in the market, check out PCMag's excellent list of budget laptop recommendations.

#3507. Lauren Graham's 2026 Colleen Hoover Movie Is Officially Netflix's Biggest Streaming Hit

Is there anyone more representative of the recent romance novel adaptation trend than Colleen Hoover? Hollywood loves a BookTok phenomenon, and Hoover's novels seem designed in a lab to appeal to the "crying, screaming, throwing up" crowds on social media, who simply cannot resist what The Guardian called Hoover's "normcore thrillers."

But the film also has some other things working in its favor. For one it stars the talented Maika Monroe, and it also features Lauren Graham, who's best known for playing Lorelai Gilmore on "Gilmore Girls." Graham does a decent job with the material in "Reminders of Him," and regardless of how you feel about the film as a whole, it's nice to see her in a modern-day melodrama.

"Reminders of Him" is directed by British director Vanessa Caswill, who oversaw Netflix's 2023 romantic comedy "Love at First Sight," after honing her chops on BBC series such as "Little Women," "Gold Digger," and "Thirteen." This was another romance movie based on a popular book, and wouldn't you know, the movie went straight to the top of the Netflix charts upon its release. Now, Caswill has done it again with "Reminders of Him," though this one had a successful box office run under its belt before taking over Netflix.

The film stars Maika Monroe as Kenna Rowan, who made a tragic mistake years earlier that landed her in prison. After serving her sentence, Kenna returns to her Wyoming hometown, where she hopes to finally meet her young daughter, Diem Landry (Zoe Kosovic). Sadly, Diem's grandparents Grace and Patrick Landry (Lauren Graham and Bradley Whitford) are completely opposed to the idea. But there's also a strapping young bar owner standing between her and her daughter in the form of Ledger Ward (Tyriq Withers). Turns out Ledger has been helping take care of Diem, and he's similarly concerned about Kenna's return. But as the two get to know each other, romance blossoms, and Kenna finally gets a chance at redemption.

"Reminders of Him" hit Netflix U.S. on November 10, 2026, and according to streaming viewership tracker FlixPatrol, became an instant hit. The film shot to number one on November 11, 2026, proving these Colleen Hoover adaptations remain perennially popular. No doubt we'll see plenty more Hoover books being adapted in the near future.

There are plenty of movies to avoid on Netflix, and "Reminders of Him" is right on the borderline. The film managed a 56% critic score on Rotten Tomatoes, which is higher than any other Colleen Hoover adaptation. But it also has an 87% audience score, which ties it with "It Ends With Us" for most popular among viewers on the site. Now it has managed to earn the endorsement of Netflixers, does this mean you should watch it?

Well, the movie has a few plus points. For one, it stars the Maika Monroe, who's able to shift from scream queen to swoon queen with ease. Meanwhile, Lauren Graham is given some of the more emotional scenes and does a solid job of bringing them to life. Otherwise, it's sort of okay for the first half? Monroe and her co-star, Tyriq Withers, manage to wring some believable emotion out of the script. Once they throw caution to the wind and just go for it, despite their previous reluctance to besmirch Monroe's deceased husband, everything starts to get a little ridiculous.

Joey Shapiro summed things up quite aptly in his review for the Chicago Reader, when he called "Reminders of Him" a "corny TV movie" that's "made with so much sincerity and conviction by all involved that it becomes watchable, if rarely 'good' by any stretch." If that appeals, or if you simply can't get enough of these romance movies that verge on providing some sort of interesting insight into human emotion only to fall short, then why not give this lesser-known Hoover adaptation a go.

#3506. WoW: Forever's 'Pointless' Early Quest Reward Hides a Much Bigger Secret

The Ancient Heirloom ring, awarded to every Skyborne character, is part of a massive quest chain players are still solving

If you start a Skyborne character in World of Warcraft: Forever — one of the blue sky elves unlocked by purchasing a DLC pack — you're awarded an item called the Ancient Heirloom very early on in the game. This ring can be equipped, but it has no stats and no apparent purpose. It's odd to receive a ring at a low level, because these items aren't usually found until later in the game; when I received one during the beta test, I figured it was just there to add a bit of flavor to the new race and didn't give it a second thought.

How wrong I was. It turns out that the ring is an instrumental part of WoW: Forever's first big secret: a huge, game-spanning questline that players have yet to see to its conclusion.

Known as the Dawn Waker Secret, the sequence was discovered by the WoW Secret Finding community on Discord, and there's a step-by-step rundown available on Wowhead. It begins at level 1 on Zephras Isle, the starting zone of the Skyborne, and extends beyond level 40 (so far). If you don't have access to the Skyborne, it's still possible to travel to Zephras Isle and find the ring lying around in a building.

The questline involves finding a special torch on the body of a guard in Duskwood, using this to uncover an ancient sword hilt on Zephras Isle, forging the hilt into a fancy sword, purifying a water globe, and much more, as you tour various spots in the game with significance to Warcraft's most ancient elven lore, including the new Mount Hyjal high-level zone. The Ancient Heirloom ring is important, because it must be equipped for the player to see and interact with elven spirits crucial to the quest, or to reveal ancient elven vaults.

Blizzard's fresh take on classic WoW is going great, but the Skyborne show just how hard it is to add new stuff to an old game

So far, the trail of breadcrumbs ends with a character called Prince Tortheldrin (an ancient, cruel elven prince), who's to be found hanging out in the Dire Maul dungeon. The Prince's dialogue suggests players will need to reach Honored reputation with the Shen'dralar faction in order to hear more.

The sequence seems to revolve around two legendary blades, Eluvi'ana (the sword discovered on Zephras Isle) and Eluvi'tor. Perhaps one of these — or both, in upgraded form — will be the chain's ultimate reward. Whatever happens, it's a great way to tie the Skyborne into the history of Warcraft's Highborne elves, and to pay off a pointless-seeming quest reward from WoW: Forever's earliest moments.

Robert Pattinson is living out a real-life ‘pinch me’ moment, and it has nothing to do with Batman. The actor has always wanted to work with Denzel Washington, who is one of his acting heroes. Well, that dream is coming true, because Washington and Pattinson are doing a movie together. However, there is one thing that surprised the Dune star.

Pattinson's first movie of the 2027 movie schedule, The Take, was an easy yes thanks to a “dream-team situation,” partnering him with one of the greatest actors of all time. The Primetime actor dished with Entertainment Weekly about what caught him off guard (in the best way) while working with Washington:

Denzel is one of the reasons I wanted to become an actor, so getting to work with him was pretty incredible. What I loved was seeing how alive the material is for him. Even after all these years of acting, he’s still looking for something new in every take. I also didn’t realize how much he liked to improvise, which made it all the more exciting. You’d start a five-page scene thinking you knew where it was going, and then suddenly you’re completely off-piste. It was really thrilling.

Sounds like Pattinson had to stay on his toes just as much as his character, Noah, who is recruited by “a charismatic thief” (aka Denzel Washington) to rob Manhattan’s richest bank. To make things more complicated, this is also the bank where his girlfriend (played by Daisy Edgar-Jones) works as a teller. The movie’s official synopsis teases that “a bank guard, a teller, and a master thief get caught in a deadly game of cons and double crosses.” This is definitely up the actor’s alley, as he tends to lean toward twisty movies, such as Primetime about To Catch A Predator host Chris Hansen.

However, this movie sounds less polarizing and more thrilling. I’m sure some of that improv worked in Pattinson’s favor given the movie’s dynamics. It’s being described as a mix of a heist film and psychological drama, and promises to keep you surprised until the end. In fact, director Fernando Meirelles assures that even the last 10 seconds are important. Part of the excitement of the movie is being credited to Washington. Meirelles backs Pattinson’s statements and shares how easy improvising is for The Equalizer actor:

He constantly surprises you. Sometimes, when I ask him where a particular line came from, he’ll simply say, ‘I have no idea.’ There are quite a few of those moments in the final cut.

While the movie is strictly from Pattinson’s POV, it sounds like Washington is going to be a scene-stealer. However, while Washington is getting rave reviews from his coworkers, the director also made sure to shout out Pattinson, calling him “one of the best actors working today.” This is definitely true, given the actor has released three movies this year and still has Dune: Part 3 set to hit the 2026 schedule on December 18. He certainly doesn’t seem to be slowing down, and I wonder if Washington gave him any advice on working so much.

Though this full-circle moment with the Gladiator II actor had to be a highlight, given Pattinson previously worked with Denzel's son John David Washington in Christopher Nolan’s Tenet. Maybe one day the three of them can do a project together. Perhaps something just as ‘puzzling’ as The Take and with just as much improvising.

Hopefully, when the movie comes out on January 15, 2027, they’ll share what lines were improvised, because I’m dying to know. At least, I’ll be able to watch it with a Netflix subscription.

#3504. In 'The Spot', Claire Danes and Ewan McGregor Unravel Together

Claire Danes was standing in the operating room, dressed in scrubs and a mask, when a surgeon’s assistant gave her the opposite of a pep talk. “You may think you’re badass, but if you think you’re fainting, you’re fainting, and we can’t have that, so just let me know,” she told Danes.

Danes, luckily, did not faint, though she says she was incredibly aware of her breathing as she watched an intricate brain surgery performed by a team of doctors.

The three-time Emmy winner was observing in preparation for her role in The Spot, a new Hulu series in which she plays a successful neurosurgeon who begins to suspect that she may be responsible for the hit-and-run death of a child. As she tries to investigate the horrific possibility, she and her husband (Ewan McGregor) find themselves falling deeper and deeper into a web of suspicion and dark secrets.

“I’ve always thought of it as an exploration of a marriage through the lens of a crime and maybe exploration of a crime through the lens of a marriage,” says Solomon of The Spot.

“I’m fascinated with this notion of what if your worst-case scenario way in the back of your head started to really look like it was true, and how could you dramatize that?” says writer, creator, and showrunner Ed Solomon.

The bold psychological thriller, which Vanity Fair can exclusively reveal will debut on January 13, follows a woman unraveling at the possibility of her worst fears coming true, and a marriage under enormous strain. There’s been a steady stream of whodunit miniseries in the last decade, but here Solomon, whose past work includes writing The Christophers and Now You See Me, has created a highly watchable, page-turning series that’s more of a “did I do it?”

“I never want it to be pretentious,” says Solomon. “I just want it to be fun and entertaining, but also elevated, respectful of the viewer.”

"I had wanted to work with Claire for years and we just had great fun acting and playing together while making this show,” says McGregor.

Danes was initially drawn to the series because of the portrait of the marriage at the heart of it, and Solomon’s particular gift for weaving the tragic into the comic. “It gets really very dark pretty quickly,” she says, “but it’s absurd too.”

She not only watched two brain surgeries in preparation but also shadowed a surgeon on his rounds, being with patients before they went into surgery and while they were recovering with their families. “I felt horrible that there I was in this room with these people who couldn’t be more vulnerable, and there I was, trying to be discreet in the corner,” she says.

But the experience gave her insight into what kind of person her character Lou Shadwick would be: intense, hypervigilant, and high achieving. “There’s a lot of marathon runners in there, and highly, highly focused people,” she says. “And they carry a lot of responsibility, and I think they compartmentalize very effectively.”

Danes had previously worked with Solomon on the 2023 series Full Circle, which was directed by Steven Soderbergh. When Kate Winslet, who was initially attached to play Lou, exited, Danes stepped in. Solomon needed an actress who could portray a mother and surgeon who is obsessed with doing the right thing and being a good person. “To be able to see someone who has a very, very present and active inner life that when you look, you can see well beyond the eyes and you can see someone who can be basically playing many things at one time, which was really important and interesting to me,” he says.

Danes had never worked with McGregor before, though they both had previously worked with Baz Luhrmann (on Romeo + Juliet and Moulin Rouge, respectively) and she thinks they had met briefly around that time. “We were definitely of a certain time, the ’90s,” she says. “So we share a lot of references, but it was just an immediate rapport.”

Lou is doing what many mothers juggling work and family have done: driving home from work, talking on the phone about dinner while also checking an unending flurry of text messages. It’s at that moment when she thinks she might have accidentally hit a child on a bike and not realized it until she heard about it later. “It’s so effective, this circumstance that he’s drawn for us,” she says of Solomon. “It’s entirely relatable, and I think it’s the fear that we all have experienced and hosted many, many times, if not on a daily basis.”

Michael Patrick Thornton as Pete Porphyry

As she tries to piece together what might have happened, a police officer (Daveed Diggs) and a detective (Michael Patrick Thornton) are doing the same, and begin to suspect Lou. Her husband, Damon, gets involved, making more trouble for both of them.

Lou and Damon met in medical school, but Damon dropped out and is now pursuing medical aid work in the shadow of his wife’s illustrious career. “I really like the idea of a man, who is charming and good-looking and therefore used to feeling very much in control when he walks into a room, having a spouse who is quite significantly on the rise,” says Solomon. “What does that do to your sense of ego if you’re a guy like that?”

Lou begins to see signs that she may be the guilty party.

McGregor says he had wanted to work with Danes for a long time, and was drawn as Damon as a character. “I think the character has an amazing arc throughout the story from where he starts to where he ends,” he says. “He has a very deeply hidden, shameful secret that gets uncovered as the story goes on.”

McGregor brings to the role a kind of playfulness. “I’ve always loved a certain quality of Ewan’s where there’s a maturity and a boyishness happening simultaneously,” says Solomon. “The boyish quality within this character is really important and the ability to cover a sense of wound.”

Set in upstate New York, the new series will take viewers on a wild ride following two people who are putting themselves in an increasingly dire situation and web of lies. “She’s a decent person, and so is her husband, really,” says Danes. “And yet, they allow their moral compass to become increasingly compromised.” Solomon hopes that even as the story gets darker and wilder, it will leave viewers with at least one big question they’ll have to grapple with: “I would hope that they’re asking questions, like what would I do if I were in that situation?”

“In Ewan, you can see the fragility in him,” says Solomon of McGregor.
